item.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
item.description: 541 points, 290 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (architectlabs.com)

→ HN comments  ·  541 points  ·  290 comments

Top #1 — shioyama:

Wow, I posted this and come back a few hours later, and the comments are... a bit depressing honestly.

Do people here know what interaction nets are? They are a fundamentally different programming paradigm, different from the most basic harvard architecture of the 1940s. Whether you think this particular implementation will genuinely support them, and whether that will bring the performance they claim it does, it another question (I'm not sure). But at least can we focus on the topic?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interaction_nets

↳ reply 1 — quaintdev:

Thanks for sharing, TIL about interaction nets. I found the article linked at the bottom easier to understand[0].

> Another issue with multi-core CPUs is the difficulty of programming them. Debuggability is a major issue, and entirely new classes of issues arise, such as race conditions. However, in interaction nets, all active pairs are independent, and so can actually be executed in any order. This property is known as confluence, and means that no matter the order in which things are executed, the result will be the same. This makes debugging straightforward and eliminates issues like race conditions. This allows Vine to be parallel out of the box; the programmer does not have to do anything special with threads, processes, CUDA kernels, etc. to get parallel execution.

[0]: https://tendrils.co/blog/2026-04-26/on-inets

↳↳ reply — marginalia_nu:

I'd be interested to see how this would pan out.

Seems to describe something analogous instruction level parallelism, which traditional CPUs made this millennium have as well via instruction pipelines, branch prediction, and speculative execution. Some of which turned out to not work too well so now we generally run hobbled CPUs with Spectre/Meltdown mitigation enabled.

The reason why we tend to reach for difficult abstractions for core level parallelism is that most automatic/safe approaches tend to stumble pretty hard on Amdahl's law, where most parallel code is consequently almost entirely designed around minimizing critical sections.

I don't fully see how inets would resolve Amdahl's law.

↳↳↳ reply — chacham15:

I think you're thinking about this the wrong way. This isnt about surpassing theoretical parallelism limits. Its about gaining parallelism without having to be explicit about it. If you look at the solve function from the page, its doing a brute force search of the 5 queens problem. In the naieve implementation, this is done serially. But with the different approach to compiling the implementation, we can essentially "automatically parallelize" it. Thats the difference between the animation on the left and right. The thing is that in order to handle fine grained parallelism like this you need better/different hardware primitives so that you can split computation at a more fine grain, which is why they needed a new hardware model/isa. This is how they achieved the 4-5x speed up: by automatically parallizing a serially implemented function. If you were to compare a parallelized function to their parallelized function, I would expect to see a smaller speedup. Or at least as I understand it. Correct me if I'm wrong.

↳ reply 2 — neerajsi:

There was also a smaller scale approach called edge/trips that could express code as a dag: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/evaluat...

↳ reply 3 — catapart:

For me, the edges are still too blurry for me to make out what this actually is. I need someone with more in-depth knowledge to let me know what is actually being proposed here.

On the optimistic side, this looks like a kind of "bigger step" in the direction that GPU/shader programming took, where you change the way you think about and break down a problem to get insanely fast results. Feels like if you target this interaction net structure and give it to this CPU that uses them natively, we could amplify the speed of computations to possibly allow for things that are currently way to slow to do. Realtime physics sims with magnitudes faster steps. That's pretty cool. And all of the downstream effects that would allow for, in product design, scientific modelling, etc. And that's just one train of thought.

On the pessimistic side, though, I have no clue how to "program for an interaction net". Seems like the authors took a "you don't need to, an LLM will do it for you" position, and I can get behind that, but that's a pretty huge step in the direction of "Natural Language Programming" in that I literally can't program it without using an LLM and natural language, because I don't understand the underlying details and probably won't have any structural support to understand it for a while, as the tooling slowly rolls out and gets iterated on, until it can do something we can recognize as "Debugging". I imagine there's some kind of "program it in C, and translate it" thing, too, but it feels like the point here is not to have me be able to debug it, and a detour through C just wastes LLM tokens.

So those are the initial impressions, but then I'm making a TON of assumptions in both sides of that. So I don't even know if my initial impressions are conceptualizing the right paradigms, much less if they are worth discussing with people who are seriously considering this topic. Only speaking for myself here, but at least my own silence is due to not having enough information myself, and not seeing enough in this paper to interest me in research in the topic just yet. Maybe if they've got something I can play with, I could get my head around it more. But, for now, it's just neat.

Top #2 — jkhdigital:

The title is a bit misleading—humans came up with all the insights and innovations here. What AI has done, which it is exceptionally good at, is take decades of brilliant ideas buried in research literature and synthesize them into a coherently engineered product. It would seem that AI is now doing an end-run around the innovator’s dilemma, or at least part of it, by dramatically lowering the R&D cost of productizing laboratory ideas.

Top #3 — pizza234:

I'm quite skeptical; their baseline is a in-order CPU, instead of a modern out-of-order design, and they're testing a small amount of programs.

Also, I'm not an expert in CPUs, but the underlying idea doesn't seem entirely novel - WaveScalar explored dataflow-based architecture 20+ years ago.

↳ reply 1 — kragen:

They're claiming better performance per watt, not better absolute performance, and out-of-order does worse on that metric than the superscalar in-order design they say they beat by 4.59×. That's why, for example, PULPino is in-order.

A third interesting metric is performance per transistor or per area, and generally the best designs there are the long-forgotten MISC designs like the MuP21 and the GA144.

↳↳ reply — adrian_b:

The performance per watt of very slow CPUs is always very good, so that alone is not impressive unless much more data is provided to prove that is really better than what is typical.

On the other hand, the performance per area of the "traditional" CPU that is used for comparison, which I assume that it is some kind of RISC-V, is very poor, so that the performance per area of the new CPU is likely to be also poor, even if much better than that of the strawman.

Their "traditional" CPU has an area that is slightly bigger than that of Cortex-A720 made with a CMOS process almost twice as dense.

So if they were made with the same process, the "traditional" CPU and the new CPU would have an area somewhat bigger than a half of a Cortex-A720.

But Cortex-A720 is an out-of-order 4-wide superscalar core with advanced SIMD and scalable vector extensions, with a good branch predictor and with many other enhancements, for which the area ratio in the same process is expected to be much greater than 2 in comparison with the CPUs evaluated in TFA, while its performance must be several times greater than that of a 2-wide in-order CPU core.

So both the "traditional" CPU and the Frostbite CPU appear to have a much bigger area than expected for their performance.

Moreover, the performance of in-order CPUs is very sensitive to the benchmark selection and to the quality of the compiler optimizations.

So the performance obtained for the benchmarks selected by them, like FFT or LU decomposition, is expected to be much better than for benchmarks that would execute an application not dominated by such regular loops, but having lots of hard to predict branches, e.g. a compiler benchmark.

They say that the ISA will be published. At that time it will be easier to appreciate whether this CPU architecture is really innovative. For now, they have done a lot of work, by fully implementing the CPU core, but the data presented is not sufficiently convincing to demonstrate that it is indeed an architecture that will be able to compete with SOTA CPU cores, e.g. with those from the Arm company.

↳↳↳ reply — kragen:

> The performance per watt of very slow CPUs is always very good

Generally this has not been my experience. Typically both very slow CPUs like the ATMega328 and high-performance CPUs like an Intel i7 are in the neighborhood of 1 nanojoule per instruction. (For operations more than 8 bits wide, the AVR is significantly worse.) Low-power CPUs like the STM32L line are commonly around 0.2nJ/insn. Ambiq's subthreshold logic gets them closer to 0.05nJ/insn.

I agree with the rest of your comment.

↳ reply 2 — rhdunn:

If you are interested in understanding how CPUs work there are a number of "build your own CPU" style video series on YouTube:

- Ben Eater's series "Building an 8-bit breadboard computer!": https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLowKtXNTBypGqImE405J2...

- Fabian Schuiki's series "Build a Superscalar CPU" (breadboard and custom boards): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLyR4neQXqQo5nPdEiMbaE...

- Polymath Unlimited's series "The CPU you can build (Tutorial Series)" (logisim): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLe8IZRJAn3oD3E2tDhNpI...

- mattbatwing's series "Let's Make a Redstone Computer!" (Minecraft): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL5LiOvrbVo8nPTtdXAdSm...

item.title: UK fridges secured from hackers
item.description: 141 points, 133 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (bbc.co.uk)

→ HN comments  ·  141 points  ·  133 comments

Top #1 — JdeBP:

There's more information in the Pen Test Partners press release:

* https://pentestpartners.com/security-blog/the-fridge-hack-uk...

This includes who talked to whom and what the responses from the manufacturer, supermarkets, and cold store warehouse operators were.

Don't expect to learn what the vulnerabilities themselves are, though. They couldn't get hold of and trace a subset of the device users, so they're holding back what the vulnerabilities are.

↳ reply — helsinkiandrew:

Interesting the company that may have manufactured some or all of the units, claimed that physical access to the devices would be required.

Perhaps, you can trigger a hard reset on the device and the firmware returns to default network password?

> Resource Data Management (RDM), the British manufacturer of the refrigeration controllers, disputed the severity of the identified vulnerabilities. The company argued that exploiting them would have required physical access to the hardware.

https://www.aa.com.tr/en/europe/uk-launches-secret-operation...

↳↳ reply — rocqua:

I read that claim as "They need to get one physical example of the hardware" and that this would them allow them to attack all instances of that same model.

Which, to me, reads like a secret stored on the hardware. Something like a hard-coded password, storing a single private key on all devices (or a public key with a crazy weak private key), or some other symmetric secret used somewhere in authentication.

↳↳↳ reply — sirsinsalot:

Pretty sure it was just an admin password hardcoded and the manufacturer claim is based on needing the device in hand to extract the password.

The same password used across all units.

Top #2 — kqr:

I'm surprised the fridges need to have far-remote control over their temperature in the first place. I can absolutely see the need for an internet-connected thermometer inside them to be able to alert when things go wrong off-hours, but that's a read-only resource.

I can also understand the purpose of centralised temperature computer control through the local network, but that's not exposed to the internet.

An internet-writeable path seems like inviting disaster.

↳ reply — aftbit:

I'm not sure about this particular case, but I believe the intention is to support remote maintenance and repair. For example, if a fridge ices up, you need to raise its temperature and defrost it. Of course, in many cases, this involves emptying the fridge, removing the evaporator fans, and spraying hot water on the coils until all of the ice is melted, which is obviously not something that you can do over the internet.

You might also want control over the temperature to react to electrical prices or grid stability, but that's pretty niche and could likely be 90% scheduled (cool slightly too cold at night, then allow to get slightly warmer (while still food-safe) during day).

I agree though - this should be behind a management VPN, not just on the open internet.

Top #3 — alibarber:

I'm quite curious to know what the actual attack was. The article is light on detail but does quote 'similar to weak password' but admits that it would have been necessary to get hold of an example device first, which isn't that hard as they're very common.

To me this spells out an unprotected private key or secret residing in the device that could be used to break the authentication checks. In which case once secret is out there - no need to posses it? Could the key/secret have been well protected, but the device could be used to sign anything given to it?

> I'm quite curious to know what the actual attack was

from the article ... back door account whose daily password algorithm was seeded from the date

↳↳ reply — jowsie:

On BBC Radio 1 during one of their news segments, they interviewed someone involved, who claimed it was as if the passwords didn't need the correct password, any password would be accepted.

↳↳↳ reply — consumer451:

Well, that's one way to reduce user friction.

↳ reply 2 — mavhc:

The attack is software for hardware is written by people who don't know how to write good software, they're still writing software as if it's the 80s

item.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
item.description: 526 points, 265 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (kottke.org)

→ HN comments  ·  526 points  ·  265 comments

Top #1 — seanhunter:

I think this idea is often misunderstood and used as an excuse by people who don’t want to make any effort to understand a complex concept and want to blame the results of their laziness on the explanation or the explainer.

There are things where you may be given an explanation in simple terms, but the concept requires effort on the part of the recipient of the explanation to really understand. I’ll give an example: compactness. Probably anyone who has done analysis is familiar with how this concept is usually taught. Typically how it goes is you do open and closed sets and then they hit you with “a set is compact if and only if every open cover has a finite subcover”. Now this definition is extremely profound but very dense and it’s highly non-obvious why that in particular is the property you want (a finite subcover for every open cover)[1], how you could go about proving that every possible open cover in a certain situation could have a finite subcover etc etc.

In this case it’s actually quite easy to give simple explanations of the separate parts of the definition (open and closed sets, what an open cover therefore means, what a finite subcover then is etc) but actually understanding the concept of compactness requires something above and beyond whatever explanation you are given: it requires the reader to get out pencil and paper, try out some sets, go for some walks, think about it in the bath etc.

You may get a really fantastic explanation in simple terms from someone who deeply understands the topic, but if you don’t put in the effort you’re not going to understand it yourself. That’s not the fault of the explanation. It’s not an easy concept to grasp so you have to climb the ladder of understanding. The explainer can’t do that for you.

[1] it took the mathematical community years to settle on this being the definition, so you shouldn’t expect to understand why this is the definition straight away.

↳ reply 1 — stingraycharles:

I like to think that a “simple” explanation doesn’t necessarily have to be a short one. 3blue1brown is a good example of that. It took multiple videos for him to explain LLMs, but it’s simple and relatively easy to understand.

Actually, Feynman himself is a good example of that as well. His explanations are rarely short, but very simple. He has a series of YouTube videos where he explains all kinds of concepts like fire, but it still takes him at least 15 minutes to explain it.

So I’d argue that thinking it needs to be condensed into one or two sentences is getting the meaning of the expression wrong.

↳↳ reply — kazinator:

A thing being more or less complex refers to the amount of information needed to encode its description.

"Simple" therefore means "reduced in information content".

The topic being explained has a certain minimal information content, and if you reduce beyond that, you are telling a fiction which bears analogies to the topic.

A simpler description is not necessarily short; rather, it is a description of something simpler.

When descriptions (of a given complexity, being held constant) are short, that can make them harder to follow, because encodings have to be clever in order to achieve compression, and that has a complexity of its own.

↳↳↳ reply — petsfed:

And there are entire categories of phenomenon that don't arise or are imperceptible in a simple context. Chaos is an emergent phenomenon that requires a surprisingly deep knowledge of a situation to predict where it will arise.

The way I understand the problem with explaining things in simple terms is this: We usually introduce quantum mechanics students to a toy model -the infinite square well- to build up intuition. However, depending on the teacher and the students, it may well take years for those students to recognize and understand that the boundary conditions we apply to literally every other QM calculation are violated by the infinite square well, and while we ultimately recover the expected conclusion via successive approximations, it takes a much deeper understanding of the material to understand why the "simple" explanation is actually wrong. That is, while it turns out that the solution to the infinite-square well is, at the limit, identical to a very deep square well, showing that is actually quite a bit harder.

The simple explanation causes incorrect intution about the situation.

↳ reply 2 — kccqzy:

Nah that is just not a good definition for beginners. It shouldn’t be somebody’s first introduction to compactness. There are other definitions that are less general but more intuitive, such as sequential compactness: every sequence has a subsequence that converges to a limit in the space. For beginners working only in metric spaces, there’s no difference anyways.

Directly teaching the most general definition misses the steps it took mathematicians to arrive at this definition and is unhelpful. In set theory classes nobody starts by teaching ZFC; instead we start by the general comprehension principle, discover paradoxes and then introduce ZFC.

That’s also the reason high schoolers taking an introduction to calculus class aren’t immediately taught the epsilon delta definition. Start with something more intuitive. Rigor can come later. Newton and Leibniz didn’t start with rigor either.

↳ reply 3 — Francute:

While I agree that the receiver needs to make an effort to understand, I don't think I agree with this explanation

Your definition; "a set is compact if and only if every open cover has a finite subcover", requires a lot of prior knowledge to actually make sense of. When you say "explain it in simple terms", you are expected to explain all the needed concepts too

So what is a cover? what is an open cover? what is a subcover? what is a set!? heck, even what is finite/infinite? and what are all the new concepts you have to introduce to explain each of those?

The idea of explaining something in simple terms doesn't necessarily mean using a short, strictly formal explanation. It means making someone who is willing to pay attention understand everything (and this can usually be a long explanation). This requires a lot more effort than people usually think. Explaining forces you to remember concepts you assume others understands because with your own experience that feels already natural

In summary: - Don't confuse "compressing an idea" with "explaining it on simpler terms" - Explain it in a way an attentive 5 years old kid could understand

Top #2 — mr_mitm:

The article is just a bunch of quotes from Richard Feynman and John Gruber. There is little insight and I even think the article is misrepresenting the quotes.

Feynman said "if you can't explain it on a freshmen level". Leaving out that qualifier distorts the statement.

The other quote about the magnets is also overly reductive. Saying "I don't understand it in terms you're more familiar with" is not an admission that scientists as a group don't understand it at all.

You could go into what it means to understand something, but unfortunately the article isn't doing that.

↳ reply — rocqua:

Besides, the claim on magnetic force already serves as a counter-example to the main claim of the article.

Unless the article means to say that Feynman didn't understand the magnetic force, they have to admit that the magnetic force was perfectly understood, but impossible to explain in simple terms.

↳↳ reply — programjames:

I think Feynman might have been referring to how spin was not understood (even by him), and magnetism is a result of a bunch of little spins adding up. I mean—even today—there are not really explanations that are correct and also understandable by a freshman. There's the belt analogy but, well, it doesn't really explain the physics.

↳↳↳ reply — mr_mitm:

That's not how I read it. Feynman started with the story of a girl going to the hospital because she broke something after slipping on ice. His point was that you can only explain things in terms that you simply accept without further explanation, otherwise you'd keep asking "why". Then he muses about imagining little rubber bands between magnets, but those only have their property in the end because of electromagnetism, so it's a circular explanation and thus unsatisfactory. To him, the magnetic field and its properties simply are, there is nothing underneath it.

Top #3 — tgv:

Explain to what level? E.g some topics common here. How do you explain NP in simple terms? "Things that are hard to compute?" That's simple, but not much of an explanation. It leaves the listener with a practically useless definition. And how do you explain even something practical as Heartbleed or Rowhammer? Etc.

And then there's another barrier, of course: the audience. You may use simple terms, and tell a lengthy story, but some things are hard to understand. Relativity and Monty Hall come to mind. They can be explained in simple terms, but how many people get them? Probably just the ones that also understand a detailed explanation.

↳ reply 1 — trash_cat:

Simple for your audience to understand. Which means you posses understanding deep enough that you can explain it any any level of detail.

↳ reply 2 — xlii:

E.g. NP is a problem that's easy to check, but not easy to solve. NP is type of a problem like one for finding people: it's easy to confirm (is Mr. X in the room?), but there's no quick way to find solution (where is Mr. X).

item.title: Carnival Cruises emits ten times more sulphur oxide than all of Europe's cars (2019)
item.description: 464 points, 292 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ecohustler.com)

→ HN comments  ·  464 points  ·  292 comments

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — tito:

One unintended side effect of the removal of sulfur from shipping fuels is a drastic reduction in cloud cover over the ocean. This is estimated to have doubled global warming in the 2020s (!).

I’m exploring how to cleanly re-create those lost clouds over the ocean. Fuel additives, spraying sea salt into clouds, modifying ship routing. If this is up your alley hit reply.

↳ reply 1 — smartmic:

Good intentions, but I would like to see a balanced discussion involving also the risks of geoengineering. It is always delicate if we interfere with a system we have not yet fully understood.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoengineering

↳↳ reply — andrewvc:

I wish we could afford to be very circumspect about geo engineering. There’s been too much warming to be slow about it.

If reduction alone was an effective strategy we wouldn’t be where we are today.

↳↳↳ reply — chriswarbo:

The main problem with geoengineering is not the unintended consequences, the unknown unknowns, etc. It's that it would require massive, coordinated effort.

The reason I say that's the main problem, is because that's also the main problem with reducing fossil fuel usage.

It's fun to debate the technical details of geoengineering (solar shades, atmospheric aerosols, enhanced weathering, etc.), in the same way that it's fun to debate the technical details of carbon reduction (energy storage methods, approaches to electrical transmission, remote work, land use, etc.).

But none of that really matters if we, collectively, don't actually do anything! It's not as fun as comparing scifi fantasies, but the problem we need to solve is that of getting humanity to actually do something, at scale, which is collectively acknowledged as necessary yet is not immediately/individually profitable.

If we could solve that, then we could do geoengineering; but in such a world, we might not need to, because we could also do carbon reduction, plus a bunch of other stuff!

However, if we can't solve that, then geoengineering is an illusion.

It's a grass-is-greener fallacy: what makes any geoengineering project seem remotely feasible, in a world where we can't even coordinate on the obviously-a-good-idea stuff?

↳ reply 2 — Timshel:

Not sure where your doubling is coming from.

https://attheu.utah.edu/research/cleaner-ship-fuel-changed-c...

Not even clear if there was a change ...

> It turned out that the clouds after the fuel change held more total water overall, which balanced out changes in droplet size and maintained cloud solar reflectivity, known as albedo. Had the albedo of Atlantic clouds reduced, they would have reflected less of the sun’s heat back into space, thereby warming the climate.

↳ reply 3 — vevoe:

Just wanted to say I saw a comment from you a few months ago in a thread about this year's El Niño where you talked about what you're doing at AirMiners and mentioned Boot Up. From there, I signed up and am in the current Boot Up class and loving it! Thank you for putting that all together.

Top #2 — nehal3m:

One of the easiest wins would be outlawing burning bunker fuel for recreational purposes, would it not? ↳ reply 1 — wouldbecouldbe:

Isn't it more effective to just legislate ships to only allow docking in EU ports if they have certain filters on their engines? Like they did with cars

↳ reply 2 — wittjeff:

item.title: "I can tell you wrote this yourself"
item.description: 386 points, 380 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (em-online.bearblog.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  386 points  ·  380 comments

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — FinnLobsien:

AI and LLMs, in my opinion, are effectively the industrialization of knowledge work.

Like it or not, industrialization brought many benefits and we couldn't imagine our modern way of living without it (just think about medicines). Industrial production made so many things so much more accessible for so many people.

But an industrialist perspective doesn't care about the process of making stuff, only about the outcome. The shoemakers deep knowledge of leathers, his intuition of all sorts of different shoes, and the pride of that competence—that doesn't matter when you can make thousands of shoes a day that cost 0.5% of something artisanal. The people working at the shoe factory only carry things to and fro and occasionally fix some machine issue.

This has tons of benefits and tons of downsides. But with physical goods, a shoe is a shoe.

With knowledge work like writing, the process is often the entire point. The point of writing a paper is what you learned in the process. The point of documented software architecture is to develop an understanding deep enough to drive coherent downstream decisions. If those things are no longer true, the asset it stands for is basically worthless.

↳ reply 1 — mrwh:

An AI design doc has all the outward appearances of a -- good! excellent sometimes! -- preAI design doc, in my experience. But it also has no reason to exist. There's no social aspect, since no one has gone through the process of actually understanding the systems involved, there's no meaningful way to review it ("why do things this way?" "Because it said to do things this way"). And it's not needed for the implementation either, for which the original prompt, whatever it was, suffices. By industrialising the output of a process, we forget why it was necessary to go to the trouble in creating it by hand in the first place. Perhaps that's ultimately how things advance, and right now we're in the absurd middle, treating proofs of work like the work itself.

↳↳ reply — mceachen:

> it also has no reason to exist.

I despised having to produce design documents for software projects 20 years ago (the last time I had to do it as a software engineer). I wanted to jump straight to coding. I begrudgingly found that, much like research papers, it's a forcing function in really understanding the problem space.

Over the last year, I've found that, at least for nontrivial things, if my agent makes a terse (under 300 line) technical design doc that describes their research and their tasks, it can highlight any disconnects between what I asked and the agent's interpretation. It also serves as context to ramp up cross-model reviews, and as historical reference material when I have to Chesterson's fence something later. I wrote up more about this here: https://photostructure.com/coding/claude-code-tpp/

↳↳↳ reply — shermantanktop:

I know a lot of engineers who hate writing design docs. I think of them as being more comfortable with ideas in code than with English. And there are good reasons for that. But ideas in code are trapped, whereas ideas in English are portable and potentially viral in how they move between people.

But all those English-hating engineers now produce shitty AI design docs, which tick a box but have less than zero influence on anyone else’s thinking.

↳ reply 2 — pegasus:

If the point of writing a given paper is learning about a subject, then it's not knowledge work, it's studying. Just like an apprentice shoe maker is making shoes mainly to learn, not to produce footwear. Acquiring more of a skill while working is incidental both when shoe making and when writing documentation. Documentation which will help others understand the system. In both cases, the main point is the finished product. I really don't see the distinction you're drawing.

↳ reply 3 — cyb_:

In software, the factory is the compiler. The code (and preceding artifacts) is the design process leading up to sending something to the factory for production.

In the shoe analogy, there is absolutely deep knowledge and a creative process that goes into designing a new shoe. This includes market research, defining the new style, selecting materials, building and testing prototypes, etc. This all happens before factory production.

Software development is the same. The factory is the compiler.

Top #2 — borzi:

Great post, author clearly has a bright future. What I realized over the past years is that people that want to "think for themselves" were already, and probably always, in the minority. It's much easier to delegate how to react to a certain event or piece of information to someone else (news anchors, then influencers in last couple years, now increasingly AI I guess). I've certainly been guilty of this...

↳ reply 1 — tegling:

Why must there be a dichotomy: "use AI/don't think for yourself", vs "don't use AI/think for yourself"?

I think we'll need to grow in our individual relationship with AI. Can't AI be that persuasive and contrarian, at times adversarial, friend? Someone you have to be somewhat wary of, but can provide very thoughtful, intelligent and challenging conversation? Such a "friend" obviously never replaces knowledge. If anything, you'll need to arm yourself with as much knowledge as possible to engage with that friend.

↳↳ reply — eloisius:

Skipping the “friend” criticism as you’ve already addressed it in sibling comments, but another reason among many that even trying to use it as an adversarial interlocutor is flawed thinking, is that even if you prompt it to debate you, you’re the one still prompting it to do that. It can never _mean_ to contradict your argument with its own unique viewpoint. It can only argue because you gave it that prompt. Ironically it’s still a sycophantic position.

↳↳↳ reply — tegling:

Appreciate your response! It was an honest question and this really helps. I think it explains my feeling of getting less "brainstorming" use of AI lately. We seem to be moving from dumber models that only provided a few different views (including stuff I didn't know) to sophisticated models that really "understands" what you want to hear and tailor for that. Any "knowledge" introduced to you in this process is only a side-effect/a strict non-goal. Rather, it wants you to feel engaged and happy with the response. Flipping this around: could it be helpful to develop some kind of "concensus models" filled with knowledge and with the sole purpose of teaching/providing you with that corpus? Or, to create some kind of mean-reversion effect of opinions at societal scale (rather than promoting "bubbles")? But at that point, we're very close to the subjects of propaganda and ideas of monoculture...

↳ reply 2 — NalNezumi:

I share your sentiment, but a recent episode made me doubt this position, and maybe you (or other HN readers) can enlighten me.

I don't want to out source thinking and therefore I'm very cautious with my AI use. This attitude caused a little quarrel with my partner, so I shared it with one of my close friend.

My close friend vehemently disagreed with me, he says AI is amazing and he have basically outsourced almost every thinking he does to it. Then he told me how it helped him:

One day he got a message about how his girlfriend was having a rough day at work. Late diagnosed ADHD as he is, he never really knew how to respond to this, so he just asked ChatGPT to write a reply to it (in his own tone). Later the day his girlfriend comes home, hugs and thank him that that compassionate message made her rough day feel much better. My friend doesn't tell her he used AI ofc, but internally thinks "wow is it this easy? Is all I needed to do, listen to the girl and validate her feelings?!" hes 35 btw.

He tells me that without AI he would've never realized this, and from his life decisions so far it's also clear that he never really had the patience to learn anything that is not of immediate interest to him. (and gf feeling seems to not have been)

I'm torn because I have to acknowledge that in the world the majority probably think like him; reading several books and listening to interviews and podcasts for 100+ hours about spousal communications after communication failure (like I did) is an outlier.

And this behavior is probably order of magnitude better than what he did before: getting relationship advice from Joe Rogan.

Edit: to clarify where I'm torn is not about my usebut the utility of it for cases like above. AI will probably (unless enshittification) HELP many people like my friend above, and probably prevent them from falling in conspiracy / online grifter scams because they now just prompt AI like "chat is this true?" and they're good at refuting bullshit. Essentially, we might have an antidote to Brandolini's law https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandolini%27s_law for the common man. I'm reserved because that's at the mercy of AI companies not enshittifying, and skill deterioration, and I have very little trust in that

Top #3 — wavemode:

> Assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which quickly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day.

College education for software developers has never been particularly good, but it seems like now they've actually just given up.

Do we accept this in any other field? Does your math professor teach you to solve integrals by asking WolframAlpha?

↳ reply 1 — Toutouxc:

> College education for software developers has never been particularly good

I'm really happy with the education I received in uni (mid 2010s). As part of my bachelor's I had to wrestle threads in C and C++, got O(N^2) code rejected for O(N*logN) problems, I got to write client-server apps in Java, do (graded) exercises in Prolog and Common Lisp, build web apps in PHP, configure Cisco IOS devices from scratch, draw diagrams of CMOS gates on paper, write Bash scripts handling newlines in file names, program robots in Python, write Lambda calculus expressions by hand, write XSD schemas, recognize a context-sensitive grammar, ...

I benefit from that a lot and I regularly notice that I'm using something or building upon something I remember from uni. It always seems weird to me when people say that you don't need any of that on the actual job. So what else do you need? Clicking through GitLab or Jira, remembering the 3 git commands you usually use and being comfortable in a particular IDE? You can learn all that on a rainy weekend, I'd be seriously pissed off if I'd spent my time in uni doing that.

↳↳ reply — ecshafer:

> It always seems weird to me when people say that you don't need any of that on the actual job.

These people tend to lack abstract thinking, and wish they had just been given a React bootcamp. They don't see it as learning networking, algorithms, files, critical thinking, software engineering, etc. They lament that they were not given specific training on specific technologies, that they then use at work.

↳ reply 2 — budman1:

My university president is pushing for AI in everything.

Personally, I a have come to the conclusion that making business apps is no longer a STEM education required profession. If your goal is to make web apps then you will be a prompter, and the the College of Business (or College of Vibecoding, or whatever) is where the education will be. And it will be finding information for the clanker. No math, no calculus, no programming.

Computer Science will still exist. It will be 95% smaller. And the 'software engineering stuff' like requirements and actual testing and design will be explained in a couple of slides in a single lecture.

In academia, almost all AI use is wrong. Thinking, understanding, expressing yourself. The AI does not help those skills at all. The work product you create has no value; rather it is what you had to learn to make the work product. (focus on undergraduate work here, there is some nuance in research).

We have to stop focusing on the work product, and move to the journey.

Also — ★ simonw:

I want to see a photo of that tawny frogmouth!

item.title: Jujutsu Primer
item.description: 197 points, 158 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ethanlowman.com)

→ HN comments  ·  197 points  ·  158 comments

Top #1 — danpalmer:

I've been using JJ almost exclusively for over 2 years now. It's great, it works fantastically with our rather large monorepo at work.

However I mostly use it backing on to a custom VCS, not git. I can't wait to see some JJ-native forges that don't try to keep it compatible with git, I think there's a lot more benefits and more UX to be explored there!

↳ reply 1 — ezst:

I doubt so, because not being compatible with the git repo format (and therefore requiring distinct hosting, therefore socially excluding from GitHub) is what slowly drove mercurial into obscurity, even though its UX was (and still is) superior to that of git (and JJ, which drew from it), not to mention the other aspects which made hg a much sounder choice on technical merits (e.g. very large monorepos), the users and decision makers both couldn't stand breaking away from the git repo format.

↳↳ reply — danpalmer:

I agree that this was a factor in Mercurial dying, but I'm not sure this holds today. Mercurial performed significantly worse than git, that was a factor at the time, but in 2026 the perception is that git doesn't perform well enough (see GitHub outages, GitLab writing on this topic, Anthropic developing their own VCS, etc). Even small teams I know (circa 10 committers) are finding Git to not scale to the speed they're working at now.

JJ has the potential to be a substantial step forward in performance. This will depend on the backend to fully realise it, but a backend that prioritises scalability could vastly outperform git and GitHub's storage.

I think in the post-Microsoft acquisition, post-Dear GitHub letter era, GitHub's shine has worn off. I see a lot more use of GitLab for open source, a lot more use of various other forges. I don't think it's a requirement for a thriving open source project in the way it was for ~2010-2020.

↳↳↳ reply — dotancohen:

You conflate Git and GitHub a few times here. I'm a heavy git user, almost never anywhere near GitHub.

↳ reply 2 — jon-wood:

I'm not too bothered about the backing store but I really want to see some forges gain support for code review based on jj changes rather than git branches and commits. The Github model absolutely sucks if you're someone who likes to keep a coherent history because if you squash the resolution of PR comments into the parent commits nobody can see what changed between when the comments were made and now.

Basing code review on changes and changesets would mean that the evolution of each change could be seen in isolation, which would also mean that you immediately do away with awkward workarounds like PR stacks.

↳ reply 3 — jkbbwr:

Hey I took a crack at this I need to do some updates on it sometime but

https://jjhub.dev/

(I am the author)

Top #2 — nixpulvis:

I'm skeptical about the no staging area, but it seems just like a HEAD commit replaces that, which could be nice.

I really don't like the automatic bookmark naming thing.

I'm also skeptical about automatic rebasing, but having conflicts not block the process could be nice, I'll have to try it out on more complex trees.

Also, I didn't see a section on workspaces, but I assume they basically do the right thing.

↳ reply 1 — ozim:

Have to say staging area is one feature that makes people better programmers. Especially using GUI tooling to pick hunks or discard parts you don’t want to go to a commit was always super useful for me. (CLI of staging hunks is not convenient at all for me)

I keep running into people who “just commit stuff” and they don’t know what they are doing.

Downside is we are heading into direction where people don’t even read code anymore so I might be just old man screaming at the clouds or agents.

↳↳ reply — rbehrends:

To each their own, but I always saw the staging area as an anti-pattern that also needlessly complicated git's mental model.

With the staging area, you don't even know if the commit builds if you commit selectively, and manual adding is error-prone.

The traditional "clean" way has been to stash unwanted changes temporarily, then commit the rest.

↳ reply 2 — adamtulinius:

I've used jujutsu for maybe half a year by now.

At first the auto-staging (or whatever it's called) is annoying. It sure is if one is used to dump random files in the repository, that haven't been ignored.

After some time, I realised it gives a lot of freedom. Working on something but not in a workspace, and need to do something else for the day? Just jump somewhere else. Everything will still be there when you get back. In other words, it's hard to lose things by mistake. In those situations it's also cool to describe (name) the work being done, prior to making a normal commit. A bit odd but one can also push `@` to a remote (e.g. iterating on something and piggy backing on a CI-system), avoiding having to squash and then push.

Having a stack of PR's, then rebasing it all to see a conflict, and only having to deal with it one is also magical.

Moving bookmarks around can be annoying.

Workspaces work fine, and there's two options:

- the normal ones, where a full .git isn't created. That works fine, unless having tooling that expects the workspace to also work as a git repository, in which case ..

- you can make the workspace collocated, less lightweight, but git tooling works

Top #3 — pkuki:

Shameless plug, but a bit related to jj:)

I recently created a project which utilizes FUSE to serve git files directly from object store without a checkout. Main motivation was to sepeedup a worktrees creation (I work on a huge monorepo). In my case it helps a lot - now I wait a second instead of a minute. But then I realised there are other interesting features which having vfs opened:

- tree structure of related branches (simplest case of that are stacked PRs) which rebases itself

- live preview of merge state or any node of such tree

- on demand creation of a new branch which merges any of the existing ones very cheaply (e.g for a throwaway build check)

- quick and simple comand which shows conflicting files between selected worktree and all others

- agents gets notified about such conflicts when they happen

I was able to design it in a way so git sees those virtual workspaces as normal worktrees, and all git commands works exactly as you would expect. So I think for some people, especially on the very big repositpries, it might solve a few problems they try to solve with jj.

https://github.com/pkukielka/gitfold

A few typical use cases: https://github.com/pkukielka/gitfold/blob/main/docs/guide.md

↳ reply 1 — jauntywundrkind:

You made it much further with this effort than i did! https://github.com/rektide/jj-workfuse

I think in truth I 50% of the reason I made it was because I was mad about Anthropic inventing a whole new vcs after blaming git clone speed. I also knew artifact-fs exists, which works lazily to get data on demand, which is cool. https://github.com/cloudflare/artifact-fs https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47792374

↳ reply 2 — IshKebab:

There are quite a few of those projects already I'm pretty sure, e.g. GitFS.

GrapheneOS, on its side, should publish a template letter for every state. They should also consider releasing evidence for Google "repeatedly reaching out to OEMs to question whether they're working with us and threaten[ing] them" [2].

↳ reply 1 — dataflow:

To make things easier for folks could you cite what specific law you feel is likely being violated and how? It'd be much more effective if citizens can say X violates Y because Z rather than "you should look into <company> because <of a rant on some organization's forum>."

↳ reply 2 — cyanydeez:

Google is basically Microsoft during windows 95+Explorer.

Top #2 — ddxv:

This was the year for me, and developer verification was the hill. I started moving all my important emails, images, etc off Google. I can't do it all or all at once, but I made a new email account and started moving things.

I bought a new phone, GrapheneOS is on it now. I started moving things there one by one.

I got a home server and started self hosting my images and my docs.

You don't need to "do it all" just do some, it feels great.

Top #3 — acd:

Strange since Pixels allow boot loader unlocking.

"The Sherman Antitrust Act[1] (26 Stat. 209, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1–7) is a United States antitrust law which prescribes the rule of free competition among those engaged in commerce and consequently prohibits unfair monopolies. It" Source: "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman_Antitrust_Act"

↳ reply 1 — aaravchen:

As of Pixel 10 this changed. Now the bootloader unlocking requires contacting a Google server first to "verify" the device can be unlocked. If it was purchased thru one of a number of vendors (e.g. most carriers), it's marked on the server side to block unlocking. Also, if someone has it on a financing plan, that's also registered with the server and blocks unlocking until it's paid off and the financing company informs Google.

I literally just went thru this hassle trying to locate a Pixel 10 Pro Fold on EBay that could be unlocked. I ended up returning at least one because someone tried to resell a device they hadn't already finished paying off , and the only way I could figure out that was the reason was dumping the ADB logs and combing thru them when the unlocking failed.

↳ reply 2 — skeledrew:

> Pixels allow boot loader unlocking

Until Google decides otherwise.

item.title: What Comes After AGI?
item.description: 148 points, 295 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (institute.deepmind.com)

→ HN comments  ·  148 points  ·  295 comments

Top #1 — bsenftner:

Propaganda? We do not have AGI, and the claims we do are propaganda.

AGI: artificial general intelligence is not a scaled up LLM, and those thinking it is are literally failed educations. They are failed because they cannot see the subtly that is what AI becomes when trained on human literature; it becomes an entirely different thing than any other form of trained algorithm. AI is a communications technology, which few to none seem to understand. AI is not automation, but it can be used to create automation with careful consideration, that is not taking place.

I'm speaking in strong terms because we are literally fighting a war against stupidity and propaganda.

AGI requires artificial comprehension which is a science that humanity does not have. When we have artificial comprehension there will be no need to train AIs beyond the kindergarten school basics, and then the AGI will figure it all out, all the rest, on its own. Human history and human literature will need to be learned in reference, but science and mathematics will require no training, beyond to learn the names of concepts we discovered earlier, so the AGI can discuss its understandings with humans and other AGI.

↳ reply 1 — panarky:

> We do not have AGI, and the claims we do are propaganda.

The linked post makes no such claim.

> artificial general intelligence is not a scaled up LLM ... artificial comprehension ... kindergarten ...

Your reasoning takes the form of "I define X to mean Y and Z, and since Y is impossible, X is impossible", which is trivially true within your definition.

But not everyone shares your definition.

A widely held definition of AGI is "a machine that can accomplish most tasks that humans do on computers as well as the median human".

This definition focuses on concrete and observable results and not philosophical or metaphysical definitions of "intelligence" or "comprehension" or "consciousness".

item.title: Postgres 19 Repack: Faster, Built-In Table Bloat Cleanup
item.description: 173 points, 29 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (snowflake.com)

→ HN comments  ·  173 points  ·  29 comments

Top #1 — jzelinskie:

I haven't used these extensions, but I like the direction of being able to extend Postgres by tailing its own internals (pg_squeeze approach) than triggers (pg_repack).

We (the SpiceDB developers) took a similar approach to solve a different problem a few years ago: implementing strict serializability in Postgres[0]. By hooking into the transactions layer themselves (pg_xact), we could layer on our own MVCC reusing the real Postgres transactions to compute visibility and total ordering. When you can just tail the Postgres internals, you don't even need to implement a Postgres extension, which can keep it portable across locked-down, managed Postgres offerings.

Do folks know of other clever implementations of behavior by "spying" on the Postgres internals?

[0]: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=_f6fHy4DWWM

Top #2 — hylaride:

I used to have to keep an eye on tuple table bloat for awhile on big PG databases, but with recent versions of Postgres the auto-vacuuming has mostly kept it in check for all but the most gargantuan, busy tables. I pretty much have stopped caring (and I cared a lot less when SSDs became the default as the fragmentation penalty that a full repack would fix wasn't as bad as it was during the spinning metal days).

Index bloat has been another story, though. Pruning b-trees is expensive and I've mostly just been scheduling reindexes (which have been able to be done concurrently for awhile) instead.

USING INDEX is interesting, though...

Top #3 — dangoodmanUT:

> You need 2x the space for the table and indexes you are repacking, since for a period, you will have two copies of it.

this feels like a foot gun. While other storage formats (eg LSMs) have lots of write amplification, it's done iteratively so you don't have massive storage and IO spikes when performing maintenance.

While this is _definitely_ better, I think the long-term solution is to replace the storage engine with something more modern.

item.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)
item.description: 356 points, 313 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  356 points  ·  313 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — amluto:

On a very very quick read, the bug is that EVP_EncodeBlock malfunctions if the input is larger than ~1.5GB. EVP_EncodeBlock is a function that encodes base64.

https://docs.openssl.org/1.0.2/man3/EVP_EncodeInit/

As a seasoned C programmer, I can immediately observe that the whole API is bad: the caller is expected to calculate the buffer length on their own, using a nontrivial formula, and the caller does not pass in the output buffer length, so the implementation cannot validate it. But apparently OpenSSL 4 also implemented it wrong and wrote (possibly far) past the end of the buffer.

You should probably assume that, if you are running anything that can be convinced to use this API to encode a very long blob as base64, then you are in trouble. I don’t know why a modern server would do this.

BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs. Stay away.

edit: Fixed my size threshold, hopefully. I was thinking of unsigned ints, but this is a signed int. I have not looked at the code, just the description.

↳ reply 1 — socketcluster:

> BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs.

Fully agree with your assessment above that line, but damn, this is a strong statement for a library this ubiquitous. You wonder; how could this happen? And yet, as an open source developer myself, I know how little people care about code quality.

↳↳ reply — Gigachad:

We have known this since at least heartbleed. The answer was that basically no one funds the project and it had only one developer.

All these trillion dollar tech companies have been leaching off open source for free and never contributed back to the projects they rely on.

↳↳↳ reply — k_sze:

Honest question: shall free software licenses be changed to force large corporations to sponsor free software projects adequately?

↳ reply 2 — vlovich123:

> BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs. Stay away.

We’ve known this for well over two decade since heartbleed yet for some reason Linux distros haven’t migrated off of it

↳ reply 3 — teunispeters:

I like to declare that industry coding standards such as MISRA exist precisely because code bases like OpenSSL (specifically) exist, as it's such a good example of breaking every sensible rule in the standards.

Top #2 — userbinator:

I think CVSS 9.8 is exaggerated. This is not remotely anywhere near as serious as Heartbleed. It's an internal function which will fail if its input is far too long, but exploitability rests on how untrusted input can reach it; the key word being "untrusted". E.g. if you operate a base64 encoding service on the Internet that just reads all the data into memory at once and calls EVP_EncodeBlock(), that's exploitable. If you have a protocol that involves a block of data with a 16-bit length field which is passed to EVP_EncodeBlock(), that's 100% safe.

For those wondering about TLS: speaking as someone who has written a TLS implementation, AFAIK neither base64 encoding nor decoding occurs in the protocol itself, and the longest length field is 24 bits (Hello stream). Certificate processing involves ASN.1 which does support arbitrarily-long integers, but that's a big hint to check that they're within a sensical range.

↳ reply 1 — jtrn:

THIS!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! THIS times 10000!

I'm starting to get annoyed about the OMG OMG BREAKING BREAKING ALARM-EMOJI crap that's not a real emergency.

Four times in the last month, I dropped everything and started investigating whether a serious CVE related to any of our dependencies warranted an emergency bump, only to be frustrated that images, even from AWS, did not have the fix yet. So then I had to worry about whether I should build from source. We actually built PHP from source and deployed it to prod, just to get ahead of the PHP2Shell vulnerability

But yesterday's PHP vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, didn't even apply to us or most people running PHP, and I don't think there are any realistic working exploits out there. I'm not saying that it's not possible, but I'm starting to feel that there's a large difference between what's theoretically possible and what's practically possible. And given the storm of patches and vulnerabilities found, this will become increasingly important to ask.

I think everything above a CVE score of 9.0 should warrant some level of “how exploitable is this in real life,” and anything above 9.5 should be proven to be easy for an attacker to execute, not just “possible in theory.” I don't see how we will survive as developers if there isn't some sort of better triage for vulnerability severity assessment. If everything is an emergency, then nothing is an emergency.

↳↳ reply — ylk:

There are more values in the CVSS vector you can fill in yourself: environmental and threat scores

So you can take e.g. a 9.3 critical down to 6.5 medium by setting CIA requirements to low and exploit maturity to Unreported.

I’m not saying CVSS is perfect but if you want to have a score that applies to your environment, you have to input some info about your environment into it.

“how exploitable is this in real life” is answered by the exploitability score, which is calculated from Attack Vector, Attack Complexity, Attack Requirements, Privileges Required, and User Interaction scores.

↳↳↳ reply — jtrn:

Good info, thanks.

↳ reply 2 — jeroenhd:

CVSS scores do not indicate priority. They give a baseline so you can pick what CVEs affecting you you should do risk analysis for first.

The score is just fine. The people misinterpreting everything with a CVSS score higher than 8 as the end of the world are panicking over nothing.

↳ reply 3 — ★ tptacek:

(I'm a broken record on this so I'll keep it brief). The problem here is that the CVSS score is in the headline, as if it meant anything. But CVSS doesn't mean anything. It's a Ouija board; VR people jack it up to get attention, vendors nerf it to chill their customers out.

Someone should design something better, and less malleable.

↳↳ reply — csnover:

A few years ago I participated in a study[0] about CVSS and apparently was very much in the minority in feeling that these scores are essentially useless. I have no idea what would actually shift the majority’s opinion on this, but I will at least echo your sentiment that everyone deserves something better.

[0] https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.15259

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

It's not an out-there opinion among vulnerability researchers, though.

Top #3 — WalterBright:

> Calling EVP_EncodeBlock() with an input length close to INT_MAX may overflow the calculation of the encoded output size and write past the end of the caller-supplied output buffer.

Haven't we suffered enough yet with lack of a basic feature in C? Why are enhancements going into C that never address this fundamental problem?

I wrote this proposal for C 17 years ago:

file:///C:/digitalmars/articles/C-biggest-mistake.html

It's a simple addition, it breaks 0 code, and provides a path forward to stop array overflows for good.

It's a foundational feature for D. We don't have buffer overflows.

↳ reply 1 — diath:

> We don't have buffer overflows.

You don't have that class of buffer overflows, but for as long as D allows raw pointer arithmetic, you still got buffer overflows, i.e. here's a simple snippet triggering ASAN: https://godbolt.org/z/qPhMKzM1z

↳ reply 2 — Matheus28:

Might wanna double check that url

Also — shepherdjerred:

It feels to me the only way to beat LLMs finding vulnerabilities is to have LLMs (or LLMs paired with other AI methods) constantly monitor your infrastructure, traffic, database, etc. to ensure that nothing out of the ordinary is happening

↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

I think so too; I think apart from pushing vulnerability research forward (which is important on its own merits just for computer science reasons), the major engineering challenge of this moment is figuring out how to make platforms resilient without rewriting everything; that could be better live-patching, it could be some weird monitoring thing, it could be automatic segregation and workload isolation.

It's not "just keep up with the patches". That's going to be a losing strat.

item.description: 191 points, 50 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (wsj.com)

→ HN comments  ·  191 points  ·  50 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — paxy:

So names and email addresses of 16,000 customers leaked from some third party marketing service.

Is this what the hackers trying to extort these banks over? They made it seem it was bank statements or something. This data has exactly zero value.

↳ reply 1 — NoPicklez:

How did they make it seem like it was bank statements?

When I see a headline that says "Visa breached in cyber security attack" I'll admit I assume its on the payment system itself. But I assume that, as opposed to the media actually saying that.

↳↳ reply — arijun:

You don’t need to explicitly say something to know people will assume it. If a headline says “so and so died today,” without mentioning that he was revived soon after, that would be a pretty egregious omission. If gp, you, and I all read the headline as Visa getting hacked, maybe this headline is misleading as well.

↳↳↳ reply — nhubbard:

My favorite example of this is reporting the death of JFK as "JFK died today of a headache".

Yes, he might have had a headache following the bullet going through his head, but the headache is not the reason he died.

↳ reply 2 — ratg13:

The data has value to the companies that own it.

Releasing it causes the company to suffer reputation loss as well as financial loss by having to pay customers for identity protection services as a mitigation technique.

The attackers are only trying to extort the source companies. They have to release the data to make good on their threats when the target companies decide either the cost isn't worth it or their security people tell them not to negotiate.

↳ reply 3 — lubujackson:

Oh shit they discovered the white pages

Top #2 — eterm:

> "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,"

A big question that I think will increasingly be asked as this sort of thing becomes more widespread: Did these customers really give informed consent to their data being passed to these "third party vendors" that are getting breached?

Even with regulation such as CCPA and GDPR in Europe, a lack of meaningful consequences has meant a complete abdication of treating customer data as a liability.

Maybe companies will be more careful with handing out data to third parties if they can no-longer trust those third parties to keep the data secure and it becomes a reputational risk.

Of course that remains to be seen, this one will likely fade into noise and have little to no effect long term, but I am hopeful that meaningful attitude change to data will happen as an effect of the continuing vuln-pocalypse.

An alternate technical point of view: there's also an argument for the need for a better way than emails or SMS for being contacted by companies with which we do business. If a contact grant was handled in a more privacy-preserving manner, then you could authorise companies to send you messages without giving up a form of identification, and this authority could then even be also appropriately delegated in a more secure way.

↳ reply 1 — oliyoung:

> A big question that I think will increasingly be asked as this sort of thing becomes more widespread: Did these customers really give informed consent to their data being passed to these "third party vendors" that are getting breached?

Our legal department is tightening PI and consent considerably, and its going to leave our marketing teams without a lot of the tools and capabilities they've been going to for a long time.

Can't say I disagree with any of it either

↳ reply 2 — makeitdouble:

In theory that should be the right framing, in practice having the information means nothing if there is no reasonable action you can take from there.

In the case of Visa and MasterCard, Amex or JCB or Diners' terms aren't better or more competitive, your only real option is to give up on credit cards altogether.

A lot of otherwise sensible concepts have little weight when you have a cartel or straight duopolies/monopolies.

Top #3 — gherkinnn:

User data should be radioactive. Leaks and hacks must be severely punished. A few companies might buckle under the fines, but such is life. The rest will learn.

Keeping user data for the sake of it will be seen as economically unviable and increasing security as business critical.

How to calculate those fines? I don't know. Maybe row*column, where plaintext passwords demand a much heftier fine than a name. Add a progression, where larger datasets are more costly than smaller ones.

item.title: Synology Security Advisory
item.description: 178 points, 136 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (synology.com)

→ HN comments  ·  178 points  ·  136 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — RetroTechie:

I've always wondered: if you take the cause of each CVE, look at underlying cause of that & repeat, how many essential root problems would you be left with?

"Can't do math" (off-by-1 errors etc)

"Sanitize your inputs" (escape sequences, parsing etc)

"What are you referencing?" (null pointers, use-after-free etc)

and error handling. Plain error codes bubbling up a call stack, or bypassing that somehow which may violate program structure.

How many of these fundamental issues are there?

↳ reply 1 — wccrawford:

"sanitize your inputs" means you have to know what the output is ahead of time, and that you'll never output any other way. It also means false positives. It can actually be harmful if done wrong (double escaping, escaping that certain systems don't understand) but there's some basic forms that probably aren't too bad. It's generally pointless, though, since...

"escape your outputs" works for all data and is actually achievable. It means even escaping data that was never an "input" from the outside the system, even developer-created data, which absolutely can (and does) cause problems to ignore.

↳ reply 2 — chias:

Boil it down enough and you get four:

1. Failure to differentiate data from instructions

2. Business logic flaws

3. Insecure operating environment

4. Incorrect use of cryptography

↳ reply 3 — fulafel:

These are bug classes that are handled by reasonable programming languages since decades ago, so can be reduced to failing in choice of tools and risk management practices.

But root cause is a flawed concept, there's almost never one root cause.

Top #2 — 6thbit:

Tied to this weakness:

  >  CWE-88: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command
So, they were building shell commands from some kind of user input in the OAuth API?

↳ reply 1 — pixl97:

These smaller consumer devices always have the worst security practices.

↳ reply 2 — formerly_proven:

Top #3 — NathanKP:

Mitigation for now is to go to Package Center -> Installed -> OAuth Service and stop it.

item.content:encoded:
