→ HN comments  ·  301 points  ·  154 comments

Top #1 — DrScientist:

Before the internet Ads used to provide a service - connecting buyers and sellers - however the internet has made this largely redundant by amplifying word-of-mouth customer to customer communication [1].

This combined with poor ad regulation ( how Google is allowed to run millions of clearly scammy ads on youtube is beyond me ), has made ads and fake word-of-mouth ( influencers ) directly in conflict with honest customer-to-customer communication.

ie ads are largely no longer serving customers or the market.

Ironically the information gap Ads used to fill would be largely gone if it wasn't for paid Ads content now muddying the waters!

[1] Think early days of Amazon reviews before they were gamed.

Top #2 — hatthew:

This analogy doesn't hold at all. Casinos are engineered for the house to win and the customer to lose because the casino is paying the customer directly. They are disincentivized to let the customer win. If the customer always won, the casino goes out of business very quickly.

Ad auctions are completely different, since they are just a marketplace. A customer's (advertiser's) win comes from a third party, and the point of the ad platform is to connect that third party to the customer. The ad platform would love to be able to make every single customer win all the time. Although, if they did that, it would create a lot more demand and even out the ROI with increased ad prices. But that's not the "evil ad platform" engineering the customers to always lose in the way casinos do, that's simply basic supply/demand economics.

COI disclaimer: My current job is a small part of an ads platform on a website you have heard of. I dislike ads but realize they are a necessity for running some parts of the internet.

↳ reply 1 — mangoceylon:

Yea, I also work in ads and the article doesn't make sense at all. A way bigger factor than anything mentioned in this article is simply what you as an advertiser can afford as a CAC (cost to acquire a customer). There are some advertisers who are selling low cost/low repeat products that advertising is nearly impossible to make profitable. Meanwhile, other advertisers are selling high cost/high repeat products to that same person. The latter can afford to price the former out of ad inventory.

Many companies are spending significant amounts of money (many millions) and not even telling the advertising platforms the actual revenue they generated from the ads, just the number of "leads" or "customers" because they are paranoid about the very thing in the article (which I don't actually believe to be true anyway).

↳↳ reply — davidfischer:

> Meanwhile, other advertisers are selling high cost/high repeat products to that same person. The latter can afford to price the former out of ad inventory.

This is correct. The best advertisers are setting the floor prices for ads within their niche. This is why StackOverflow, before their fall, had just a few advertisers like Google, IBM/RedHat, and Azure. Those advertisers were willing to buy pretty much the whole inventory at a price a startup focusing on say a single niche SO tag couldn't compete with.

Disclosure: Work on an ad startup I helped build. I talk to over a dozen advertisers every day. We have similar problems with advertisers trying to buy most/all of our inventory and we explicitly cap the max percentage we'll sell to any one advertiser.

↳↳↳ reply — PaulHoule:

In the 2000s my political activism and business involvements had me in contact with people involved in local newspaper and radio ads in my community.

I always had the impression that there is a tranche of advertiser who is "made of money" who doesn't care what ads cost and... that person drives the market.

For instance in my town there is one guy who owns all the new card dealerships in town and he saturates the airwaves, I think because he loves to hear his name on the radio. For the rest of us it just reminds us that the next time we buy a car we're going to drive 50 miles to a town where one guy doesn't own all the new car dealerships.

If a radio ad costs him $20 I am sure he gets at least $20 of pleasure from hearing his name and he makes monopoly profits so he can afford it!

A similar story was that a tiny ad in the local newspaper cost $100 a day and it was stupendously difficult to make a case that this was worth it for most small businesses, especially when you could get a storefront for that much or hire a part-timer. I'd talk to people who sold ads for the paper and they told me, "we tell them that their customers will think they went out of business if they stop advertising!"

Some of the rapid collapse of "old media" was that the foundations of it were pretty rotten and people didn't see the value they were getting out of it and were ready to pull out of it as soon as they could.

↳ reply 2 — danielmarkbruce:

You have picked one dimension, incentives, and say the analogy doesn't work because on that dimension it's different. Analogies aren't supposed to be exactly the same.

The point of the analogy stands - most players using paid advertising can't win. They don't realize the entire structure of the market makes it close to impossible for them to win. Google (and a small number of others) have an extremely strong position in what is effectively the distribution channel for a lot of businesses, and a pricing mechanism which enables them to take a giant chunk of economics of the transaction.

Top #3 — davidelettieri:

I help my father and it's 2 business partners to run ads on adwords for their tow hitch/bar installation business. The money are well spent and if something is off on the campaign they notice it immediately by the drop of calls, emails and such.

I also have no marketing background at all. I was just the only one able to set it up.

item.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
item.description: 508 points, 237 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (anthropic.com)

→ HN comments  ·  508 points  ·  237 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — chunky1994:

From a cursory glance the bootstrap paper is really hard to read, however the blog post is easier and seems more human written.

The first result is cool (but basically a complex error-prone calculation), the second is much much cooler, Claude proved the upper limit for the mass of a black-hole which is consistent with a given central charge. (thereby making it a consistent theory of quantum gravity), any theory predicting above this is not a theory of quantum gravity of that universe. This is very exciting!

↳ reply 1 — cvoss:

> thereby making it a consistent theory of quantum gravity

Careful. Thereby making a not-inconsistent-via-bootstrap theory. Such a theory could be inconsistent for other reasons shown by other methods. The article expresses a desire to show inconsistency for M1 above c/12 for example, but it's now been shown that the boostrap method can't get you that far.

↳↳ reply — chunky1994:

Agreed on the correction.

↳ reply 2 — dguest:

Proved it in a 2d universe.

Top #2 — turzmo:

Physicist here. I don't have time right now to read the papers in depth, nor are the results directly in my area, but I would say a few things.

One is that there are a near-infinite number of "open problems" in physics because the surface area of research programs in theoretical physics is extremely large. Before I was in the world of physics, I would have thought that "solving an open problem" meant that physicists around the world would be rejoicing and discussing the result. In reality, other than for the big, field-defining questions, only a small handful of people might care about any problem being solved. That holds true even for the Millennium problems.

Even if I were to read these papers in depth and understand them, without talking to somebody that knows the area and what has been done in it already, I would have no sense of the significance. The way to assess significance is to see how the community responds. Only time will tell whether people care about these results enough to cite them, incorporate them in future work, etc.

And so, like many other people I know, I plan to ignore all of these results until somebody I know comes and tells me to check one out: the cost of assessing any of them is too high, and there are too many other papers to read.

↳ reply 1 — sashank_1509:

Why is it so different in maths compared to theoretical physics?

↳↳ reply — _mjk:

Maths starts from axioms / existing proven work, and extends knowledge with newly proven facts.

Theoretical physics starts from (incomplete) observation and compatible theories plus targets an open question. There often are many solutions, but the real question is, which one holds up if the broader field is examined?

Consider what happened to the observation of the Higgs boson? There were numerous string theory flavors, all (more or less) consistent with current observations, but predicting different mass for the Higgs. Clear path for elimination of a lot of previously "correct" models.

In that empirical approach, making experiments and comparing to old/current/future work is a necessity to judge a models in a given regime. In fact, it is the differentiating factor in maths and theoretical physics.

↳ reply 2 — bluerooibos:

> significance

Presumably Anthropic wouldn't have chosen to work on these if the problems weren't significant?

This seems carefully timed with their IPO.

Top #3 — ★ simonw:

It tickled me that this was a bullet point in the Fable 5.2 announcement. I like that we're now at a point where "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes" is the kind of thing that shows up in a frontier model launch.

↳ reply 1 — bananaflag:

Copying my comment from that discussion:

Those theoretical physics papers look like the real thing (i.e. not mathematical physics like the OpenAI Yang-Mills result). It looks like AI is finally branching out of math.

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50430239

> It looks like AI is finally branching out of math.

Is it really, though? It's still a heavily mathematical domain, rather than one involving empirical research, where AI still struggles.

https://xkcd.com/435/

I have strong, complicated feelings about it, and I understand you may not feel the same way, but "I like" is not a good description in my case.

item.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
item.description: 787 points, 136 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (newscientist.com)

→ HN comments  ·  787 points  ·  136 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — epistasis:

I was trying to figure out what the actual intervention was, and what clinical trial this is from based on the extremely limited information, and have not been able to yet.

In the mean time, here's 25 clinical trials for oncolytic viral therapies for pancreatic cancer:

https://clinicaltrials.gov/search?cond=Pancreatic%20Cancer&i...

And here's a review article on the general concept from the lead physician-researcher in this article:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6186423/

Adenoviruses are very easy to make with custom contents, and are used for many many purposes. However they rarely make it all the way to become a therapy in practice.

It's always fascinating what hits the front page of HN when it comes to bio!

↳ reply — chasil:

Kurzgesagt has mentioned oncolytic viruses in their recent videos.

This general discussion of the human virome mentions Newcastle disease and Reovirus:

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=SbvAaDN1bpE

A full episode followed on a biologist who injected her tumor with Measles:

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=0NY2gAftzJE

Edit: The main article identifies an adenovirus that has been modified to replicate primarily in cancerous cells.

"The only cancer-killing virus that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in the US is T-VEC, a genetically modified herpes simplex virus that is injected directly into melanoma tumours, causing the cells to rupture and die."

Top #2 — tombert:

My favorite uncle died from pancreatic cancer when I was a teenager. I remember at the time I quickly looked up the survivability rates of pancreatic cancer and was immediately sad to see it was nearly zero [1].

For the next few months, there was a roller coaster of hearing about his new treatments, sometimes seeming effective where we would convince ourselves that he's going to get better, only for him to take a turn for the worse. This kept happening until, of course, he died. I was sad he was dead but the combination of the cancer and the chemo seemed really miserable so I was at least happy he wasn't in pain anymore.

This happened around the time Patrick Swayze died from pancreatic cancer, and a bit before Steve Jobs, and it was at least a little reassuring that this disease didn't spare even obscenely wealthy people. I hope we figure out better treatments for it, and this seems promising.

[1] At least when caught late, which it often is and was for him.

↳ reply 1 — elromulous:

Worth noting that the cancer Jobs had is _very_ different from the kind Swayze had.

Jobs had a PanNET tumor[0]. That's the pancreatic cancer you "want". The survival rates are incomparable (iirc localized PanNET survival rate is around 95%!). Jobs chose woowoo bullshit over science, until it was too late. With his money he would have almost certainly been in the surviving group.

Edit to add: Generally when people refer to "pancreatic cancer", they are almost exclusively referring to Adenocarcinoma - the deadly one. That's what Swayze had.

[0] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_neuroendocrine_tumo...

↳↳ reply — globular-toast:

Too many people repeat this about Jobs. The truth is the experts are split on whether he could have survived or not. Some say what you are saying, but others say he was doomed anyway and any treatment would have just made his limited time even less pleasant.

If you ever find yourself in the situation you'll quickly realise it's a catch-22. You might refuse the deeply unpleasant treatment then question whether you could have survived if you had taken it. Or you could get the treatment, and die anyway with much more pain and suffering, possibly drawn out over more time, all the time being a burden on those you love.

If you've never been there yourself or with someone you love it might be hard to understand. But at least try to understand you don't know all the details of someone else's decision, even if they're a public figure.

↳↳↳ reply — elromulous:

I wouldn't say experts are split, that implies it's somewhat 50:50. Experts just can't say with certainty.

https://www.gawkerarchives.com/5849543/harvard-cancer-expert...

https://www.latimes.com/health/la-xpm-2011-oct-20-la-heb-ste...

↳ reply 2 — soperj:

Pancreatic cancer is almost always caught late, because the main indicator is that it's spread to other places. Very rarely, you'll get jaundice from it and then it can be caught early. Survivability in those cases are still really low.

Top #3 — dopamean:

My father died from pancreatic cancer in 2016. He was 54. I don't think I'm ever going to get over it. Otherwise healthy guy starts not feeling great, goes to the doctor, gets misdiagnosed a few times. After a few months of that gets told that it's pancreatic cancer and he has 10-12 months. 15 months later he was gone. When I see news like this it gives me such hope for other people.

↳ reply 1 — lexandstuff:

Sorry for your loss.

Misdiagnosis is very common with pancreatic cancer, it seems. My mum was complaining about stomach pains and sickness for a long time before they finally tested her for pancreatic cancer; before that, they had all sorts of theories about what it was, including tropical sprue. By the time she knew it was cancer, she was stage 4 with months to live. Thankfully, chemo kept her alive just long enough to meet her grandson, and also for assisted dying laws that had just passed in Victoria, Australia.

Hope that one day no one else has to go through what we did.

↳↳ reply — devilbunny:

There's not a "test" in the sense of a blood draw for pancreatic cancer. Diagnosis is made by getting a piece of tissue (not easy) and having a pathologist review it.

At a bare minimum, you will need to have a mass large enough to be seen on CT scan, and then an endoscopic biopsy (among GI scopes, the endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography or ERCP is one of the most difficult). And even that may not get enough tissue for a diagnosis.

So, yeah, failure to diagnose it is common - largely because it's almost impossible to diagnose early. I'm a doctor. We feel sick when these things happen. It's horrible for our patients.

↳↳↳ reply — robotresearcher:

Same with gallbladder. A common way to find out you have it is to have tumors elsewhere that are not liver/breast/lung cells when biopsied, ie. it’s metastatic and you are doomed.

‘Cancer of unknown origin’ is a grim diagnosis.

↳ reply 2 — jamier1978:

Very similar story to you and the other replies. My mum passed away in August this year from pancreatic cancer. It was detected at stage 4 and she was two weeks from diagnosis to passing away. She was 74 but very active and still had a lot of life to live.

In the same way, the doctors went down a lot of different paths before a later CT scan picked up the mass on the pancreas which has also spread to other organs.

While two weeks was short, she did struggle and I'm glad she didn't have to endure it for too long. I'm not sure life will ever feel the same again but I am learning to cope with the loss as the weeks go by.

Sorry for your loss and all the others who have commented.

↳ reply 1 — guar47:

I think we long passed the massive moment. Right now, it looks more like an attempt to save the sinking ship. I think Anthropic and OpenAI they hit the wall in their business.

Yes, in the last 4 years, we got a massive disruption in our industry and we work with the highest abstraction ever. But I feel like SWE was always moving that way.

Now, I only see how AI tools stagnated in the last few years. To me, Opus 5.x solves all the issues I've had with programming. I no longer need more.

They also failed with massive adoption of non-tech people beyond using AI tools as simple guidance and search tools with some simple programming capabilities.

I don't see any way for them to grow more (maybe I am blind), and open weight models are only going to get better, which will sink them further.

Only time will tell I guess.

↳ reply 2 — elgertam:

I came close to thinking that way a couple years ago, but I've become more optimistic. There is no shortage of problems that can be solved (in fact, wants are infinite), and LLMs may actually enable our profession to reliably deliver them better than 50% completion.

I've also seen non-technical folks in the corporate and government worlds glom onto vibe coding, only to start flailing like they were caught in a rip current when the underlying technical debt is too strong, even with strong and capable models.

For a certain type of engineer who enjoys really arcane technical problems, yeah, the gravy train may be over, or at least will involve a lot more machines than it used to, as Alan Turing predicted about "mechanical work" becoming a "drudge."[0]

And I think Big Tech is for the foreseeable future a sink for capital in the form of specialized hardware rather than human capital.

[0]https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Alan_Turing#Quotes

↳ reply 3 — betterunix2:

> Genuinely a massive moment in human history

Is it? It looks more like a forgettable moment to me. We're talking about an IPO, how many headline-making IPOs can you actually remember?

> as a SWE the gravy train is basically over in my view

That is not a result of the IPO even if you are right, and I have my doubts.

> they figured out how to make a program that does the job

No they figured out how to make software that makes the job easier. How is this any different from the introduction of optimizing compilers or type systems or any of the other software tools we all use? It makes programmers more productive, which means programmers can take on larger projects.

Coding agents have limits and the managers who forced their SWEs to use them are starting to figure that out. Using agents to both write code and review code sounds cool in theory but in practice it is not such a great idea -- it means that nobody actually understands the codebase and therefore nobody can actually debug the code when things break. No, you cannot just assume that you can also throw an agent at the problem when things break -- because the breakage might mean you lost access to the agent or the agent lost access to your system and cannot help you.

> difficult to grasp how much life will change in the coming years

Not too difficult to grasp. Shareholders will demand returns and Anthropic will have to deliver those returns. All the sky-high dreams about RSI and the next phase of human existence are going to evaporate and profit is going to be front and center.

Another possibility: Anthropic fails to survive the next recession and the companies that did not allow their employees to become dependent on Claude will be the winners.

item.title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
item.description: 656 points, 308 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (macanorak.com)

→ HN comments  ·  656 points  ·  308 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — natch:

Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. People will point out that your key is created on your device, lives on your device, and never leaves your device, but that is just your key. Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with. There can be other parties (UK government) with their own KEK that opens a copy of the actual key. In this scenario, Apple can have no access to a KEK that opens the actual key, but they are forced to make the wording change they did, if they want to stay honest.

I say the statement is arguably deceptive because it presents the same feel of assurance that the old one did, to most people.

Note John Ternus in a recent event (WWDC keynote if I recall correctly) used the old wording. I think this was a slip-up (I’d hate to think it was a calculated lie posing as a slip-up).

↳ reply 1 — happyopossum:

This is just not true. Apple's current platform security white paper clearly states what you're complaining they took away:

"many Apple services use end-to-end encryption, which means the user’s iCloud data can be accessed only by the users themselves, and only from the trusted devices where they are signed in with their Apple Account."

And: " If a user chooses to turn on Advanced Data Protection, their trusted devices retain sole access to the encryption keys"

Also, there's no need to make suppositions such as this: > Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with.

The details of keys are clearly outlined in the same white paper: "Most iCloud data is first encrypted on the user’s device, using device-generated iCloud keys, before being uploaded to iCloud servers."

So no - there's no layer of keys that Apple or the UK or whatever can use to bypass e2e where it's enabled.

↳↳ reply — kps:

> "If a user chooses to turn on Advanced Data Protection, their trusted devices retain sole access to the encryption keys"

The implication is that if a user does not “choose to turn on” Advanced Data Protection, then something else also has access to their encryption keys.

Users in the UK cannot “choose to turn on” Advanced Data Protection.

↳↳↳ reply — TimTheTinker:

> if a user does not “choose to turn on” Advanced Data Protection, then something else also has access to their encryption keys

That's exactly the case. Without it, Apple Support, anyone with a valid warrant/subpoena, insider threats, successful phishers, etc. could access iCloud data.

Previously, Apple did not support E2EE for user data in iCloud, but later added it - that's what "Advanced Data Protection" is, after all.

But I believe when it was introduced, it was a news item (not from Apple, but from industry watchers) that it wasn't available in the UK, likely because of UK laws that harm privacy. It is the foremost surveillance state after China and North Korea, after all.

↳ reply 2 — s3p:

This isn't related to the article, and it's not true? iCloud ADP still exists in its original form, there was no modification allowing 3rd parties access to ADP decryption keys.

↳ reply 3 — raxxorraxor:

I think the wording should explicitly say that third parties can access your data if that is the case.

Top #2 — fweimer:

Primary source: https://investigatorypowerstribunal.org.uk/judgement/1-mr-vi...

The key finding seems to be that the media learned of the technical capability notice through confidential security briefings, and not a leak (“one of those irregular verbs”).

The contents of the note remains secret for now.

↳ reply — exe34:

"I give confidential press briefings; you leak; he's been charged under Section 2a of the Official Secrets Act".

↳↳ reply — Y_Y:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotive_conjugation

↳↳↳ reply — peterclary:

https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0751832/quotes/?item=qt0174103

Top #3 — puppycodes:

Sorta thought this was alreay common knowledge? Unfortunately the UK has never respected privacy or free speech as a right.

↳ reply 1 — ChrisRR:

The US has really been fed some propaganda about the UK making out as if the UK population is being silenced at every turn. The US has laws against inciting violence just like the UK does

item.title: Pete warden on local AI, open models, voice interfaces, the future of hardware
item.description: 250 points, 222 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (thedataexchange.media)

→ HN comments  ·  250 points  ·  222 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — lrvick:

I run 8x r9700s at home which lets me run up to 2x 1M context sessions of GLM 5.3 flash at ~50tps or 12x sessions of qwen 3.8 flash next at ~100tps.

I exclusively use this setup for all AI usage from fixing obscure reproducibility bugs in software that once took me weeks, to compiler bugs, to kernel hardening and hardware drivers, to building a complete unprivileged and security hardened replacement for systemd in rust. Most of that was done using Qwen 27b back when I had only 2x r9700s.

There is literally not a single problem I have faced in 25 years of systems engineering that I cannot solve now 10x+ faster using my local LLM setup.

I turned down the free OpenAI and Anthropic tokens in my YC batch because I have absolutely no interest in being reliant on third parties to do my job.

↳ reply 1 — lrvick:

For those asking in threads. 4x r9700s will cost about 6-8k depending on how patient you are with ebay auctions.

From there any motherboard and CPU that can give you 4x slots of 16x Gen 5 P2P capable PCIe slots positioned such that you can install 4x cards is probably fine. Ideally with a CPU capable of memory encryption.

My latest pairing is a ASUS Pro WS W890E-SAGE SE For $800 open box, and a Xeon 654 for $1300. My first build was an AMD EPYC rig for similar cost a few months ago using a Gigabyte ME03-PE0 and a AMD EPYC Siena 8224P for about 2k combined. I specifically wanted one amd and one intel machine for reproducible build diversity which most probably do not care about.

Do not get too attached to specific cpus and boards. Get what is available for cheap with the needed pcie bandwidth open box on ebay from reputable sellers to save thousands of dollars.

Be sure to get a power supply that can handle all 4 cards. I run Silverstone Hela 2500s at about $800. Do not go cheap on power supplies. It will end in pain. Can confirm.

Then 2-3k for 64gb in DDR5 RDIMMs. This is the most painful thing to purchase but it is what it is.

Not only do I recommend this setup, I plan to build more of them to share with my team.

If you are patient and buy used, a 10k budget can get you a very powerful local AI rig running 100% FOSS software/drivers even today.

↳↳ reply — gravypod:

Would you be willing to buy a kill-a-watt meter and posting the power usage of such systems? I am thinking of building something like this eventually and would love to know if I'm going to trip breakers.

↳↳↳ reply — lrvick:

Rack has a dedicated power meter and runs about 1kwh average but spikes to 1.5 so more than one residential outlet can support.

I initially had to distribute across circuits to avoid tripping breakers, but in the end I just had a dedicated 50a 240v sub-panel installed just for the server rack.

Biggest problem is heat, but 3d printing a bunch of 3U panels that hold 3x 120mm fans each for the back of the rack so I can fully close it without thermal throttle issues.

↳ reply 2 — mportela:

Kudos, my friend! This is the real hacker way, in the old school sense of the word. Feels like going from proprietary programming languages to open-source ones.

It's a shame how expensive it is to run this rig for now, but I guess the hardware will eventually catch up and get cheaper over time.

↳ reply 3 — wez470:

How cost effective had it been? I don't want to rely on 3rd parties either, but my experience is it's super expensive to run locally versus using a provider (both in terms of hardware costs and ongoing electricity usage).

Top #2 — giancarlostoro:

If Nvidia didnt abandon consumer GPUs we all could be running better models locally by now. The moat is companies like Nvidia not releasing better consumer hardware so they can partner with bigger companies so they can sell us overpriced hardware.

They release a new RTX series every two years, last time was 2022. (edit: I mistakenly quoted the year wrong, not sure why, but it seems obvious to most that Nvidia doesn't care about the local consumer market anymore)

Meanwhile major AI companies are investing in their own chips, if Nvidia wants to survive they really should not abandon consumers.

Hoping AMD steps up to the plate. Meanwhile the nextXbox and PlayStation consoles are going to have a rough time with their next consoles which will likely cost a thousand dollars or more is my gut feeling.

↳ reply 1 — Tuna-Fish:

GPU-style platforms (lots of compute connected to a big shared pipe that connects to a large pool of fast memory) are inherently more efficient for centralized inference.

Local inference gets truly interesting when the proper next-gen, natively AI and not just a repurposed GPU, stuff starts to land. Initially things like compute-in-memory and fancy flash, and later possibly the truly exotic stuff like various RMM (read-mostly-ram, for example stacked FeFET on logic) tech.

IMO there is no chance for ubiquitous local AI to happen if that means people using GPUs. But the industry is chasing all possible solutions for more efficient inference platforms, and if something like pachinko machine architecture with FeFETs ends up winning, suddenly buying a local ai inference solution in a box is no longer as insane.

↳ reply 2 — winwang:

If consumers were willing to pay more for GPUs like datacenters do, NVIDIA would have sold plenty of consumer GPUs. Or would you press a button to halve your revenue for some reason?

(I say this as someone who would have liked a 5090...)

Top #3 — paxy:

I don't see any difference between the conversations around self-hosting local AI and self-hosting regular software, which have been going on for decades.

Yes, there are a hundred valid reasons to self-host. But 99%+ of consumers aren't going to care.

People don't even care when the cost of hosting is ~free, like a simple home server. How many are ready to buy thousands of dollars worth of AI hardware, which could very well be obsolete a couple of years from now?

↳ reply 1 — abdullahkhalids:

One of my favorite stats is that Limewire used to be installed on 1/3rd of computers worldwide [1], i.e. people were self-hosting.

Why? Because Limewire was easy enough to install that even grandma could do it. There is not a single way to self-host even a simple html website without learning half a dozen software skills. People will self-host when it is click-and-play.

[1] https://marquettewire.org/3777966/tribune/marquee/the-life-a...

↳↳ reply — rockostrich:

> There is not a single way to self-host even a simple html website without learning half a dozen software skills.

1. Set up port forwarding on your router

2. Open a terminal

3. Run `python -m http.server 8000` in the directory with the html file

I'm not sure you could really count any of those 3 as software skills, but even if you count all 3 it's still half as many as you said it would take.

↳↳↳ reply — abdullahkhalids:

I encourage you to explain this to a 60+ year old person or a 15 year old who have never used a computer to do anything except edit office documents, watch movies, or browse the internet.

Then grab a windows XP computer from 2008 and explain to them how to install and use Limewire. You will see the difference.

↳ reply 2 — nsbk:

Hard disagree. I'm running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next using Strata on a Mac Studio and it covers all my needs. One drag and drop install. Nothing like self-hosting your email.

item.title: Cooling buildings is overtaking heating them as an energy need, IEA says
item.description: 161 points, 110 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (maccus.fr)

→ HN comments  ·  161 points  ·  110 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — nikodunk:

This is an ok development in my opinion because cooling buildings with heat pumps or AC overlaps the demand curve with the solar production curve better than heating does.

Heating tends to be during shorter days and less solar production, making it trickier to cover the power needs with new energy alone.

Of course this doesn’t mean heating is going down, just that cooling is going up (unless populations are moving to warmer climes).

↳ reply 1 — mixdup:

>cooling buildings with heat pumps or AC overlaps the demand curve with the solar production curve better than heating does.

>Heating tends to be during shorter days and less solar production, making it trickier to cover the power needs with new energy alone.

This is a key issue with renewables, particularly solar. At summer peaks, the electric demand peaks at the part of the day with the highest solar production (mostly). It's hot when the sun is at the maximum. This isn't 100% true because the peak is actually a little later when people get home from work, but close enough

In the winter peak, it's usually coldest early early in the morning when it's been dark for hours and people start to wake up but the sun isn't up producing solar yet

↳↳ reply — kube-system:

> This isn't 100% true because the peak is actually a little later when people get home from work, but close enough

Also because of the thermal mass of buildings themselves.

↳ reply 2 — TremendousJudge:

well, climate is getting warmer in general, so in a sense populations are actually moving to warmer climates. heating is probably going up anyway, but less than it would be if there was no global warming

↳ reply 3 — boothby:

Notably, heating a building adds heat to the local environment (heat your house and your neighbourhood gets warmer). Also, cooling a building adds heat to the environment (cool your house and your neighbourhood gets warmer).

> unless populations are moving to warmer climes

Rather: warmer climes are moving to populations

Top #2 — mw888:

What's this headline mean?

That everywhere is warmer now so we need more cooling? (Implies global warming)

That developing countries need more cooling than heat? (Buried lead)

That datacenters make up the majority of new demand? (Misleading headline)

I see many comments here assuming it means continuous energy needs. From the article, we see the headline implies my second question:

> That growth comes mostly from hot countries that are getting richer.

↳ reply — warmwaffles:

More like the demand for air conditioning in Europe is increasing.

↳↳ reply — thinkcontext:

It is but its still pretty low, last year the whole EU installed less than Japan. China is by far and away the leading installer.

Top #3 — torginus:

The great news is that its usually only hot when the suns out, and AC units can be run from solar panels essentially for free. So we can sit in our air conditioned rooms without having to feel guilty for killing the planet.

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

Electricity demand peaks after sunset in many markets.

It's called the Duck Curve because the graph kind of looks like a duck if you squint https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duck_curve

It's a familiar problem to everyone in the energy industry. Solar alone isn't enough, you also need energy storage to time-shift the generation and the load.

On an individual scale, if you're into home automation you can do some tricks like pre-cooling the house below your target temperature while you're gone for the day. At one house where we had significant excess solar I briefly entertained the idea of having a cooling vent into the attic to try to make that space cold on days with excess generation available during the day.

↳↳ reply — bob1029:

> I briefly entertained the idea of having a cooling vent into the attic to try to make that space cold on days with excess generation available during the day.

My attic has spray foam insulation and the HVAC system (also in the attic) already does this to a mild extent. I can go up there in the middle of an August day and not feel it at all.

Allowing the ceiling above your living space to reach 140F+ starts to get into radiative heating issues. You don't need to cool the attic to 72F. Anything would make a huge difference. Radiative heating scales quartically with temperature.

https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/articles/unvented-cond...

↳↳↳ reply — Aurornis:

Insulation should be a high priority, of course.

My idea was to use excess electricity generation to cool the attic somewhat below the temperature of the living space. That space would then sink some heat after the sun went down, reducing the cooling demands in the evening.

An analogous idea would be to have a large water tank in the basement with a chiller attached. You run the chiller when you have excess electricity to get the water colder than the house, then let it passively soak up heat later.

It was all shower thoughts, but the idea of storing excess energy generation during peak as coldness (wording which makes pedants cringe) for evening cooling is not new. You can pre-cool your entire house, but having to wear a sweater for a couple hours every day during the summer is not fun after a while.

↳ reply 2 — __MatrixMan__:

The less great news is that solar panel efficiency drops as temperatures climb. Peak solar power generation is in spring and fall for this reasons.

item.description: 310 points, 61 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (krthr.co)

→ HN comments  ·  310 points  ·  61 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — staplung:

For the curious, the generalized process of reordering and potentially rotating pages so that when printed and folded (and optionally gathered into signatures) is called impositioning. There is specialized software with a variety of options that will do this for an input document.

Bookbinder JS is a nice web-based tool that will do this for you too, though I'm not sure it covers the exact folding algorithm described in this article.

https://momijizukamori.github.io/bookbinder-js/

↳ reply 1 — compiler-guy:

Similarly, the term printers use for a sheet that has been printed after imposition is a "signature". Sometimes called a "sig" for short.

The result of the imposition here would be considered an "eight-up sig", because you get eight usable pages on one side.

Books and magazines are typically bound from several signatures.

↳ reply 2 — remyp:

Thanks, I had no idea it was called that. I guess you could say I didn't expect the imposition.

Top #2 — addled:

My high school geometry teacher would let us use an index card of notes during exams.

She had a student years prior show her this folding technique and asked if he could use it for the test. Not only did she allow it, but she taught it to every class going forward for those that wanted to put in the extra effort.

My buddies and I spent so much time trying to come up with modifications to use more area of the page. Some of them even worked!

↳ reply 1 — raudette:

I loved the whole idea of the 'cheat sheet', and seeing my kids put them together - I'm not in education, but I suspect the value of the cheat sheet is having the students make them, its essentially material review (vs say for example "open book" or "supplied formula sheet").

↳↳ reply — burningChrome:

Its interesting, I worked as a TA in the early aughts helping teach what was an intro to anthropology class. When I allowed a double sided 4X6 notecard, students did reliably well. When you didn't allow the 'cheat sheet' I would still find scraps of paper that had notes on them after tests. A majority of the time, the notes just had bad or incorrect information on them.

I just figured the students who scored well when I allowed the cheatsheet took their time rehashing and reviewing the information for the test so it stuck with them better. When students were just trying to cheat and rushing to get what they thought was going to be on the test, it was almost always wrong.

Interesting experience for sure.

↳ reply 2 — ohlookcake:

How did folding allow access to more area of the page? Unless I've misunderstood something, it should just be the same area folded up in booklet form?

Top #3 — knlb:

↳ reply — WillAdams:

Similarly, I would fold a legal-sized sheet of paper so that it would fit in a small leather notepad case I use as a pocket blotter --- it's very handy and a lot less expensive than custom notecards or even an equivalent of index cards.

item.title: Unblockable communication with gravity
item.description: 165 points, 64 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (science.org)

→ HN comments  ·  165 points  ·  64 comments  ·  comments as of 22h

Top #1 — aetherspawn:

It seems like they missed the opportunity to put the big heavy thing on a rotating disk and then encode the data as changes in velocity (frequency domain) which is way easier to do than an elevator, especially with a PM motor. This is basically FM vs AM.

Intuitively if the thing is heavy enough it should have decent range, for example humans can “feel” an object of 100 tons spinning at decent distances one way or another. Not sure if this is a gravity phenomena or a vibrational one though. The rising/falling edges will be even more detectable than the mass itself, and intuitively increasing the energy level (speed) might increase the range? Wondering how far that scales, for example does it scale to 100,000 rpm - several megawatts? Can it be detected 1km away at that energy?

↳ reply — hnuser123456:

Humans would only feel vibration through the ground. On top of that, you can only directly "feel" gravitational waves by having a heavier, more stable point of reference. By its nature, you cannot feel your own acceleration due to gravity, unless there's macroscopic changes in the field across the size of your body, which requires being next to a black hole or neutron star.

Some of the most precise clocks can detect elevation differences of 1cm or less based on varying speed of time at varying depths in the gravity well, but our biology cannot.

Gravity is so weak, that if you were standing on an asteroid less than about 10 miles wide, you'd be able to jump to escape velocity with your legs.

Top #2 — marmakoide:

Would it be easy to jam the signal ?

Say, you have a big, heavy double pendulum moving close to the emitter. The moving mass would disturb the signal, and predicting the evolution of a double pendulum is not easy due to its instability (it's not periodic for example, so no Fourier analysis)

↳ reply 1 — cryptonector:

> Would it be easy to jam the signal ?

The answer has got to be yes.

↳ reply 2 — cvoss:

> While this communication method cannot be passively blocked in the manner of EM shielding, it can, in principle, be affected by active signal degradation strategies. A malicious actor, Mallory, could attempt to jam the signal by moving other nearby masses or generating environmental vibrations, reducing the SNR at Bob’s gravimeter.

Top #3 — DavidSJ:

The key idea seems to be:

Since mass cannot be negative, there is no gravitational analog of charge cancelation and hence no way to hide or screen the presence of mass.

Perhaps they address this in the paper, but it occurs to me that the obvious countermeasure is to shield with a large positive mass, and then to selectively remove some of this mass to cancel the attempted message.

↳ reply 1 — tomxor:

> Perhaps they address this in the paper, but it occurs to me that the obvious countermeasure is to shield with a large positive mass, and then to selectively remove some of this mass to cancel the attempted message.

It is, about 1/3rd down the page, they distinguish passive from active degradation:

> While this communication method cannot be passively blocked in the manner of EM shielding, it can, in principle, be affected by active signal degradation strategies. A malicious actor, Mallory, could attempt to jam the signal by moving other nearby masses or generating environmental vibrations, reducing the SNR at Bob’s gravimeter. Mallory could also attempt to locally block (spoof) Alice’s signal by moving a nearby mass so as to counteract (reproduce) the change in gravitational field at Bob’s location. In this case, Bob would observe a modified or misleading signal rather than the one generated by Alice.

> In a more elaborate scenario, Mallory could attempt to block the signal entirely by constructing the gravitational analog of a Faraday cage. This would require surrounding either Alice or Bob with a continuous distribution of controllable mass and dynamically reconfiguring it in response to Alice’s motion so as to cancel at all times. Such an arrangement, while not forbidden by physics, would require Mallory to have extraordinary capabilities with regard to control and coordination of mass distributions. We explore this possibility further in the Supplementary Materials.

↳ reply 2 — markhahn:

and the quoted statement doesn't actually follow, since there is a gravitational analog of cancellation: movement of mass on the opposite side of the receiving gravimeter. the opponent needs to know the receiver's location, but you can use a "phased array" of counter-emitters to zero the signal. or make it anything you want.

Top #1 — black3r:

The very first referenced issue in that PR discussion sheds a bit more light on this: https://github.com/adoptium/adoptium-support/issues/1480

This PR's author says there on October 1st: "Got an email from Oracle asking me to NOT proceed with a PR until receiving approval." and then on October 28th: "It's taken over by Oracle. Nothing required from us."

↳ reply 1 — mzs:

should have known at this point it's a potential security issue and maybe the AI regurgitated this:

https://github.com/adoptium/adoptium-support/issues/1480#iss...

edit: also oracle is big enough to have one of every modern gen to test on

↳↳ reply — pron:

We did know it was a potential security risk, and that is why it was handled exactly how security-sensitive issues are supposed to be handled (not to mention that the reporter is a well-respected OpenJDK contributor and former Oracle colleague).

I don't know if people here understand how these things need to be done in the most important and critical open source projects, such as Linux or OpenJDK, but there are two things you must not do when an issue is suspected to be a risk until you've researched the matter and decided on a backport and release strategy: You shouldn't communicate publicly, and you absolutely shouldn't merge a patch.

↳↳↳ reply — guiambros:

> You shouldn't communicate publicly, and you absolutely shouldn't merge a patch.

I (still) agree, but I don't think these rules will be valid for much longer, though.

With new models capable of finding vulnerabilities faster than ever before, if you (or your AI) was able to find a critical bug, it's only a matter of time that the bad guys will also discover it - if they haven't already.

Human skill and ingenuity used to be the limiting factor, so it was the universal equalizer. Now the game depends on how many tokens you want to throw at the problem, and there are many bad actors with incentives to outspend every white hacker out there.

Responsible disclosure will still be important, of course, but timelines will need to be compressed into days, instead of months.

↳ reply 2 — znpy:

I’m usually a java supporter because i have fond memories of working with it and great experiences from working with high throughput/low latency stuff written in java… HOWEVER: I’ll frame that comment as a smoking gun the next time somebody says java is fully independent from oracle (btw this used to also be me, but i clearly have to change my position)

Top #2 — dlor:

I also found this independently ahead of disclosure and reported it to Oracle last Friday. My harness found it after a fuzzing run and then turned it into a full RCE chain in the target app I was actually scanning.

The harness itself doesn't run with Internet access and I confirmed it didn't access this PR directly, but who knows if this was in the training set itself.

Either way, these simultaneous disclosures are incredibly common now. The Ruby issue affecting Gitlab was not only known about for 6 months, it was publicly fixed for 6 months before someone turned it into an RCE. The fix sat on the Ruby dev branch, and it was never pulled into an actual Ruby release until after Gitlab disclosed their own 10.0 vulnerability through it.

It's very common for reporters to not realize the impact of a bug, models are very good at turning bugs into RCE chains, and the volume everywhere now means security teams are basically only focused on RCEs.

↳ reply — AlexCoventry:

Which model were you using?

↳↳ reply — dlor:

Mythos 5.2

Top #3 — wood_spirit:

So the implication is that the LLM that assisted the Calif researchers might have read this previous bug report and not independently discovered it?

↳ reply 1 — dlenski:

I don't think that's a reasonable implication at all.

There are lots of bugs in lots of software, and lots of them get ignored when reported.

I personally aware of multiple security vulnerabilities in major pieces of software that everyone has heard of, which I very quickly and easily stumbled on while working on this software as an AWS engineer several years ago. I had never used an LLM of any kind at the time.

I presented my findings both internally and externally, and the reactions ranged from shrugs to delays to hostility towards me for "getting distracted" or "being overly negative."

Those bugs that I discovered still exist, last time I checked.

↳↳ reply — larodi:

> I don't think that's a reasonable implication at all.

the contrary is very likely thing the agent may have done, given they... like agents dig the web, don't they. and if im a security researcher digging through Oracle's shit, the open issues sure does look a good starting point.

↳ reply 2 — cryptonector:

Idk that u/notmine1337 meant that. I have questions:

- why was this not a secure vulnerability report, why was it public?

- why was this closed [by the submitter]?

For the second question, I suspect it's because they were told a different fix was coming.

Top #1 — c-fe:

Within my friend group, we also switched now to Matrix. One of us is hosting it on their server, and we also use ElementX as clients. We did this to try get away from lack of privacy on Whatsapp and Telegram. It was also fun to tinker around with a selfhosted solution.

In particular I love that I can now share my live location with this friendgroup and be very confident that noone is harvesting this data. With whatsapp, I was always very uneasy allowing live location access.

Apart from one friend having issues receiving notifications, overall, we are having a positive experiene on ElementX/Matrix. I like especially how clean and well designed the iOS App looks. It simple and it just works.

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

> Apart from one friend having issues receiving notifications, overall, we are having a positive experiene on ElementX/Matrix.

My experience started like this: Good at first, but there was a slow burn of people encountering random issues with no clear solution. Fixing the first few was a team effort. Then everyone starts to get tired of debugging the latest issue someone has. Then that person needs to talk to someone so they talk on another platform, with others following over time.

Group chat is a product where it has to work for everyone in the group. Unless you have a dedicated IT person for the group who will tirelessly solve everyone’s problems for them when they don’t have time or energy to do it, the slow attrition from random problems either splits the group or nudges everyone to an easier platform.

I hope they’ve made progress on fixing some of the random issues and user unfriendly sharp edges over time because it could be a great platform.

Because, otherwise, even if you went crazy and did the most naive implementation:

    Storing for every User
    User -> List <User Contacts>
And the reverse: User -> List<Users who have you as contact>

↳ reply 1 — burnte:

↳ reply 2 — lnxg33k1:

https://www.aikido.dev/blog/critical-vulnerabilities-in-php-...

https://www.aikido.dev/blog/php-security-release-19-november... ( from today)

Top #2 — beberlei:

Most excited about the ZTS overhead reduction. If you are unfamiliar PHP can run either with or without thread safety (think using pthreads in PHP requests).

If the overhead can be further reduced (and people have ideas) then it could be that we only need ZTS mode anymore in the future and that can open up one avenue for PHP to get native async support similar to the existing parallel extension: https://github.com/krakjoe/parallel

More "hands-on" is the stream error handling improvements. This greatly improves the old file stream APIs to now allow throwing exceptions instead of returning false on errors:

  $context = stream_context_create([
    'stream' => [
        'error_mode' => StreamErrorMode::Exception,
    ],
  ]);

  try {
    $config = file_get_contents('/etc/app/config.json', context: $context);
  } catch (StreamException $e) {
    // handle error
  }

↳ reply 1 — jmyeet:

Spawning threads in PHP is a mistake. The beauty of PHP is that a given request is single-threaded. Any IO/network bound calls allow off-thread code within that same async-await model. If you want to spawn threads, put it in an extension.

↳↳ reply — whalesalad:

you are assuming that the work is happening inside of an http request context. what about background tasks? workers? cli tooling? etc.

↳ reply 2 — calvinmorrison:

That's certainly a use case but I worry async opens the door for all the non PHP to come on in

Top #3 — p4bl0:

I'm a bit sad that there's still no way to limit the number of arguments of a user-defined function in the type system. The internal functions have that.

I know that introducing such a behavior by default could break existing code, but it seems relatively easy to introduce this feature in a backward compatible way by using the void type. For example :

    function foo (void) {}
    foo(42); // fatal error: foo() expects exactly 0 arguments, 1 given

    function bar ($a, $b, void) {}
    bar(1, 2, 3); // fatal error: bar() expects exactly 2 arguments, 3 given

    function baz ($a, $b=null, void) {}
    baz(1, 2, 3); // fatal error: baz() expects at most 2 arguments, 3 given

> I know that introducing such a behavior by default could break existing code

Specifically because older versions of PHP didn't have "..." arguments - variadic functions used func_get_args() to access their arguments.

item.title: Do not buy RAM, compress
item.description: 260 points, 210 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (curiousbits.nl)

→ HN comments  ·  260 points  ·  210 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — varenc:

As others have said, macOS does this by default and it's quite impressive. I have a long running daemon with a memory leak. By its nature, the leaking memory is very repetitive and easily compressed. Right now this daemon has tried to claim 2.5GB of memory, but it's been compressed to a mere 450MB of actual memory! And because it's a memory leak, it never accesses this old stuff, so it never gets decompressed. Only 20MB of RAM is held that isn't compressed.

Of course, it would be far better to just not have the memory leak...but in the mean time, macOS memory compression is making the leak nearly a none issue.

↳ reply 1 — cpeterso:

A new take on the OOM killer: if a long-running daemon hasn't touched some heap pages for a very long time, perhaps the OS could assume it is leaked and unmap the pages. If the daemon tries to access that memory, let it crash.

↳↳ reply — kevincox:

This sounds like a bad idea. No one has logged in via SSH for a while so the daemon hasn't touched any pages (or only pre-auth relevant pages) then when you log in it gets killed. Or if someone sends a rarely used request to an HTTP server then it crashes accessing some data unique to that request.

Sure, they will get restarted, but not great.

↳↳↳ reply — cxr:

It's a good example of perverse outcomes. Rather than simply following the contract and functioning correctly, we would be:

going through extra effort to accommodate/enable buggy, poorly behaving programs, and meanwhile—

punishing those (and the programmers of those) that are well-behaved and functioning exactly as intended but that now have to contend with evading some heuristic of badness.

↳ reply 2 — davidkwast:

It's like having a room that shrinks everything to 1/5th of its size but you never come back to get anything. It will work until gets full.

↳ reply 3 — fl0ki:

The BackRAMs

Top #2 — Lio:

RAM compression sounds very useful but the thing I really need extra RAM for is local inference.

Since the models are effectively highly compressed data already my assumption is that RAM compression won't help improve that much (I'm assuming unified memory here as per the Framework Desktop). A bit like trying to compress a JPEG in a zip file.

Could anyone comment on that?

↳ reply 1 — vlovich123:

You are correct, compression doesn’t help reduce a model. That’s why quantization is inherently a lossy operation although there’s tricks to limit the perceived loss. That’s the only way to further compress the data.

One way to think about it is that if the weights were compressible, it’s a clear signal that better training could make the model smarter as there’s redundant information in the structure that could be used to store other meaning.

The other challenge with compressing weights of course is that you have to decompress them before you do math with them. Dequantizing weights is significantly cheaper and supports random access too (not that that matters too much but it helps in terms of leveraging SIMD techniques to do it in an embarrassingly parallel way)

↳ reply 2 — matja:

> A bit like trying to compress a JPEG in a zip file

Interesting comparison, I wonder if there are loss-less compression schemes that are "weight-aware", about the statistical properties of model weights.

Back to that line - because (Huffman coded) JPEG images can be lossless recoded using arithmetic coding, which makes them smaller than if they were compressed with the best general-purpose compression algorithms/tools (e.g. `jpegtran -arithmetic < input.jpg > output.jpg` beats `xz -9 < input.jpg > output.jpg`). AC takes advantage of the properties of the image coding better than general-purpose compression tools on the output of the Huffman coding.

Top #3 — hedgehog:

As others have noted zswap is usually a better choice than zram, additionally depending on your situation it may be worth checking which algorithm it's using as there are a few choices (zstd, lz4, etc) and the defaults vary by distro. zstd is the right choice IMO unless you're in a situation where you know better.

↳ reply 1 — seabrookmx:

I have a Framework 13 (AMD, 16GB) running Ubuntu. After some struggles with heavy multitasking, I bumped the default swapfile from 4->16GB and enabled zswap with zstd. I basically don't think about RAM usage anymore. It's been working flawlessly.

zswap actually compresses the memory _in RAM_ (just like zram) first before swapping it, so you actually get more runway out of it before it hits the disk. But you still can spill over to the disk when necessary.

↳ reply 2 — deathanatos:

My frustration with zswap is that, when content is spilled to disk-based swap, it gets decompressed. There is, AFAICT, no way to have compressed swap¹ on Linux.

(¹on disk. A lot of these "z[foo]" projects are compressed memory.)

item.title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite
item.description: 265 points, 69 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (zerodha.tech)

→ HN comments  ·  265 points  ·  69 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — anacrolix:

I spent years trying to squeeze this use case out of sqlite. All roads lead to tears, it is not made for this use case.

I wrote https://github.com/anacrolix/possum for this exact use case. It has a few rough edges but it absolutely hauls ass for caching on disk. Incidentally it uses sqlite for transaction/TTL metadata which is more suited to sqlite but it's still the bottleneck.

sqlite transaction commit overhead is too high and uncompetitive without batching but it's a design flaw specific to being multiprocess.

↳ reply 1 — mbreese:

Yeah, I'm not sure how well this will work. I've always dealt with data blobs with data on the filesystem (or s3), metadata in the database. Anything else starts to get a bit too much like a filesystem in a database, which has lead many smart people to tears.

Or is there a better way?

↳ reply 2 — mightyham:

At the end of the day durable transaction commit in any OLTP database will always be slow because fsync is an expensive operation (~1000 IOPS on a decent SSD), so as you mentioned batching is the only way to make significant increases to throughput. That said, based on assorted benchmarks I've seen online, sqlite doesn't even get close to max fsync IOPS because it has a ton of overhead. Other embedded systems like rocksdb or lmdb are going to give better performance.

↳ reply 3 — adev_:

> Incidentally it uses sqlite for transaction/TTL metadata which is more suited to sqlite but it's still the bottleneck.

Why sqlite instead of RocksDB ?

What you need at the end of the day for a blob storage is a transactional key value store.

Which RocksDB will give you with much better throughput (and latency) and solves your transaction problem.

Top #2 — sgarland:

> What we learned along the way… Deleting rows doesn’t shrink SQLite files

This is true of every RDBMS I am aware of. It would be horribly inefficient to constantly run page merges in order to be able to free some of them.

Whenever I read things on posts that are a. discussed in documentation b. should be apparent from first principles, I immediately lose faith in the product.

↳ reply 1 — tomasol:

Everybody learns. Coming from other databases it might not be obvious that you need to enable vacuum explicitly.

↳↳ reply — sgarland:

In other databases, you also don't get the space back (mostly [0]). Postgres requires VACUUM FULL (or REPACK CONCURRENTLY, as of Pg19), and MySQL requires OPTIMIZE TABLE, neither of which is commonly done.

This is my point; if you're coming from other databases, it should be obvious that you don't get space back unless you ask for it.

0: Postgres can, under the specific circumstance of pages at the end of a table being completely empty, release them back to the OS with a normal VACUUM.

↳ reply 2 — ★ simonw:

The problem with that attitude is that you're actively encouraging people to not talk about things they've just learned that might be obvious, for fear of being judged negatively by people like you. That harms the discourse.

Top #3 — sneilan1:

Earlier in the blog post, Sarat writes about how many databases can't store multi-megabyte blobs. That makes sense to me but later on, he writes

> While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.

My question is, were the other databases not tried with compression on the application side?

item.title: Ruby2ßhell: Pre-authentication RCE on stock Rails
item.description: 385 points, 166 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (verialabs.com)

→ HN comments  ·  385 points  ·  166 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — circularfoyers:

Thought this was another vulnerability for a second, but for anyone else who thought the same, this is already covered in the Ruby advisory being discussed here https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50554038 (which covers six other vulnerabilities).

Top #2 — djha-skin:

I remember being a kid in a small town. My dad got into an auto accident, and the next day the DJs talked about it on the radio. Then we moved to the Chicago area and the morning news only ever talked about how many accidents we'd see that day on our theoretical morning commute during the traffic segment.

At what point will we stop considering individual x2shell ultra-critical CVEs news in the age of AI? Like, how many of these are we finding per hour?

Top #3 — barbegal:

More interested to see how you can use just a single byte overflow to trigger RCE. Definitely achievable but sounds tough.

↳ reply 1 — cyphar:

There was an even more restrictive single NUL byte heap overflow in glibc in 2014 that the ProjectZero folks managed to turn into ACE and thus an LPE in setuid binaries[1]. The final section that talks about bickering over exploitability seems particularly pertinent today.

[1]: https://projectzero.google/2014/08/the-poisoned-nul-byte-201...

↳ reply 2 — ★ tptacek:

The simplest core mechanism of these kinds of exploits is that you can groom the heap by triggering lots of similar-sized allocations, so you have a good guess as to what the heap will contain where your wild write occurs, and then you can trigger specific allocations to land juicy victim structs in the heap where you want them.

It's an evolution of the old "nop sled" idea from stack overflows (and viruses before that), where you don't know exactly what the stack addresses you're targeting are, but you can in your exploit trigger payload include data that will carpet bomb the stack with NOP instructions so that you have a big window to guess.

↳↳ reply — kyledrake:

I was under the impression that everyone adopted the OpenBSD randomized memory heap by default. Does this imply that it's not enough to prevent this sort of attack from working? If this is even slightly repeatable then the mechanism doesn't seem to be sufficiently random. I'm not an expert on low level memory allocation but at a high level it seems like we need to do a better job of randomizing the heap if this sort of thing is still possible.

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

All the heaps are (probably) randomized. I haven't seen an exploit for this (but know them to exist). ASLR is not a reliable countermeasure for these kinds of flaws. Here's a good starting point:

https://azeria-labs.com/grooming-the-ios-kernel-heap/

Also — cowlevel:

So the recent RCE wave seems to be people finding more single byte overflows and such, but reporting them as RCEs because AI can do the tedious grunt work of finding the rest of the vulnerability chain.

If any single byte overflow can be converted into an RCE with minimal human effort then we have no choice but to prove the whole software stack is memory safe.

↳ reply — boomlinde:

From my understanding it's only a single byte overflow if your payload only contains a single ß.

↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

No, from my read of the code, it's a single-byte overflow because the casing code works 1 character at a time and doesn't account for the ß->SS expansion case. Not only is it a single byte, but that single byte has a fixed value; you can't use ß->SS to push some other character off the end of the string.

(Correct me if I'm wrong!)

↳↳↳ reply 1 — boomlinde:

Yeah that seems right on a second look

↳↳↳ reply 2 — jascha_eng:

No this is correct I think. And it's not easy to control what lives next to that buffer. But AI probably can figure out a chain of requests that this then changes the length block of another object or flips a pointer or something, so it's tedious but can be used to escalate to basically arbitrary memory corruption. That's kinda the issue with AI, this would have been extremely tedious to exploit before LLMs but now anyone with an unlocked good enough model can do it.

That's why hiding the POC still helps a bit, because any model probably will require quite a bit of wall clock time to actually build one itself. Then making that work on e.g. a running gitlab instance with other traffic... much harder yet again I'd assume since that should alter memory state without you having control over it.

Still if someone builds an exploit with even 1% success rate they just need to run it on enough instances in parallel and will eventually break through some of them probably.

↳↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

Right, I'm not talking down the severity of the vulnerability; if anything I think people are underrating it. But it's a constrained 1-byte overflow.

Also — weinzierl:

There should be other codepoints other than ß that in principle could be used for a vulnerability like that. There are even ones that expand to three codepoints, like ffi.

↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

I went looking last night and found only the ß in Windows-1252.

Applying the speed impact to Gemini Carbon is particularly interesting, though, because it's the top model in our leaderboard when you exclude early votes (https://agentduel.com/leaderboard?excludeEarlyVotes=true) but mediocre when you let developers vote. ↳↳ reply — wasabi991011:

What makes something an "early vote" and a "developer vote", as opposed to just a "vote"? And what makes those categories meaningful to agent duel?

↳↳↳ reply — seizethecheese:

> What makes something an "early vote"

When you run agents in a battle, one always finishes first. We let users vote for the finished agent without waiting for the agent that's still working. This is contrary to typical Arena methodology (like Arena.ai) but I think it's appropriate for agents since they can take dramatically different amounts of time to finish tasks.

This is why DeepSeek 4.1 Flash is doing so well on our leaderboard, it's super fast and often sufficient.

> and a "developer vote"

This is confusing, sorry. Inspecting our data it's almost entirely people doing software developments with agents. It's just a vote.

This is a pivot from Bottomless (YC W19). That business is doing okay and funding our runway, in addition to fundraising back in 2021.

item.title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
item.description: 326 points, 126 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ruby-lang.org)

→ HN comments  ·  326 points  ·  126 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — ★ tptacek:

There's what I think is probably an awesome bug here.

Windows-1252 encoding has a representation for lowercase German sharp 's' (ß), but not one for the uppercase. If you upcase a string containing a sharp 's', it gets normalized to "SS", which increases the length of the string by one character. The 1252 case conversion code doesn't handle this; it looks like it checks for headroom in the buffer one character at a time. So if the last character of a string you upcase is ß, it looks like you get a one-byte overflow (of 'S').

If that's really the bug (there's a claimed RCE POC), the heap grooming for it must be really fussy! I couldn't find any other character pairs that expand like this.

You can feed strings in 1252 to a Rails program through multipart POSTs, which get to pick their encodings.

The great thing about this bug, apart from how it illustrates how doomed we all are (if I'm right), is that it should by rights have the best vulnerability name of the year, because you get to work 'ß' into it.

↳ reply 1 — ludovicianul:

In my API fuzzer I use a bunch of similar cases that can expand when lowered/uppered: https://github.com/Endava/cats/blob/master/src/main/java/com...

It's interesting how people start discovering these edge cases again, now that AI can be put to work to find vulnerabilities like this.

↳ reply 2 — bee_rider:

Haha, that exact character caused problems in a programming class I tutored for. Got to throw the first year students some curveballs.

↳ reply 3 — xp84:

↳↳↳ reply — eru:

↳ reply 4 — testplzignore:

↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

↳ reply 5 — dwattttt:

It must be noted though that Excel exports CSV as Windows-1252 by default in France (and other countries).Apps that ingest these files and run regexps over them are quite frequent.

↳ reply 6 — ykonstant:

↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

At this point I think we're pretty sure "I was right", though, like, I had a lot of hints to go off of here --- "Windows-1522" and "case change" were in the official notice!

Top #2 — pentestercrab:

  str = ("\x82\xA0" + ("A" * (2**32 + 4))).force_encoding(Encoding::Shift_JIS)
  
  puts "str.bytesize: #{str.bytesize}"
  puts "str.encoding: #{str.encoding}"
  puts "str.valid_encoding?: #{str.valid_encoding?}"
  
  new_str = str.downcase
  
  puts "new_str.bytesize: #{new_str.bytesize}"
  puts "new_str.bytes:    #{new_str.bytes}"
  puts "new_str.encoding: #{new_str.encoding}"
outputs on an unfixed version:

  str.bytesize: 4294967302
  str.encoding: Shift_JIS
  str.valid_encoding?: true
  new_str.bytesize: 6
  new_str.bytes:    [130, 160, 97, 97, 97, 97]

also I'd suggest you check out CVE-2026-128084 (GHSA-4fqr-96q8-xrfx) if you are interested in C bugs impacting Ruby on Rails

I'm worried that this can be used against a standard rails app somehow, as I'm sure there's regex parsing and downcasing somewhere in the stack.

However, if you need to do an operation on a malicious multi gb string to trigger this, it makes me slightly less concerned that regular rails apps are vulnerable.
