item.title: Software companies are trying to kill home computing?
item.description: 174 points, 141 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (lateblt.livejournal.com)

→ HN comments  ·  174 points  ·  141 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — EvanAnderson:

I think enthusiast computing is dying. Home users will be able to buy packaged laptops and some desktop PCs, but I think the era of enthusiasts building "gaming rigs" and such is coming to an end. I think it's being ushered out by a feedback loop of high prices driving market contraction and, in turn, driving prices even higher as demand shrinks. Gaming will move to real-time streaming and there won't be a need or a market for GPUs and high performance CPUs in the enthusiast market.

Home computing, in the context of having a marginally-powerful computer or phone / tablet with minimal storage and RAM in the home, will continue just fine. Subscriptions for storage and applications are already becoming the norm, and with the skyrocketing cost of storage the market for large capacity storage targeted at enthusiast and home users will dry up, too.

The industry wants users to rent everything.

Storage rental is particular pernicious, to me, because being able to store your personally-created works in a manner that maintains confidentiality is to cornerstone of digital sovereignty. Being forced to store your data in systems that will use your data for model training is definitely desired by the industry. If they can con users into renting that storage and giving up their data to model training so much the better.

↳ reply 1 — Exmoor:

> I think the era of enthusiasts building "gaming rigs" and such is coming to an end.

I've been hearing this for over two decades and yet gaming desktops are more mainstream than ever. Certainly the current market is negatively impacting pricing and availability, but those same factors are also pushing their competition just as hard. I'm not even sure cloud streamed games was a profitable idea when prices were sane, but it certainly isn't now.

↳↳ reply — cyberrock:

I think gaming desktops are mainstream but have a longer lifespan now, as AM4 and RTX10xx hardware is perfectly fine for most gamers who play Big Walk or Queen's Domain rather than 8k 240fps Forza. In contrast when I bought a $600 GPU in 2013 (outrageous price back then) it wouldn't be able to handle a medium quality 1080p game in 3 years. So I think both assessments are right: an enthusiast top end rig is more expensive but most gamers simply need less top end rigs every year.

↳↳↳ reply — dormento:

I was using a GTX1060 up until last year, and it still played pretty much everything on decent settings. PC hardware has been long lived for a while, in fact, I think this is one of the factors in the attacks on personal computing.

↳ reply 2 — webstrand:

I've never lived anywhere with low enough connection latency to accommodate real-time streaming of an action game, and my bare packet latency is 20ms to the nearest data-center (that I know of and can ping anyway). Add any latency in the input processing of the game, time to encode/transfer/decode the frame, and any local input latency on the client and you’re easily looking at an extra 50-100ms over playing locally, which is well into the range people can actually feel in anything twitchy. Turn-based or slower games would probably be fine, but I don’t see shooters or fighting games moving to streaming for anyone who doesn’t happen to live next door to a data center.

There might be some unexploited latency-masking tricks in client-side cursors and client-side reprojection (the timewarp trick some VR uses to rotate the camera without receiving a new frame), but I suspect the legacy internet connectivity of rural and suburban homes in america will be a serious barrier to widespread adoption of real-time streaming. If local hardware gets priced out of reach, it could rather mean the end of gaming as a widely accessible hobby instead of a switch to real-time streaming?

↳ reply 3 — Aurornis:

> I think it's being ushered out by a feedback loop of high prices driving market contraction and, in turn, driving prices even higher as demand shrinks.

Shrinking demand makes prices go down, not up.

Demand for gaming and consumer gear is higher than ever. Gaming GPUs were expensive before the AI boom. Remember when everyone was shocked that the 4090 was $1500 or the 5090 was $2000, but they were sold out anyway? Remember the extreme competition for 30 series GPUs and scalping before that?

I have yet to hear a good explanation for these beliefs that consumer PCs and gaming are going away, because they’re all driven by incorrect economic ideas (like shrinking demand raising prices) or fear imported from some other ideas, while ignoring the ever expanding market for gaming and consumer PC gear

Top #2 — chupchap:

This is a cycle. As of now the companies with server farms are buying up everything that can be manufactured, but this is not a forever model. The companies that are in the business of making things will always want to make more in the future and they will need to come back to general consumers to soak up that supply. The only question is how long it will take. I was hoping the GPU situation to normalise after the blockchain hype started to die out, but AI picked up that demand and shot it up to the stratosphere

↳ reply — asdff:

When all this is done, will general consumers even be interested in general purpose computers, vs say walled garden devices that can run their office apps and slack client? Will the hobbyist market of people building little linux home servers to run their containers or whatever be even large enough to justify investing in that sort of business at all? It is already a market where many people participating in it are buying hardware second hand, bevvied by the fact that enterprise has at least up till recently bought their own compute and replaced it every three years, creating plenty of constant inventory suplly of anything from capable enough clusterable i5 usff pcs to xeon powered rack servers.

But that was then, this is now. I've been realizing lately how perilous general purpose compute has been, and how much of its continued access depends on things remaining exactly as they've been for the last 25 years.

↳↳ reply — chupchap:

The market shifted to iPad centric back to laptop centric for work in the last decade and a half, so I still have some hope for change.

↳↳↳ reply — Gud:

The iPad never dethroned the laptop.

Top #3 — ivanjermakov:

Who is buying home computers besides gamers, students, and programmers? For general public smartphone does the job.

↳ reply 1 — pixelpoet:

"Does the job" implies an equivalence, which couldn't be further from the truth in the case of PC vs phones.

Smartphones are what's responsible for the death of the internet as a place where knowledgeable, can-do people congregated and built a free utopia together. Once the normie hordes arrived and the marketing / advertising / propaganda / doomscrolling / mindless passive consumption people completely hijacked their brains with things like Instagram, the good old internet promptly died, and was replaced with the VC money-soaked online world we have now.

Gamers don't buy computers anymore (despite their consoles being computers, they are completely uninterested in those capabilities, same as phone users), students don't have a clue about files and directories anymore, and as for programmers... as a lifelong low-level programming enthusiast, I'd better stop there.

↳↳ reply — kulahan:

For many, many people in particularly low-income brackets, a phone is literally their only access to computing if they’re not in school or somehow getting a free laptop from work (all traffic monitored by HR-attracting IT department). A large number of (at least public) sites take this into consideration and have very robust mobile sites.

↳ reply 2 — sodapopcan:

Ya, I was born in 1981. It really surprised me around 8 years ago, I met someone my age who did not own a computer and did everything on her smartphone. I still don't really understand how people do this, but they exist in a wide range of ages, apparently. (Full disclosure, her computer was stolen, but she was in no rush to get a new one).

item.content:encoded:
→ Article (anthropic.com)

Top #1 — blfr:

People are saying that Anthropic has no moat which sounds right but at the same time they have left everyone behind: Google is trying lately but seemed very lost over the last years despite inventing the thing; OpenAI cannot match Opus 5.5 and Fable atm; and it seems like anti-distillation efforts really did put a dent in the speed of Chinese model development.

Meanwhile Claude is getting really good. It's a decent harness now, even the remote control over a couple servers is quite OK. They're adding artifacts left and right, new features. And all without making the product seem bloated, they stay focused.

The prediction markets don't show anything on the horizon either: https://releaseoracle.xyz/

I am not a big AGI believer but business- and product-wise it seems like ANT has something that others are missing.

↳ reply 1 — bob1029:

> OpenAI cannot match Opus 5.5 and Fable atm

OpenAI is absolutely crushing Anthropic regarding cost of running models.

A lot of real world scenarios have already been completely solved with models released months ago. My clients don't need more powerful models anymore. They need faster and more affordable models.

OpenAI has been aggressively pushing on both fronts. Where is Anthropic's 750T/s wafer-scale compute offering? Where is this on their roadmap?

↳↳ reply — heartbreak:

It seems like everyone I know outside of tech uses ChatGPT “Chat” on the free tier.

Of the people I know in tech, other than those who don’t use either, everyone is paying for Claude.

↳↳↳ reply — roncesvalles:

It's pretty obvious that OpenAI is dieselgating* the benchmarks. Even 6.2 Astra is nowhere near as good as Claude models for coding. Any software engineer can do a side-by-side comparison (as many of us do) and figure it out.

*Also consider the possibility that Anthropic may be dieselgating it down ("benchminning"?) instead of OpenAI doing benchmaxxing. It might make sense from some game theory standpoint - If you are significantly better than your enemy, it might be in your interest to lull them into believing that you are only slightly better.

↳ reply 2 — tkgally:

They don’t get so much attention on HN, where the focus is naturally on coding, but the new Claude features being steadily rolled out for office work could, it seems to me, become a real moat. Anthropic has lately announced integrations of Claude into whiteboards, online meetings, etc. As people get used to using those and to having Claude as a collaborator who is knowledgeable about their work, they will become reluctant to switch to other providers.

↳ reply 3 — lm2s:

The question is for how long? Maybe OpenAI doesn’t have it right now, but won’t they have it in a couple of months? That’s been the recurring theme. Anthropic has had a noticeable advantage before, and others did catch up and momentarily surpassed it.

Top #2 — purple_ferret:

I am totally blown away that a company that was formed in 2021 will have a 1.5 trillion market cap on the public market... to put into context, a valuation not achieved by Apple until 2020

↳ reply 1 — mcv:

It doesn't say much about the company itself, but about the state of the economy, where all the money has been concentrated at the top, in the hands of people who have nothing else to spend it on than on more financial assets. So there's enormous amounts of money available for more stocks.

It's why stock markets and corporate profits are at an all time high, while most people struggle to make ends meet and governments are woefully underfunded.

That $1.5 trillion IPO is the result of a completely lopsided economy.

↳↳ reply — pembrook:

The K shaped economy trope is directionally correct, but you have the cause backwards.

It's not that governments are underfunded, the K economy is a direct byproduct of government stimulus across all developed economies for the last 15 years.

When you inject the market with QE, the money printer and most importantly; 0% or negative interest rates for 15 years...it massively inflates the value of assets. Rich people own assets.

This is why things in the US with the prospect of generating future cash flows are at historically high valuations relative to GDP: public companies, private companies, real estate, etc.

If you think government is 'underfunded' and the solution is giving it more money to dump into the economy, ironically, you're going to inflate asset values further and make the K economy worse.

The stimulatory tools that are easiest for government to use are monetary policy, not fiscal policy.

But let's say you do manage to pass populist fiscal policy, like, giving first time home buyers $20k to help with a downpayment on a house.

Surprise! Turns out you've simply raised the value of all starter homes by $20K by increasing everyones capacity to pay for a scarce asset, inflating the value of the asset and handing the money to the person selling it.

The solution is to increase the supply of assets (build more real estate and competing businesses), not stimulate demand for existing ones. But that requires a much more rational, long term policy view than dumping blankets of cash on angry populist voters.

↳↳↳ reply — polshaw:

You are describing, almost fairly well, issues of accumulated wealth at the top -- particularly the effects of covid handouts[1], where all the money ended up with landlords that were not allowed out to spend it all, significantly increasing inequality and asset prices.

And somehow you try to turn it into an anti-tax argument, when taxing the wealth at the top is the only solution, the way to control the money supply, time machines aside. Give out too much you have to take some back if you don't want to devalue.

1. which is why the stock market and housing market went crazy at that point, not a steady 15 years, $5tn was created

↳ reply 2 — flowerlad:

I am blown away that a company spun off from OpenAI is now worth more than OpenAI and is going IPO before OpenAI.

Top #3 — 6thbit:

  The offering consists of 980,000,000 shares of Class A common stock

And they're taking around ~105B in cash.

81.34B from the 980M shares at $83 and 26B from Google/Nvidia/etc, minus 1.9B the existing holders selling 23.6M shares.

Perhaps they were expecting to be more oversubscribed? Like they increased the number of shares offered to keep a target amount of money. Likely they see the rough few months ahead. Ramp.com AI index shows spend on Anthropic AI was in decline/flat July 31 - Oct 31

Likely they're best bet is to weather the continued devaluation of tokens and cheaper models until they hit on a better business model, which honestly is probably not that hard.

item.title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
item.description: 293 points, 74 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (slowchronicle.com)

→ HN comments  ·  293 points  ·  74 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — saidinesh5:

Yesterday night, i reverse engineered the cloud connection plugin to my cctv camera in about 2 hours with Gemini.

Started off with me searching for what Chinese OEM made the product. Then tried out existing GitHub projects to see if it works but they were failing.

Spent 15 minutes to write a script that started their desktop software on a different network namespace and ran tcpdump in it. Captured exactly only the things i needed without any noise. Turned out it was using a different server url and credentials than the GitHub projects. Opened Ghidra to inspect the dlls that matched the strings i was looking for.

After that, I got lazy and handed over the task to Gemini to find the username and key they use to authenticate with the servers. It took about 30 minutes or an hour. A lot of it was me changing models because the llm servers were busy. It simply wrote a little script that ran through various strings it fetched from the binary to see if it can generate the authentication credentials.

Now my Home Assistant will be detecting if my car is parked in the parking lot or not. Life is good.

↳ reply — vachina:

How did you manage to coax Gemini to cough up the creds? Whenever I touch anything that requires reversing auth I get stone walled. Close to useless for me.

↳↳ reply — saidinesh5:

Last time I ran into quota limits very quickly when debloating my tv... I think it's just luck this time though. Debloating my TV took slightly longer and i ran out of tokens.

This time I manually filtered all that data it needs to search through.. like instead of going through the full tcpdump logs, i had a 50 line file with only the data it needs, stripped out of all headers. I specifically told it to only read these two dlls. And to understand the login protocol "only read through these 2 source files".

Plus half the research i did , i was just using the free search in Google instead of antigravity this time..

Top #2 — hexapus:

I have zero experience reverse engineering and very little with software development. Most of my work has been in DevOps/SRE space with an emphasis on infrastructure. I am surrounded by code, but other than terraform, and the occasional python script, I don't really write much of it.

Not too long ago, I successfully reverse engineered an abandoned audio effects plugin, as well as a discontinued instrument with an onboard DSP for virtual instrument modeling. I had no idea what I was doing, but it was still amazing to get to open the black box and see what's inside and how it worked.

The plugin is nearly 1:1 as far as sound, and while I'm not going to use the code or the techniques of the instrument, peeking into them gave me the insight I needed to start trying to replicate the functionality on a modern DSP.

I have my issues with generative AI as a technology, but busting open propietary software - particularly when it's abandoned and unsupported, is one of the cooler use cases I've seen for it.

↳ reply 1 — kccqzy:

Busting open proprietary hardware is also a cool use case. There have been very many Claude-assisted efforts recently at making Linux run better than it ever did on obsolete Intel Macs.

↳↳ reply — Pokepokalypse:

working on a 2013 macbook pro running Mint, right now. I remember slogging through this exercise about 2015, trying to get the nvidia drivers to build, trying to get power/thermal management to work properly, getting it to wake from suspend properly. I eventually gave up and went back to Mac OS X on this device. But I had to stop using it when Apple stopped shipping security updates. Now with gemini, it's been a snap getting everything functioning and optimized.

↳ reply 2 — darksim905:

what tooling did you use?

Top #3 — jedjonesuk:

Reverse engineering is one of those areas where the depth of the knowledge and the trouble solving really shows up for me. Two things I reverse engineered this weekend:

1) My kid has a toy from china where you put a USB cartridge in and get stories in Chinese with pictures. This is itself a rip off of another product of which I forget the name. the cartridge is just a normal USB but the file on disk was just a .dat file so you could buy more stories online, and then download them. It figured out in about 15 min, they just had a combined format which just concat all of the input together with all text base 64 encoded. So manifest|pagetext|image1|image2 and everything just had to be just the right format and then it would work. It wrote a script to make a story from a folder input, but also wrote a skill to write a story, make pictures etc from the idea.

2) I was looking into a shelf my wife wanted, but didn't want to spend the money on. I took the 4 or 5 product images from the websites, dumped them into Claude with mcp to freeCAD and an hour later it has completely recreated a working cad design of the product, produced a pdf on how to assemble it, and allows me to make edits and changes to tweak the product to my preferences. The interesting thing about this one is while following its work, it clearer identified the actual original product at some point despite there being zero obvious indicators in the pictures.

↳ reply — Oxodao:

I want so hard to like freecad but every time I try it I just can't. I'd love to have a proper software to make my 3d models for my printer..

Yesterday I decided to design a 7-segment display from led strips and for some reason my sketch with the segments just would not extrude / dig into the back plate, spent nearly an hour debugging with ChatGPT to no avail. At some point it asked me to give the file which I did and even it could not simply make it work without weird workaround. For such a simple task it's weird I can't get it to work. I saw a few people on youtube to use it so there's definetly something I do wrong but I have no clue what. Maybe I'll try using an MCP for it but in the mean time I have to get by with my windows VM just for Fusion...

↳↳ reply — jedjonesuk:

It does feel hard to use, truth be told I rarely use it and mostly just have Claude do it now. I Imagine furniture is much easier than some other things. I only used it because the friend with the CNC and the experience to review the results uses it.

I imagine you get similar results with other CAD systems. One key thing which does help is to encourage the model to screenshot its output as well as just reading whatever textual representation there is. I noticed with the shelf it would rotate the shelf to match the base pictures and screenshot, I guess for a better side by side comparison? but I've no idea if it "looks" at two images at the same time in the same way it would 2 parapgraphs.

Top #2 — impulser_:

Is there any theory on what is Anthropic's secret sauce? I have been using the latest Gemini models and they just don't seem as good as Opus 5.5 despite the benchmarks. Yeah it comparable on some tasks maybe slightly better but as an overall general intelligent model nothing compared to Opus 5.5 and it hard for me to understand why. Opus feels like human level intelligent like I'm talking to a coworker basically while GPT and Gemini feel like I'm talking to an AI and have to change how I talk. It hard to explain and maybe I'm the only one that feels this.

Is it because Anthropic put a ton more effort into the character of the model that it basically roleplays as a human and that why it tends to think better when giving tasks that it might not be trained heavily on.

I have used Carbon more than most model to try and get the same results but it just feels like i'm talking to a smart AI. Which is fine if you are asking questions, researching an idea, but if you actually want to work on something, build something, it just falls apart. Like Opus can run for days on a task and it feels like it understand what it was doing 2 days ago even when it might not be in it context while other models feel like they breakdown and get lost or falter as the task grows.

↳ reply 1 — svara:

I think Gemini 4 (Argon is the one I've been using) is very clearly better at writing English than any Anthropic model. It's not better otherwise but in that the difference is vast.

To the point that I now use a workflow of delegating from Opus or Fable to Gemini4 to write commit messages and PR descriptions, it mostly solves the Claudese problem.

↳↳ reply — qalmakka:

Agree. Claude sucks at writing, you can pinpoint it's Claude from a million kilometres away and it always sounds like it's writing in slogans or something. Both GPT and Gemini are way better at writing text

↳ reply 2 — ehsankia:

Every day I'm just more and more amazed at Opus 5.5 and how ahead it was. Even with the insane pace we're going at, it's amazing that two months later, we're barely putting out models that hit the price/speed/quality of Opus 5.5

On that latter category, I find Gemini superior to Claude for many tasks. Of course Google has an advantage when it comes to reaching places in the internet via its index and things like YouTube, but Gemini is really more useful than people give credit for the tasks I use it for.

item.title: DaisyRose-27B
item.description: 247 points, 103 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (radixark.com)

→ HN comments  ·  247 points  ·  103 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

Top #1 — chriddyp:

Very excited to see more post-training happening on these open models. Looking forward to trying this one out once it makes its way onto OpenRouter.

Qwen 27B really punches above its weight. 27B is small enough to fit on a Mac Mini / Macbook Pro which is very exciting.

Starting to see more promising examples of companies post-training. From my evals [1], I've tested 3 so far:

1. Fireworks' Ember-1 (postrained on Kimi K3, improved score by 10% in my evals)

2. Particle AI's Particle-1 (fine-tuned on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, also a 10% improvement and a bit cheaper and faster)

3. Nex AGI's Nex-N2.6 (post-trained on GLM 5.3 Flash. Didn't show an improvement in my eval, and had a couple runaway loops that made it expensive).

With Thinking Machines' western open model release (Inkling Small) a few weeks ago, I expect we'll see more of this, especially out of western companies.

[1] https://plotly.com/blog/nex-n2-6-plotly-data-analytics-bench...

item.title: Teaching robots to carve marble sculptures
item.description: 125 points, 91 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (eleanorwiesler.com)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  91 comments

Top #1 — mauvehaus:

Two things:

1) A great podcast about why we're bad at statues in the US:

https://slate.com/podcasts/decoder-ring/2026/07/how-taste-po...

2) This isn't a particularly interesting model to sculpt. The parent model is a scan of a ceramic rabbit, and it doesn't have crisp details like really good marble sculptures do.

I have seen Venus Victrix[0] in person, and the detail in the mattress the figure is lying on is absolutely transfixing. You would swear the marble would softly yield if you put your finger on it. There's a detail rendered around the edge of the mattress that likely represents embroidery and it's unbelievably crisp, even as it follows the folds and creases in the mattress.

If we're going to have robots sculpt marble, that is the standard we should be reaching for. If we're reaching for that, I think we're going to find that modeling the finished product in 3d is going to be a significant fraction of the work of actually carving it in stone. I think we're also going to find that the mastery also lies in the tiny decisions the sculptor makes as they work, informed by how light plays off the material in different directions in real time throughout the day.

Can the process in the article achieve results suitable for mounting at the top of a building and viewing from ground level? Probably, and if not now, certainly with time. Can it sculpt something that will command your attention in reverent, slack-jawed awe for hours? I don't see it happening.

[0] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_Victrix_(Canova) Seriously, this and Bernini's David, also at the Galleria Borghese, are worth the trip to Rome to see. If there were nothing else in Rome worth seeing and the food was terrible, they would justify the pilgrimage on their own.

↳ reply 1 — dekhn:

One of my best art moments was the Vatican museum. At one point, there's a garden, but most people instead head past it. I walked into the garden and came across https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laoco%C3%B6n_and_His_Sons with nobody else around and spent ten minutes inspecting it in detail (including around the sides). This is somethiing that was carved 2000 years ago! Absolutely stunning, and much more appreciable in a quiet, relaxed setting.

I fully expect that robots will be able to carve novel masterpieces in 10 years.

↳ reply 2 — stronglikedan:

There's also the one with the veil where they carved the marble so thin that it's translucent. Amazing

↳ reply 3 — krisoft:

> modeling the finished product in 3d is going to be a significant fraction of the work of actually carving it in stone.

Of course. But what is the problem with that?

We have the same situations with many other things. With printers: It takes way more effort to write a book worth printing than the actual effort of putting in the reams of paper into the printer and hitting the print button. Same with 3d printing. People spend days, weeks, months, or years modelling something interesting and then it is relatively easy to get it printed once it is designed.

> Can it sculpt something that will command your attention in reverent, slack-jawed awe for hours? I don't see it happening.

I don’t see why it couldn’t carve a model which evoke those emotions into stone. And i used my words deliberately there. Because i would call the person who made the model the sculptor. I wouldn’t say that the machine sculpted anything.

The machine is a machine. It carves the stone. We can talk about how accurately it does what it does, we can talk about the surface quality it leaves behind. We can even talk about what geometries it can or can’t tackle due to the particular arangement of the arm and the spindle.

If those “datasheet properties” are good enough, then all you need to do is get a good artist who is handy with some modelling software let them play around with it and you will get your “awe inspiring”.

Top #2 — runxel:

Reminds me of the link to the Carmelites[0] that was on HN a few weeks ago.

But they do it in stone (they don't seem to mention what kind of stone, tho). I think marmble is a different experience, and I wonder what the implications are. Often enough marble requires an experienced master to "read" it. Since it's a natural stone there will be veins, imperfections etc. Sometimes you'll have to work around it and alter your design slightly while carving - which is not possibble if a robot just does its lusterless job.

While I admire this task, and I hope that we will see more carved stones in our buildings and surroundings again, I also hope that we can use technology as our aid, not as the end in itself.

There is a manufacturer in Germany who does exactly this, btw (rough cuts by robot, fine tune by human masters). So there is a lot of prior art out there - I wonder if there was anything new at all.

[0] https://carmelitegothic.com/cnc-stone-carving/

↳ reply — buildsjets:

Came here to post this, but you already have. So I will just add that everyone should visit the link just to see a berobed monk with a tonsured haircut (think Friar Tuck) running desktop CAD and multiaxis CNC.

Top #3 — barbariangrunge:

Sculpting teacher here. Ceramic and oil clay--marble is scary.

On the one hand, there is something special about an artist made sculpture. But on the other, in north america we have almost no cool sculpture around us day to day. So few people can make them and there is seemingly limited demand due to costs

If companies start producing millions of sculptures and selling them at walmart or dollarama in bulk, will they still be cool? Or will we make them in our garages in 2036 with robot arms and ai generated designs informed by amazon ring camera footage of our neighbourhoods?

As an artist, what does your role become? Does anything remains scarce in art? Would love to hear some speculation

↳ reply 1 — jszymborski:

I'm not an artist, so maybe I'm missing the mark, but I feel like the hard part of making art should be learning how to express or project your artistic vision or complex emotion or some other aspect of human experience into physical space. I'm not sure I subscribe to the idea that the difficulty of the medium you choose is necessary. Sometimes it's the point of the work, but I don't think you're getting the most out of the Pietà if your take home is "wow, that must have been difficult" (although that's just my opinion).

We can look at other art forms that are pretty accessible w.r.t. barrier to entry. Most folks learn creative writing as school children and master the fundamentals quite quickly. Sure, there's reams of bad (and good, don't come at me) fanfic at ao3 as well as middling pulp at the gas station, but I don't think that stops great works from appearing or being any less special.

Similarly, we see pretty terrible statues in public places quite frequently (I'm thinking the derpy Ronaldo statue or the Lucille Ball statue in Celeron).

So all that to say, I'm optimistic that if something like this meant statues were easy to make and you can design one in your underwear in a few hours and hit "print", sure the volume of shite statues would explode, but I think that just raises the floor on quality a bit and leaves the ceiling in tact.

↳ reply 2 — david927:

The Walmart effect doesn't worry me because we can already have that with prints of the masters and few do it.

Instead, I'm inspired. Could we democratize and evangelize culture this way?

The American city I live in has 300,000 people. Why can't it have a large building that has full replicas of the great works of art? The Mona Lisa, Whistler's Mother (or Falling Rocket), Van Gogh's Sunflowers or self-portraits (with impasto). Marble sculpture replicas of Canovo, Bernini, Rodin. A small, one-stop shop of some of the world's great works, for people who will never see it otherwise.

Used to play quite a bit with Mastra (not Factory) and it was a very pleasant experience. Cool launch, congrats!

Couple of questions:

1. Did you experiment with not having a separate design/plan phase? From my experience agents usually don’t really know what the plan is until they start editing files and executing tests (in other words, implementing), so the initial plan is usually not great and changing it mid-flight is overhead. I also find reviewing tested code to be much easier than reviewing plans/designs, which are often full of ungrounded assumptions.

item.title: Seven new models at scalable price-performance
item.description: 546 points, 355 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (microsoft.ai)

→ HN comments  ·  546 points  ·  355 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — athrowaway3z:

I was on the fence on jumping into the Anthropic IPO - but i think i'm going to skip it even though it's a product I actively pay to use and am happy with. Its just too overpriced.

Yes Anthropic will be leading for a while with the best model; but first the Chinese models, yesterday's OpenAI's Sol & Astra, and now even Microsoft getting Opus 5 performance. Remember that even Anthropic's own Opus 5.5 is _way_ more efficient than the models that were active in their “profitable” quarters.

I do not see a business that is going to do triple digits growth consistently to justify their valuation.

It is just too much of a fungible utility — and there is too much demand for any single approach to capture a market. Hell, AI is the perfect tool for any customer to 'uncapture' themselves.

↳ reply 1 — rayiner:

It's increasingly looking like AI companies have invented electric motors. Incredibly valuable technology that will be in everything. But nobody ever built a moat around electric motors. At least as to LLMs, AI is a competitive, efficient market where the basic interface is the most plug-and-play, standardized thing imaginable: a text stream. Literally anything that can produce a 9600 bps serial TTY stream is basically interchangeable with Claude, GPT, etc.

↳↳ reply — svara:

The essay "AI will not make you rich" by Jerry Neumann makes a similar point, but uses containers (the shipping kind) as an analogy.

It's well argued and the arguments are worth considering.

https://colossus.com/article/ai-will-not-make-you-rich/

↳↳↳ reply — seanhunter:

The idea that shipping containers never made anyone rich is a weird myth. The Møller family (owners of Maersk) certainly got pretty rich.

↳ reply 2 — namjh:

I'm also skipping the IPO, so essentially having the same conclusion, but with a different reasoning. I don't think Chinese AI companies, Meta, MS(and even OpenAI with very low confidence) will outpace Anthropic in intelligence or cost per intelligence in the foreseeable future.

My guess is Anthropic is way ahead towards RSI(based on the recent METR report spotlighting their internal model 4/5 and AECI) so this is the systematic, and concrete moat against other competitor.

The reason I don't think that the IPO is favorable is, just a short- to mid-term macroeconomic impression that the current scale of the global economy cannot spend that much fortune to use their AI services. In short, I have no doubt that Anthropic is going be the winner, but skeptical about whether they can extract enough return from the consumer chain and the economy.

↳ reply 3 — PaulKeeble:

Given the progress we have seen in local AI as well this year its quite possible that the bulk of programming needs might soon be entirely met by models that run in a 16GB consumer card as well. The audience here is enterprise looking to save money, and there is no natural monopoly preventing this from gaining traction.

↳↳ reply — danudey:

Not to nitpick, but Windows Phone also failed because Microsoft released the first generation of devices with Windows Phone 7, convinced a bunch of people to buy them, and then released a second generation of devices with updated Windows Phone 8, a version that the first generation couldn't upgrade to meaning that anyone who got in on the ground floor got locked out immediately.

The phone comparison doesn’t apply, IMO. Phones are entire ecosystems and they’re very sticky. People don’t switch phone OSes casually because they only buy a phone every several years. Getting locked into a phone you don’t like is too risky.

Even my wife’s big company technically has a contract with one AI provider for the company, but teams across the company are getting extra spending to use on Claude or other models of their choice and the favorites are changing every few months.

Don't disable nested, it's still better security than everything else, and having it on means access to real hardware virtualization. Second, the article is AI-written. It really should be rewritten by a human.

↳ reply 1 — xmodem:

Outside of development and CI, I have yet to hear a compelling use case for nested virtualization.

↳↳ reply — JoshTriplett:

> I have yet to hear a compelling use case for nested virtualization.

AWS instances are slow to launch; they take whole seconds. Nested virtualization allows running something like firecracker/crosvm/rust-vmm atop a normal AWS instance, without needing a bare-metal one.

↳↳↳ reply 1 — xmodem:

If you need as-fast-as-possible guest start, AND you have to be on AWS, AND you can't use any of their native microVM-based services, AND you can't use the bare-metal instances - whether due to cost or some other reason, then nested virtualisation might be the least-bad option. That doesn't make it compelling.

↳↳↳ reply 2 — ★ tptacek:

If you're segregating internal workloads, by all means use nested virtualization on EC2 or DO or something. Your threat model is different and you probably have a lot more room to maneuver when a KVM escape is announced, because you have some level of trust in all your workloads.

If you're running multitenant for mutually-untrusting customers, that excuse goes out the window.

↳↳↳↳ reply — exceptione:

Do you mean that you would run each tenant on separate (physical) hardware? If so, I presume that you enforce this only for workloads where you run code outside your control. I guess the average SaaS does not install hardware boxes for each tenant separately.

Also, how could VPS hosting still be a thing if KVM is that easily escaped?

EDIT: I am talking about KVM in general, not nested virtualization.

↳↳↳ reply — MajesticHobo2:

↳↳ reply 2 — ★ tptacek:

I hate these meta conversations on crunchy technical topics and feel like we should be digging into the KVM security model more than this general security prognostication stuff. Having said that, I will hypocritically further this debate by pointing out that the determinant of software security moving forward is not so whether AI is drastically better than humans at avoiding common vulnerability patterns, (or instead just a little better). Rather, it's that AI will make it much easier to move subsystems or whole projects to memory-safe programming languages and towards formal verification.

↳ reply 2 — TZubiri:

Have you ever been told that you are problematically optimistic?

Also — ★ tptacek:

Another nested KVM bug. We debated enabling nested KVM for many years, and held the line every time, because the only post-2020 KVM vulnerability we knew of required nested VMs. That decision aged well: we've gotten at least 2 more nested KVM escapes in the last year.

Don't allow nested KVM.

Considering the LLMs have ~15 years of nested virtualization to catch up with, it's not in an awful state. These bugs are extremely complicated to exploit, which means that the past ten years of fuzzing with syzkaller have already found the low hanging fruit.

doesn't change the value of what's writen, if true and actionable that's all that should be needed

↳↳↳↳ reply — tsunagatta:

Time to dig this one out again https://marc.info/?l=openbsd-misc&m=119318909016582

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48883089

↳↳ reply — eddythompson80:

He is right. It’s just that selling bare metal doesn’t scale and we must sell VMs instead, so we can't understand his point.

Since he made that comment there has been numerous virtualization vulnerabilities in KVM, Xen, HyperV, and all other hypervisors as well as all their device virtualization helpers/ecosystem. ↳ reply 1 — JoshTriplett:

I use Zulip every day, and it works incredibly well. There are still rough edges, but it's improving regularly.

The model of having threads within channels provides great organizational help. But also, these days, if you want to have a "general chat" in a channel that isn't in a thread, you can optionally do that. (I'd recommend not jumping to that just because you're coming from Slack/Discord and not accustomed to threads; give yourself some time to try them. But it can be useful for a subset of channels; some people like it or casual/social channels, for instance. I personally like threads for those too, though.)

Also, the integration and API are easy, and bots and similar are easy to write. You can also arrange to have emails turn into posts on a channel.

Despite what the site says, you don't have to self-host. The software is Open Source, and you absolutely can if you want to. But you can also use the hosted version, either free or paid, and save yourself the trouble, knowing that you can always move to self-hosted later.

I think properly-trained AI agents will have a huge advantage against humans in such contexts: They will have no intrinsic tendency towards laziness. I think most humans have a natural inclination to optimise the amount of work we do in a professional setting, unless we really happen to enjoy it doing it for the sake of it. We can fight against this by setting up processes and incentives, but we'll always be going against a tendency deeply ingrained by evolution to minimise our mental energy expenditure and to avoid repetitive, tedious or boring tasks.

On the other hand, with AI we'll use reinforcement learning to create agents without such evolved-in tendencies. Where (so long as we can solve alignment and cheating) they are trained to do the job, no matter how much effort it takes, or what's involved.

↳ reply 1 — dasil003:

Just as laziness is an energy saving technique with high evolutionary value, so is busybody makework for AI agents. Have you noticed how claude always has a couple loose ends and a suggestion for next step at the end of every session? Nothing is ever done—that's good for token spend, and can easily create an illusion of productivity.

But when it comes to audits/compliance, it's mostly a cost center meant to mitigate risk. Going deeper may be valuable, but it can also add costs in terms of time and attention that just aren't worth it—this is the balance that human auditors walk every day, and it's in a squishy human domain where AI really struggles to demonstrate any common sense let alone street smarts, instead acting like an extremely precocious 13-year-old with no sense of human incentives or tacit understandings.

item.title: Inside Deutsche Bank
item.description: 708 points, 240 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (inside-db.com)

→ HN comments  ·  708 points  ·  240 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — ltrg:

I was involved with this project as a reporter, though others from my organisation did most of the work.

HN readers may be interested to know a bit about the tech stack. The 15 million or so documents, mostly Outlook mailbox exports, were provided to partners in the consortium via a tool called OpenAleph [1], which is maintained by DARC and based on ElasticSearch and a schema called FollowTheMoney [2], developed specifically for the investigative journalism use case. A lot of the original work on this was done by Friedrich Lindenberg (@pudo), who now runs OpenSanctions [3].

The timing was v. interesting given where we are with LLMs -- it's the first major leak I've worked on where it was possible to leverage local models to do some of the heavy lifting, and this only got more possible as the project went on. The coordinators provided a centrally hosted chatbot with RAG, but I also managed to get some surprisingly useful material using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my 24GB M2 MBA via a custom agent harness for Aleph/OpenAleph. [4]

Happy to answer any questions about techy stuff, though I'm not a spokesperson for the project by any means. Seen a few people saying "just release the data!", but I think that slightly misunderstands what this work is. The whole point of forming a consortium of hundreds of journalists and sifting through the dump is to identify the bits that are in the public interest to report on -- especially important in jurisdictions like the UK, where I'm based, which have very strong defamation laws. Think Panama Papers, not Wikileaks.

[1] https://darc.li/openaleph/ [2] https://followthemoney.tech/ [3] https://www.opensanctions.org/ [4] https://github.com/data-desk-eco/sift

↳ reply 1 — AdamN:

This tech stack probably is the inheritor of alot of work done with the Enron Corpus - the first big body of text data from a large company that could be analysed using machine learning techniques:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enron_Corpus

This is the reason why their web address is darc.li, because darc.de is used by the ham radio people.

And if I read their impressum right, they aren't some "Data and Research Center", they are "IDIO Daten Import Export GmbH" based in Berlin.

Weird.

↳ reply 2 — mentalgear:

This news outlet has a good introduction:

> Deutsche Bank's business dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, now US President Donald Trump, and a host of Russian oligarchs.

> Gleaned from nearly 15 million documents leaked [...] the e-mails and meeting minutes trace the bank's aggressive pursuit of business deals in Russia, and with high-profile Russian oligarchs, right up until Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — despite risk warnings from numerous managers.

Top #3 — mlmonkey:

> The Data

> Our reporters will continue to evaluate the material journalistically over the

> coming months. We will not publish the raw data online.

One of my biggest gripes about journalism today is that biased actors will change the narrative to fit their biases via selective omission of facts, thereby putting forth a misleading version. One doesn't have to actually _lie_ to deceive the public; one can just hide extenuating facts and let the public form their own (misguided) opinion.

This is why I feel like the raw data should be released so we can do our own analyses. Why should I blindly trust a random self-selected, possibly anonymous, group of people?

↳ reply 1 — Traster:

I really strongly disagree with this. Let's say you have all the data. You release it. How many people are going to go audit it? Not many. So instead of you, a journalist who actually has a professional interest in this and a reputation to build, you're handing analysis off to clout chasers. Suddenly whoever can find the most explosive viral take will win. Not the most accurate take. The most viral. And the most viral is often something just wrong enough to engage those who want to believe it whilst also engaging those who know enough to refute it - that's where you hit the sweet spot of engagement. Sure someone could go back to the original published data and debunk it - well done, you're driving engagement and uninformed people aren't going to see you debunking it, they're going to 90% see the original false claim, and 10% see a debate they know nothing about which is 50:50 on what they end up believing.

Far more effective is for you to listen to different journalists opinions and reporting over time and answer two questions: "Is this person acting with integrity?" and "What are their biases that I need to factor into my analysis". It is much more important to be listening to journalists who have clear ethical standards - even if you disagree with them.

↳↳ reply — rsync:

This is a well formed and convincing justification for not initially releasing the raw data.

I don't agree with it but it's not crazy ...

However there is no good justification for not releasing the raw data eventually, which it appears will not occur.

↳ reply 2 — probably_wrong:

No one else mentioned protecting whistleblowers, so I will:

We all know that our printers carry tracking dots, and similarly there's a good chance that all kind of fingerprinting shenanigans are going on inside these big companies. Or maybe there's a file that only five people are supposed to have and everybody knows who the other four are. Every time you release an original document you risk it being traced back to the leaker.

This is not theoretical, BTW, this is (as far as we know) how Reality Winner was identified:

item.title: F-22 Next-Generation micro–Data Transfer Cartridge (mDTC)
item.description: 183 points, 118 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (sam.gov)

→ HN comments  ·  183 points  ·  118 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — jotux:

Cool coincidence. In a past job, I specifically made replacement PCMCIA cards for these (and other) planes. Instead of making cards with a controller and onboard storage, we made cards with an FPGA/microcontroller and a microSD card soldered to the PCB. We did this specifically because these aircraft use (at least partially) broken implementations of the PCMCIA protocol, and we'd update the bus protocol per aircraft to work around the limitations. None of these planes can just go buy stuff off the street because some large portion just doesn't work because their protocol isn't fully implemented and isn't flexible to deal with variance in timing/speed/etc.

A fun story: Our cards had whatever industrial-spec microSD card we could find (16GB, 32GB, etc.), and we'd internally limit the disk size to whatever the platform needed. Almost every aircraft had some specific number of MB they wanted because all of their CONOPS listed it, and they didn't want to update documentation or software to put a different number there. We had a plane that could only use EXACTLY 128MB, but they were currently using 256MB cards and partitioning them to 128MB. We updated the disk size to present as 128MB so they could skip this step, and they specifically told us to put it back to 256MB because they didn't want to update the commissioning process to remove the partitioning step.

It was rewarding work, and the card we designed was cheap (~$500 each, which is literally nothing for major platforms like this) and 100% US-designed and made (with the exception of ICs manufactured in the usual places). Still, the procedural and cultural practices of these program offices made it a real struggle to get traction and deploy them widely. Government acquisition is just generally designed around funding primes for current development and then paying through the nose for sustainment later. It was hard to design something for widespread sustainment use because by the time you were done and ready for production, a bunch of parts would be obsolete. Then you'd have to rev the design over and over. We were never allowed to stockpile anything, even if it was trivially cheap, to facilitate production later.

↳ reply 1 — jotux:

Another story:

PO came to me and asked if our card would work on their plane. We ship them a prototype and it doesn't work. They ship it back and send along a card that does work in the plane. We test it, and the card is just faster. We get the designer of the data box (works at the prime) on the phone and talk to him. Explain that our card works within timing specs but isn't working in the plane reader. He says something along these lines: "Oh, our reader implements the communication specification just fine, but only for fast cards. When we designed the box we wanted to hit a certain read/write speed, so we went out and bought a bunch and found the fastest cards and wrote our VHDL to talk to those cards." After we collected our jaws from the floor we updated our card to run a little faster and it started working. They had a lot of trouble finding commercial cards that worked.

And another:

One of the hardest parts to find for a PCMCIA card is stamped sheet metal cases. When we made prototypes, we bought case kits where the PCB just dropped in if you followed the PCB outline and used the right 68 pin connector. Around 2020 the companies that made them started to discontinue them, sent out a notice to offer final production batch ordering to do final lifetime buys. I BEGGED a bunch of groups to go order a few thousand, or tens of thousands and just put them in a closet somewhere (they were like $9/each). No one could make the decision in time, they went obsolete. We ended up designing a new machined aluminum case with super tight tolerances and features and it was like 80% of the total $500 cost.

↳↳ reply — CobaltFire:

I would have killed to be able to use the machined aluminum case.

The number one reason we had to retire PCMCIA cards on the flight line was the stamped steel case getting caught on something and bending one too many times. We could fix it a few times, but they wouldn't fit in the aircraft after a while (tighter tolerances than the laptops).

↳↳↳ reply — jotux:

When we designed the prototypes with stainless steel cases we potted the internals (and case) with thermal epoxy to make them more rugged. It made them super strong and durable. We had a lot of issues with machined aluminum cases not fitting well in a bunch of readers because of the tight tolerances.

↳ reply 2 — RogerL:

Cool. I was in the game during the period when DTMs were still being used, and ended up doing sw mods to support the PCMCIA replacements, which was a real hair puller because of lack of documentation and difficulty in getting Windows to work with the cards (a lot of work was more on the pc side - planners/loaders).

for others - the DTM was a solid black "brick" that weighed a few pounds and was maybe 128MB of solid state memory. About the size of a brick, but half as thick. Very expensive (I think we were paying ~6K at the time), with long lead times. The SCSI devices we used to read/write from the PC were even harder to acquire; you had to get a spot on the manufacturing schedule, and we were a small defense contractor, so no real way to get moved up the list. Made for difficult contract deliveries, and of course absurdly expensive bids due to all of this.

Everyone was really excited to the change to PCMCIA, except the ones of us implementing it!

edit: i may be conflating a few memories, I do remember fighting with microSDs as well, I think. Trying to remember; I think the DTM 'bricks' had a version that accepted a PCMCIA or micro card as the memory, so the interface hardware/sw didn't need to change. I have no idea if the DTMs are in use anymore.

↳ reply 3 — inamberclad:

Cool coincidence, since I'm writing a storage driver for an airplane at the moment! Software reuse is very difficult in aerospace since the hardware and software were both qualified in a very specific combination, in the context of an aircraft program, and any change or adaptation is a huge effort.

That means lots of 'clean sheet' driver rewrites from a spec document for your specific environment and hardware, and lots of hand rolled drivers that work well enough, but not great, because the burden of certification is too much to justify incorporating fancy features, like driver interrupts or multiple speeds. Just hard-code exactly the settings you need for your project, you'll save weeks of extra V&V effort.

Top #2 — spicyjpeg:

It's worth pointing out that there are actually two main types of PCMCIA memory cards. The most common by far are the ATA cards mentioned here, which are basically CF cards in a different form factor (equivalent to a CF card in a CF-to-PCMCIA adapter) and work by emulating either an IDE hard drive or an ISA IDE controller depending on wiring. While uncommon at this point, CF controller chips are still available and some specialized suppliers do manufacture these cards brand new using modern NAND flash.

The much more problematic ones to find a replacement for in 2026 are the so-called "linear" memory-mapped cards, consisting of one or more banks of raw parallel NOR flash with no controller IC. Linear cards were never standardized and the protocol used to interface to parallel flash can vary greatly across chip families, so the vast majority of devices that use them are hardcoded to only accept cards with a specific manufacturer and device ID. Many NOR flash manufacturers from the turn of the century have long discontinued their products and emulating parallel flash using modern FPGAs and microcontrollers is also non-trivial due to their memory-mapped nature, so owners of legacy telecom equipment and original Dance Dance Revolution arcade cabinets [1] are left with pretty much no viable replacement option once the stock cards fail.

[1] https://psx-spx.consoledev.net/konamisystem573/#flash-chips-...

↳ reply 1 — Waterluvian:

Oh! I have one of these. Except it’s only 2MB and my Newton is currently using it.

↳↳ reply — andyfilms1:

When you get a chance, you should throw it in an F35 and see if it works!

↳↳↳ reply — Waterluvian:

I see no PCMCIA port in my F-35. And I’m fresh out of F-22s.

↳ reply 2 — Melatonic:

So your saying that Dance Dance Revolution and Fighter Jets might be competing for the same stock of legacy hardware?

Top #3 — CobaltFire:

For anyone wondering what these are used for:

All current US military aircraft (at least up through the F-35) use CF cards to take mission planning from the laptops in the SCIF (or whatever unclass space they are using) to the aircraft.

As an aside, LCACs (among other platforms) also use these systems and cards. So this is a pretty widespread use case.

↳ reply 1 — happosai:

I heard recently The F-16 updates are known as "tapes". So like "M6 tape brought this and that feature but there was a serious issue so had make a M6.2 tape". The source did not clarify if the fighters literally load software from tapes and I was too afraid to ask...

↳↳ reply — Animats:

The F-16 also uses PCMCIA cards.

It's the right size for the job. It's small enough to be easily carried around, and big enough that it can be handled while wearing heavy gloves. They're big enough to have labels on them. The drive encloses and supports a PCMCIA card on five sides, and locks it into place, so it stays seated while fighter planes do fighter plane things.

PCMCIA cards were an excellent choice for military purposes. MicroSD cards are too tiny to handle with gloves or outdoors. In this application, you want a visible label on the device, since the card contains mission specific data and there are other similar cards around. USB drives supported only by their own connector are not well supported against G loads and vibration.

So they had a great solution. It just became obsolete because everybody wanted tiny laptops and phones.

↳↳↳ reply — 0_____0:

I concur with this, and it's the same reason I've standardized around the Samsung external SSDs. Come to think of it, they're kind of a similar volume to PCMCIA cards, albeit not as long, and I have each of mine labeled. I also know, positively, where they all are, which I can't say about any of my microSD cards.

Make Data Big Again

↳ reply 2 — andyfilms1:

"128MB of mission targets ought to be enough for anybody"

item.title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
item.description: 1406 points, 604 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (wiz.io)

→ HN comments  ·  1406 points  ·  604 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — black3r:

The bug was apparently fixed in open source repo a week earlier, this could've been abused by anyone smart enough to monitor repos like this for exploitable bugfixes for a week (the commit message even included "Reported by Xint.io" and I'm guessing skilled black hats would know about Xint)

Given that in this case the workaround is as simple as disabling http2, there is honestly no reason why F5/Nginx or any of the reporting teams couldn't at least put out a PSA to disable http2 for the time being before basically telling the whole wide world this exists and how to exploit it.

Especially for software like Nginx which powers a huge part of the internet.

↳ reply 1 — verst:

Disabling http2 can be a big deal. My service is primarily made up of gRPC APIs. Not an option for me to disable http2. Luckily I'm not using nginx at the moment - but I easily could have been.

↳↳ reply — weitendorf:

If you're using grpc, http2, etc you're so much better off using Envoy proxy

You basically get to piggyback off of a large chunk of big tech's infrastructure and security work. Obviously everything has the risk of security flaws (and I kind of hate that default Envoy builds ship with half-baked filter impls) but it's a generally more mature ecosystem than projects with a lot of smaller/legacy users like nginx

↳↳↳ reply — trey-jones:

I'm not 100% informed on this, but it seems very unbelievable to me that Envoy could be considered more robust or widely used than nginx at any point in history including today. I started using ConnectRPC instead of GRPC almost entirely because it didn't leave me subject to (what I consider to be) an unnecessary dependency in Envoy.

↳ reply 2 — brunoborges:

> this could've been abused by anyone smart enough to monitor repos like this for exploitable bugfixes for a week

And here lies the risk of AI agents in cybersecurity: the speed of processing for monitoring, scanning, identifying security fixes in open source, writing exploits for affected versions, and attempting infiltration, is a matter of minutes now.

It is not "by anyone smart enough". It is by "anyone ill intentioned enough". They don't need to be super smart anymore.

↳ reply 3 — SubiculumCode:

How bad are these CVEs? Could any of these be related to some of the recent outages (not claiming, asking) in the last week, coinciding with when this bug was fixed in the repo? Monitoring such repos seems a given for nation states.

Top #2 — fduran:

Small consolation but HTTP/2 is not enabled by default in Nginx and "only" 12% of servers run it (still huge at Internet scale) https://w3techs.com/technologies/segmentation/ce-http2/web_s...

↳ reply — jonenst:

Not enabled by default in upstream nginx yes, neither in most prepackaged nginx (e.g. debian), but enabled by default in some, for example kubernetes community ingress-nginx (the popular but deprecated one)

↳↳ reply — kuschku:

I still hate that they deprecated it, just because it gives anyone with write access to the cluster write access to the cluster.

Chainguard still updates their fork, by letting AI try to apply and backport the nginx patches, and I'm using that at the moment while switching to gateway API, but I'd have preferred if ingress-nginx was still maintained (the one by F5/nginxinc for example is still being maintained, just not entirely compatible).

Top #3 — malikNF:

Hey so, does anyone know of a good tutorial on getting in to woodwork?

↳ reply 1 — cfn:

I tried, didn't succeed so I am back.

↳ reply 2 — hi41:

I felt your post was off topic. But maybe it was on purpose because we are getting bored of so many vulnerabilities being discovered by AI security tools. So your post is important because of that.

I see a lot of interest in woodworking on HN. Is that because Jesus was a carpenter and HN folks are interested in woodwork because of the larger context and history shaped by Christianity? What is your motivation for woodwork? Is that because we see a concrete finished project instead of vague intellectual stuff which has no seeable boundaries?

Also — fn-mote:

AI is burning down the internet. This is insane.

Are we going to discover in a year that every server online this month had a rootkit installed? There’s got to be thousands who are too small time to wipe and reinstall.

↳ reply — codedokode:

Not AI but poorly designed programming languages ignoring integer overflows.

↳↳ reply — vlovich123:

I don’t know any systems programming language that doesn’t ignore integer overflow/underflow in release builds. IMHO this is a CPU design flaw - integer operations should carry a flag indicating if the operation is allowed to wrap or if it should generate a trap. Then there wouldn’t be a performance penalty for this and languages like Rust could have it be trapped by default.

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

No. Memory safe languages still have integer handling issues, but the consequences are different. In a memory-unsafe language, integer mishandling often nets out to bad copies and memory corruption.

↳↳↳↳ reply — vlovich123:

I wouldn’t be sure that a Rust equivalent would be immune because it’s not hard to imagine an underflow/overflow from reaching an unsafe block that’s used for performance (the implicated TLS path would be a hotspot worthy of such a choice).

item.description: 217 points, 79 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (youtube.com)

→ HN comments  ·  217 points  ·  79 comments

Top #1 — judge2020:

Isn't it the case that DMCA takedowns are a mechanism of 17 USC 512, and thus takedowns submitted for 17 USC 1201 therefore aren't legal takedown notices?

Nintendo only cites section 1201 in their DMCA takedown request: https://github.com/github/dmca/blob/master/2026/11/2026-11-0...

Same thing seems to have happened with Take Two submitting takedown requests yesterday[0] for software projects that enabled you to run GTA 5 on Apple hardware if you bring your own copy, although this is a much less legal-looking takedown.

0: https://github.com/github/dmca/blob/master/2026/11/2026-11-1...

> We adamantly request that GitHub disable the repositories and all associated forks from the platform. We emphasize that “bring your own files” disclaimer does not automatically shield the user from secondary copyright infringement through clear intent to facilitate the act.

↳ reply 1 — judge2020:

Going to reply to myself here that apparently there is Universal City Studios v. Reimerdes, 82 F. Supp. 2d 211, 217 (S.D.N.Y. 2000)

> Section 512(c) provides protection only from liability for copyright infringement. Plaintiffs seek to hold defendants liable not for copyright infringement, but for a violation of Section 1201(a)(2), which applies only to circumvention products and technologies. Section 512(c) thus does not apply here.

So in essence taking down a repository would not absolve GH of liability for the 'trafficking' of said circumvention technology.

Although it looks like GitHub has their own policy for handling circumvention claims: https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/content-removal-polic...

I do wonder if this extra circumvention review was undertaken by GitHub though, given I haven't seem any evidence of the extra process happening (giving the repository owner a chance to respond or modify their repo / referring the developer to legal consultation via GitHub’s Developer Defense Fund).

↳ reply 2 — ndiddy:

AFAIK Github voluntarily chooses to process 1201 claims as a risk mitigation strategy. The DMCA prohibits trafficking in circumvention mechanisms and doesn't include a "safe harbor" provision for them, so Github could conceivably also be named in a lawsuit if they chose to wait for a court order to take them down.

Top #2 — haunter:

Or did they? The main repo is still untouched and available on Github and it's up since 2023.

They took down a fork which had a lot more than the firmware itself.

item.title: The x86 CPU: From 4004 to 486
item.description: 170 points, 57 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (pikuma.com)

→ HN comments  ·  170 points  ·  57 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — jgord:

Learned to program on an 8088 machine with Hercules mono graphics card, first in GW-Basic which was godawful, then in A86 assembler and finally Turbo Pascal which was a pinnacle of human engineering, a portal into a wonderful future ahead.

There was great excitement and relief when the 80386 came out with its 32bit address linear memory model. Everything suddenly became possible - serious compute on the desktop.

Also remember fondly the workhorse that was the Core2Duo and the i4700k beast, and Mike Abrashes Black book on game programming.

LLM-style AI doesn't yet seem to be the growth technology we need to bring back the economic prosperity of the 80s-90s - but if RL can figure out a stable plasma fusion configuration and layout chips for much better data-flow, then we might see the level of prosperity and innovation we saw in those decades when Moores Law held sway.

↳ reply 1 — lproven:

> serious compute on the desktop.

The late great Guy Kewney wrote, I think in his original review of the IBM PC/AT in 1984 or 1985 (so roughly when I was doing my 'A' levels), something along the lines of...

"I got this sudden feeling that sitting there right in front of me was... Raw. Computer. Power."

The caps were his. The phrase has lived in my memory for 40 years.

He also had a wonderful description of WordPerfect 5, that went something like...

"I can only imagine the conversation at WP head office, when they sat down and tried to work out what they could do to top Wordperfect 4.2. And somehow, what came out of the meeting was: 'so, what we have here is the world's greatest bicycle. We know it, everyone says it. So what we're going to do is: we're going to put 11 more wheels on it."

These days WP 5.1 for DOS is held up as The Greatest DOS Word Processor Ever.

It was much more usable, because it had CUA menus. So if you didn't have all the f-key combinations memorised, you could just use the menus.

But that meant 3 complete UIs. At the time, it was seen as a bloated mess to existing WP users.

WP 4.2 was the sweet spot and ran from one 360kB floppy on an 8086. WP 5.1 needed a 286 with a hard disk.

But that's sort of my point...

At one point, if you were used to CP/M, an IBM PC with an 8086 and two 360kB floppies was a powerful computer.

Then came the PC/AT... 1.2MB on a floppy and anyway a hard disk as standard! It could take a meg of RAM, if you were insanely wealthy, and amazing multi-colour EGA graphics!

Raw Computer Power indeed!

Then the 386. I remember that era. Insane unimaginable power, in the MS-DOS era. 2 or 4MB of RAM! DOS 3.3 or 4.0 had no useful way to use all that. You could have a disk cache, and EMS as well, and it was still wasted.

These were computers so powerful one could stick 2 more serial ports in the back on an ISA card, and it was instantly a multiuser UNIX minicomputer serving 4 dumb terminals as well as the console. A £5000 PC that could replace a £250,000 minicomputer.

What could 1 person do with all that power? Nothing useful.

Then, in 3 years, came Windows 3.0, and suddenly this departmental-scale powerhouse wasn't fast enough any more... and you needed more RAM and a better graphics card and a bigger faster hard disk...

↳ reply 2 — bartread:

> 80386 came out with its 32bit address linear memory model. Everything suddenly became possible - serious compute on the desktop.

I wasn't really in the PC world at the time but I do remember this. I remember the first time using a 386 and feeling that, finally, PCs were genuinely powerful machines capable of genuinely impressive feats of computing.

↳ reply 3 — bananaboy:

I used A86! That was a great little assembler!

Top #2 — petercooper:

This is a neat history. However, going to be a bit nitpicky since they put this in bold re the 8008: "Intel did not design the instruction set of this chip" .. kinda true in a broad sense, but Intel engineers including Stan Mazor did change and enhance it, like adding increment and decrement operations and some other stuff mentioned in https://archive.computerhistory.org/resources/text/Oral_Hist...

↳ reply — adrian_b:

The increment and decrement instructions were the only enhancements, according to what is said at your link.

They removed from the ISA a branch-on-bit instruction and reduced the address size from 16 bits to 14 bits, because at that time Intel could not use bigger integrated circuit packages, with enough pins for a complete address.

↳↳ reply — wk_end:

The link describes increment/decrement as “one of the enhancements we made” (emphasis mine). The other things rattled off there aren’t necessarily “enhancements”, so I don’t think it’s clear that Mazor is giving an exhaustive list of changes or enhancements.

Top #3 — kens:

One thing I'd emphasize is that the 4004 is not related to the 8008 at all, except that many of the same people worked on both chips.

↳ reply — adrian_b:

Yes, the only relationship between 4004 and x86 is that the team which designed 4004 practically learned on it how to design PMOS logic circuits and by the end of the project they had a methodology of how to design such logic circuits in a more efficient way, which then they applied in their next project, which became Intel 8008.

In my opinion, not only 4004 is completely unrelated to 8008 and x86, but it also does not deserve to be called a "microprocessor", which is intended to mean "monolithic computer CPU", while it can be argued that the 4004 chip set was neither monolithic nor usable as a general-purpose computer CPU.

↳↳ reply — nwallin:

> In my opinion, [...] it also does not deserve to be called a "microprocessor", which is intended to mean "monolithic computer CPU", while it can be argued that the 4004 chip set was neither monolithic nor usable as a general-purpose computer CPU.

Somebody wrote a MIPS emulator in 4004 and used the emulated system to run linux. (it took a week to boot) I'd argue that if it runs linux it is a general purpose computer CPU.

I agree that it is not monolithic; you can't do anything without the associated ROM+IO chip. But I'd argue that's largely semantics. You can't use a modern x86 CPU without a motherboard full of associated chips either. Although it's not the Platonic ideal of a single monolithic IC, 2 chips to run programs is good enough.

↳↳↳ reply — lproven:

> Somebody wrote a MIPS emulator in 4004

[[citation needed]]
