item.title: The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026
item.description: 281 points, 214 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (cam.ac.uk)

→ HN comments  ·  281 points  ·  214 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — thimabi:

> Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines

If only it were that simple to define what a job is and which jobs are “worthy” or not of being reserved to humans.

I’m against dreamy proposals like this one because they miss the forest for the trees. Like previous technologies, AI can do lots of things that humans don’t really care about automating. But deciding which things won’t be subject to AI hinges on personal preferences, class interests, and even market pressures. It’s not something that can be reasoned about on a global scale, and trying to push this agenda might sow even more division among humans than we’d think at first glance.

↳ reply 1 — cassonmars:

As someone who has seen many caregivers of elder family – both family members serving as caregivers, and hired caregivers – as well as a caregiver to my spouse with a lifelong physical disability, Gates is so wrong for this. Caregiver burnout and fatigue is a thing. And sometimes it can be exactly these human circumstances that something is missed, or someone is injured – if we had caregiver robots that could serve at peak human caregiver capacity at all times, we should do everything in our power to make them as affordable and accessible as possible.

↳↳ reply — Rebuff5007:

The fact that caregivers burnout under the current economic model of funding care is completely orthogonal to the idea that caregiving should be a human reserved job.

IMO, a more reasonable argument against reserving caregiving for humans is that robotic caregiving can actually empower those that need the help.

↳ reply 2 — Finbel:

Plus, personally. When I’m old, if AI and robotics is really good I might truly prefer being taken cared of by a robot that takes gentle care of my crippled body while carrying stimulating conversations and remembering everything I’ve said.

Compared to the, sadly too common, current hellscape of some underpaid and over worked person who comes by and does the bare minimum (if that) in a rush before hurrying off to their next client.

↳ reply 3 — relyks:

I disagree with Bill Gates. If future androids can take care of people in their old age, they absolutely should. I'm hoping this will be the case. I was a caregiver for my grandfather. It can be very stressful. If androids can take care of my future aging family members, that will allow me and younger family members to keep them in our places of residence rather than having to move them to an assisted living facility or nursing home. That is great. There is also the bonus that humans won't have to wipe 100-year-old butts and change diapers.

Top #2 — trentnix:

The use of "human" instead of people or person is a peeve of mine. When someone says "he/she is such a good human" or "one of my favorite humans", it sounds (to me) impersonal and demeaning. A person is 3-dimensional. A person has agency. A person has purpose.

A human is just a person-shaped clump of cells.

I know I'm a bit ridiculous with my over-analysis. I know people say "human" mostly because it's a trope. But it grinds my gears nonetheless.

↳ reply 1 — devindotcom:

I would say this construction works in a context where one is comparing (overtly or not) with _inhuman_, which has its own connotations but could imply alien, machine, sub-human, etc.

Cambridge's highlighting of the word is clearly setting it in opposition to machine, or imitation humanity. To be human is a different matter than to be a person - the former is broader and a designation, the latter more, well, personal and descriptive.

But these fine distinctions do matter and attending to them makes us more conscious of how we use language.

↳ reply 2 — moffkalast:

People and person also includes aliens and sentient machines though if you count how it's used throughout scifi anyway, so it may not be accurate enough for the situation. Human is very specific.

Top #3 — ourmandave:

Of my friend, I can only say this: of all the souls I have encountered in my travels, his was the most... human.

Adm James T Kirk

item.title: Show HN: Type Fighter 2
item.description: 134 points, 59 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (typefighter2.com)

→ HN comments  ·  134 points  ·  59 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

Top #1 — richardcrng:

This is fun, nice work! Just blitzed through a few things to try it.

I've got a background in pedagogy and I'm curious about the 'sequencing'.

- I think it's probably the right call to introduce letters incrementally

- I don't know whether teaching nonsense, rare combinations is the right start

The interesting educational questions for me are:

- which are the right letters to expose people to at the start?

- what's the right way to expose people to those letters?

e.g. some heuristics to consider off the top of my head:

1. look at common words in the English language

2. look at letters that occur frequently in those words

3. teach those letters

e.g. maybe `a` and `m` are plausible starters: `am`, `ma`, `mama`, `maam`, `ama` are not nonsense (vs `dj` or `fk` or whatever it was)

To motivate that more clearly:

- I'm a touch typer but I sometimes fumbled on e.g. 's;k;;l;;;;f;j` (to exaggerate) whereas when it starts being actual words, I fumbled far less on those.

- What this demonstrates is "being able to touch type in a way that's useful practically" is a different skill to "being able to touch type arbitrary character strings".

- i.e. I'm probably substantially slower at touch typing on very rare character combinations and that's almost certainly less useful for a novice to learn

(From a learner engagement perspective, it's also probably motivation-reinforcing when they're actual words as much as possible)

Great work though! I'm a bit of a 'sequencing' nerd when it comes to education; I think the core idea, theme + UIs etc are all very strong

↳ reply 1 — OrderlyTiamat:

> I'm a touch typer but I sometimes fumbled on e.g. 's;k;;l;;;;f;j` (to exaggerate) whereas when it starts being actual words, I fumbled far less on those.

I had this exact experience. typing `mam` and `mama` etc would've been a better start I think. I have no pedagogical background though.

↳ reply 2 — XenophileJKO:

This is following the most common teaching method because hand placement is the most important component of traditional typing form.

I find it really weird we would propose learning anything but the "home" row of keys in the beginning. The whole exercise of high speed typing is having a solid orientation of the hands relative to the keyboard and returning to the home row seems pretty integral to that.

Teaching "a" and "m" without building the muscle memory of reseting to a known point seems like a recipe for disaster. You can type words better then those key combinations likely because you have already consolidated that mental process to something you don't think about.

Top #2 — WesleyJohnson:

Not a review of the game, but I'd like to just skip to typing words. I never learned home row. I tried in grade school, but it never stuck. I've been a software engineer now for 20+ years, been zoned out on computers for 30+ and I just never learned. I type well enough, ~120 WPM according to MonkeyType, but I was falling behind by the 3rd level on TypeFighter2 because home row just doesn't fit how I type.

Interestingly, and thankfully, I've avoided any form of RSI and I do attribute that largely to NOT confining myself to home row - but that's just an unverified anecdote.

↳ reply — vikingerik:

Same here. I've avoided any RSI from 40 years of typing, and I'm certain it's because I don't force my wrists into the home row position. I keep my wrists straight with the forearms so the hand is angled about 30º from perpendicular to the keyboard. My home positions are more like QWDC and NJIO (but not exactly, more like in the crevices between them, at whatever angle feels most natural for the wrists.)

I agree with the other posts saying that the home-row first levels in this game feel wrong, no actual typing works like that, give me words.

Top #3 — Kuyawa:

I wish I had this 40 years ago, still can't type without looking at the keyboard. A coworker 25 years ago could type looking at me while talking, I thought he was a kind of geek god and I wished I could do that. Well, after all these years I still can't

↳ reply 1 — commakozzi:

We had typing class in high school as an elective back in 1992 (10th grade for me), and i didn't want to take any of the other electives. Everyone made fun of me for taking what they considered a "girl's class", but I enjoyed it so much that I took it again the next year. Glad I did, because I've been a touch typist since high school AND i got to be around all the girls. edit Also, Mario Teaches Typing was a great game that helped me practice. It seemed to follow what we were doing in typing class fairly closely.

↳ reply 2 — vasac:

Even after almost three decades of using computers (counting the ZX81 and ZX Spectrum in there :) ), I still couldn’t touch type. Every few years, I’d give it another try, but the proper hand position made my wrists hurt, so I’d always have to stop. A few years later, I’d forget why I’d stopped and make another unsuccessful attempt.

Then I built a split keyboard, and it turned out that was all I needed to learn to touch type in just two weeks. I wish I’d had one in the eighties.

item.description: 303 points, 52 comments. See description for top comments.

→ HN comments  ·  303 points  ·  52 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — Topfi:

Recommend checking out Logical Intelligence, chaired by among others Yann LeCun, for more context on EBMs [0]. Has great potential in areas that LLMs traditionally do not perform that well in and, because they want to show the advantages of EBMs, also tends to be a great source of examples LLMs struggle with, like primary school level maths and counting (while ironically providing Millennium level Lean proofs). Does of course open the not unreasonable discussion of whether it matters if LLMs can accurately count when writing code to do the calculation is reliable and fast...

[0] https://logicalintelligence.com/blog/energy-based-model-sudo...

↳ reply 1 — Isamu:

Thank you for this reference, the first article summarizes what I am seeing myself:

>LLM reasoning is strong in problems where useful planning happens through language; conversation, summarization, translation, and code generation. They’re good at producing syntactically valid solutions that do roughly what you requested. LLM-generated code mostly performs, translations are mostly correct, and if they happen in a language one doesn’t likely know well (Haskell, Tagalog), the improvement over typical human performance is tremendous. But many of the problems that matter the most in the economy do not look like language.

↳ reply 2 — abeppu:

> We disabled code execution for all models in the demo, to prevent the LLMs from writing a brute-force backtracking solver in Python and running it, which would tell us something about their coding ability but nothing about their reasoning ability.

This seems sketchy. Reasoning how to solve the problem with a program is still reasoning, and if it yields programs which are more efficient (bc even a slow interpreter is faster/cheaper than an LLM) and potentially reusable, then so much the better!

↳ reply 3 — nilsherzig:

> See the live benchmark

broken login wall. truly agi.

Top #2 — program_whiz:

A clarifying way to think about this for sudoku:

For every clue, mark the probability of sampling its number in the row/col to zero. Also mark the probability of selecting a "clue cell" for modification to 0.

Pick a random cell for modification, based on its "energy" (higher energy get modified first):

    1. Every conflicting cell gets energy +1.0 (try to resolve conflicts before new empty cells).  E.g. two 7s on the same row both get +1 energy.

    2. Empty cells have small energy 0.1

    3. Filled cells with no conflicts have energy 0
For the selected cell, choose a digit. Look at numbers in its row/column, every occurrence of a number in the row/col drop prob of sampling by 90%. Example:

    | No. of 7s | chance of 7 |
    | --- | --- |
    | 0 | 10% (equal to other digits) |
    | 1 | 1% |
    | 2 | 0.1% |
Obviously this would get more complex with more numbers on the line (this is just checking 7 on otherwise empty line).

This is essentially what these models are doing. It provides a kind of "wave function collapse" search with random exploration based on "energy", but energy is just defined as conflict / unsolved. For something like a maze, energy is disconnected path segments or walls, etc.

Top #3 — mocmoc:

I've spent a year on this. EBMs while ... how to say it, they are impressive validators , it's insanely hard to train them. They are very niche specific. While LLMs , being not right all the time and clumsy and so on, they help the people to get the job done at the end.

EBM sudoku is not that hard in a small scale, and Logical Intelligence sudoku solver doesn't scale , if I'm wrong , I want to see them offering as big of a sudoku as you want.

also, after months and months training EBMs , you come to realize... it's really worth it?

↳ reply 1 — xgk:

What makes EBM hard to train?

It took a long time (including the development of GPUs, then TPUs, not to mention domain-specific languages like JAX and PyTorch with associated compilers) and scale to train LLMs. EBMs have not yet seen this level of decades of 'full-stack' optimisation.

↳ reply 2 — m3kw9:

item.title: AI is killing All About Berlin
item.description: 762 points, 686 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (nicolasbouliane.com)

→ HN comments  ·  762 points  ·  686 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — jeppester:

How do you all feel about the situation?

Is it just okay that these humongous companies just took all our work without paying us a dime?

Is it okay that they are replacing our jobs with tech that would never have existed had they not taken all that work? (or would have moved slower)

Do you feel good supporting these companies by giving them money every month?

What do you think will happen if these companies become profitable? Do you think it will have a positive effect on our society?

Personally I feel that I'm living with severe chronic cognitive dissonance - and have been for many months at this point. But I'm not sure what I can do, I have rent to pay and children to feed.

Do you all just not have this feeling? How do you combat it?

↳ reply 1 — shinycode:

I have a deep feeling that it’ll never be for our good. The strategy is “get them addicted first”, then “remove human thinking and understanding” (junior don’t learn like we did in 2000-2010) then they’ll do whatever they want. They will provide the cloud and the code and the voice for anything software related, eating up everything that is in the middle.

We can’t escape it. They are too powerful and because there is positive side effects as well, and they know it, there will always be a debate.

I feel that, the common mindset in software that you rarely see elsewhere, like in big pharma, is to open and give knowledge very broadly. But OpenAI, Anthropic absorbed everything and are not playing along. They should have continued giving free knowledge of everything as well. That’s only fair, but that’s just one way to see it.

↳↳ reply — juujian:

The problem is that the information gets stale, and nobody will have an incentive anymore to write down more up-to-date information. Then, the models will provide inaccurate information. We may be living through the glory age of AI right now if that happens.

↳↳↳ reply — boringg:

Its the forever problem of AI - its like a one time reaping of high quality data and then information goes stale because few people will provide information for free, fewer people will be motivated to build any content online, most things will get protected and locked down, open source is saturated with agents.

This is 100% the "glory" days of AI. The price is highly subsidized by investors, govt but thats going to ramp up and the product quality will dilute as they need to drive revenue for the markets. Its the same long lived strategy of every great tech company that has VC returns to feed. If OpenAI can stay private for a longer period of time they could ostensibly continue to build a better product and not be handcuffed to wallstreet in the near term.

Cost of AI will get subsidized for 3-4 years while corporate america gets addicted, then pricing will ramp up and corporate ameria will be dependent. This has been said millions of times over.

↳ reply 2 — dspillett:

> Do you all just not have this feeling?

I certainly do.

> How do you combat it?

I handed my notice in last Friday. The newest CEO wants "AI at the heart of everything we do" and so it is at the heart of my departure. Actually I've been unhappy in tech since 2020, full time remote work is bad for my mental health and even though I go into the office I'm still remote because most of the people I work with are elsewhere. I never wanted to work for a large company (and refused job offers for more money for that reason in the post) for similar reasons and have been "forced" into that as we were bought by an international outfit just over a year ago. AI is just the final bale of hay.

This is professional suicide for me, of course. I'm not qualified for anything else that isn't also going to be remote, fully AI infused, or both, so for some time at least I'll most likely end up stacking shelves or waiting tables for a third (maybe a half with long hours) of what I have been earning. I have the luxury of a paid mortgage (it is a small flat, but it is all mine), no debts, some savings, and no dependents other than the cats - others are not so lucky so couldn't make this choice even if they wanted to.

↳ reply 3 — glimshe:

I don't like hearing that AI is bringing you and the article's author hardship. But I think it's more complicated than tech companies taking away work through greed. Technological progress is the culprit here and this time you're the victim, unfortunately.

That site's business model is similar to the many paper magazines you'd get for free in tourist welcome centers, hotels and on the street. Companies (usually very small) who published those guides got replaced by the website. Some small publisher likely felt the same a few years ago.

A family member used to own a magazine about arts and crafts that went bankrupt because of Youtube creators and free Internet articles - well before AI. It was a small magazine and profits were just enough to maintain a middle-class lifestyle. Random people online, relying on technology, destroyed his livelihood and he has been struggling ever since.

You can try using laws and spreading the word against progress, but it's certain you'll lose in the end. I'm not saying it's not worth it because you may delay it long enough to give you time to settle elsewhere, but change will come against our will.

Top #2 — nicbou:

Hey, I'm Nicolas from All About Berlin. This post is a few months old. I went through a psychological rollercoaster since I wrote it. Things got worse, but so far, I can still live from the website. Next year might be my last year running it full time.

I'm traveling at the moment, but I'll grab a drink and read this thread later today. In the meantime, feel free to email me. Reader mail would be a lovely break from the flood of LLM-generated outreach emails.

I rarely comment here, but this warrants a comment. I've been a big fan of All About Berlin since I moved to Germany. Such a well-put, precise, concise and reliable source of information for immigrants. I appreciate you and your work, and I'm really sad to see how things are turning up for developers like you, and valuable projects like these.

↳ reply 2 — lnrd:

Your website was a lifesaver when I moved to Berlin, finding reliable information about how to deal with all the quirks and customs of Germany really made my life infinitely easier. I still use it from time to time.

It sucks what's happening. Not sure how to reach your audience, but your work is still relevant. Maybe you could publish it as a book and get it distributed around the city where newly coming people might find it.

Also you should consider translating your content into video format and establish a social media presence. Your content is still valuable for newcomers (and expats in general) so you could find a new way for your audience to find you now that Google search is dead.

Top #3 — adamddev1:

People are being conditioned to think that all the answers come from AI, or that AI knows everything.

But AI is only getting (inaccurate shadows of) the info from these sources which it is simultaneously working to kill. (Websites like this, StackOverflow, human written code)

What happens when there are no more sources and everyone just expects AI to answer everything or write everything? Recursive self-improvement? I doubt it.

↳ reply 1 — MrScruff:

While I know what you mean, the reality is that for many types of query the cost of extracting relevant information from the web has been trending upwards as a result of people gaming the attention economy. There are of course exceptions like wikipedia.

AI has cut through that trend and that's why people use it.

↳↳ reply — nitwit005:

> AI has cut through that trend and that's why people use it.

Likely temporarily. Those same people are trying to get the AI to show the result they want, just how they tried to get Google search results to show the result they want.

I don't see any particular reason to think Google will succeed this time when they failed before.

↳ reply 2 — ironborn123:

Exactly. For factual stuff that updates occassionally like the local scene or local laws the models will have to source original content from somewhere.

I wonder if the solution is to stop giving free updates on your website, and then contact the big model makers that you have been using my content for free but its no longer updated. If you really want updates i will provide a paid api or rss feed for you to consume. or just sign a retainer contract with me.

I would like to think most model makers should agree to this or risk providing outdated/hallucinatory info to their users.

some kind of collective action where a lot of popular content owners form associations and negotiate together may work even better.

item.title: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
item.description: 259 points, 135 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (kernel.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  259 points  ·  135 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — tristanj:

It's pretty obvious that Gemini 4 Carbon is not token efficient. It also has relatively low tokens-per-second compared to other models. I can think of several reasons why this is the case:

1. Google has huge amounts of cash and compute. Their goal was to train a model that that has the highest quality & frontier performance, not create a model that's efficient to run and serve. They have other models for that, like Hydrogen.

2. Google created Carbon without caring for inference costs. DeepMind is subsidized by the rest of Google's empire. Selling inference is an insignificant part of Google's revenue. But for Anthropic and OpenAI, selling inference is their entire business model. Anthropic and OpenAI have enormous incentive to sell as much inference as they can in the most efficient manner. Google doesn't have this incentive.

3. They are one of the few companies that can be inefficient. Out of all the frontier labs, Google DeepMind is probably the least constrained by compute. Chinese labs have around 10 to 100 times less compute, so they must release highly optimized models.

↳ reply 1 — kyrra:

1) "Gemini 4 Hydrogen is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon." From https://deepmind.google/models/model-cards/gemini-4-hydrogen... . Also, the Agy team is pushing is that Carbon is a great planner, and then use hydrogen as the worker. They want people to use it.

2) lots of people inside Google use carbon. If they didn't care about it, it wouldn't have been pushed on all of Google.

3) Deepmind is competing with cloud and others. they are the only Frontier Lab that actually has to compete with other business units within an org for compute. GCP and others want that compute as well.

(Googler, opinions are my own)

↳↳ reply — zamadatix:

1. Small, efficient models are often derived from "the best" models. That doesn't mean "the best models" are efficient too.

2. GP said they don't care about cost, not they don't care about the model

3. Competing for existing compute + being able to assign the projects own capex investment for new compute provides more compute than needing to assign all compute via new capex investment. But it's hard to say if that's actually the type of case or not unless Google wants to tell everyone publicly - so I'd take that point with a grain of salt in either way.

↳ reply 2 — aberoham:

Google's frontend web servers routinely time out connections from agy (the antigravity cli) when using Carbon, wasting tons of work. Like any effort level more than "low" is completely unusable.

It looks as if Carbon often takes more than 240 seconds thinking, which I'd guess appears as a silent connection to Google's load balancers, which then drop what it thinks is a stalled connection.

One hopes that Gemini's serving stack is smart enough to cancel these torn-down connections, but maybe they're not and this is leading to all sorts of ghost TPU load.

Disclaimer: We spend millions on GCP per month and have a dedicated customer engineer. Even they are horrified at the glacial pace of the Gemini fixes.

↳ reply 3 — npn:

4. they are so behind that they can not create effective datasets like other frontier labs do. So instead they do all the tricks the Chinese labs do: using RL with the single purpose of benchmaxxing the AA score.

Look how all Chinese models, or haiku/luna class US models behave, you can see the same pattern: they think too much and only work well with a subset of tasks

Top #2 — hetspookjee:

Might be the only one in the thread but ever since Gemini 4 Argon. I’ve become a huge fan of the Google models. I do use Carbon most of the time since it’s become available but notice that i also am falling back more and more on Argon again without much difference. For security purposes argon has far fewer triggers. I only use the Google models as orchestrator for how they talk and analyse. I let it delegate everything to Astra / Fable / Opus models

↳ reply 1 — eitally:

I've also become a fan. For most of my current projects I'm using Agy with the Carbon orchestrator, but switch to Hydrogen when I'm bantering back & forth. It's convenient, with things like Swarm, to have an orchestrator that can automate the selection of models for sub-agents. I've used quite a few harnesses -- both for local and cloud dev -- and although Claude Code has some clear feature benefits over Antigravity (for desktop/sandbox control & interaction), I'm generally very happy.

↳ reply 2 — wronglebowski:

I do like Argon, but usage continues to be an issue for me. The economics of everything pales in comparison to the value you get with DeepSeek. I'll end up using my limited opaque usage based limit with Antigravity to have Argon review something or maybe write a plan, but the bulk of the work has to be done with cheaper models.

Top #3 — fwee:

Carbon is slow, but I've also realized that it works really well. I don't need to get involved or keep checking the results over and over again. I think it's pretty close to Opus 5.5 in terms of work quality.

I have no doubt that Google will adjust its training to find a better balance between speed and intelligence, just like they did with Gemini Flash (3.7 -> 3.8, slower but smarter).

The orchestrator and swarm modes are also interesting. Even though Carbon is slow, it can delegate tasks to other models. (They're both as slow as Carbon, but I think they have potential.)

Anyway, great article!

In "Empire of AI", the author mentions that when OpenAI included public GitHub repositories in its training data, the resulting model achieved better results even in fields unrelated to programming.

Aside from the obvious applications in biochemistry, could protein sequences also be used as a new training data source to improve overall model quality? Software is used in all fields, and github issues and PRs are going to contain detailed reasoning about all sorts of things when adding features or fixing bugs.

Right

> GitHub repositories ... in fields unrelated to programming

About as surprising as training on books and improving in fields other than writing.

↳ reply 2 — dekhn:

It seems not entirely unreasonable to expect that training on large biological sequence repositories could uncover structure that is applicable to information theory. There has been a great deal of cross-pollination between those two fields.

Claude just blocks from anything in this field. Can't even work with my own DNA without triggering opus 5.5 50% of the time

I'm told by colleagues in the life sciences and pharma space that it isn't just "safety" but more like artificial market segmentation. Claude has no way of knowing whether the DNA you're working with is yours. And you probably wouldn't want to change that.

item.title: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
item.description: 677 points, 526 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (revscope.co)

→ HN comments  ·  677 points  ·  526 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — pcarolan:

When you typed who is on snl tonight? You used to get 10 pages of clickbait that made you scroll down endlessly for the answer. The best product for most questions is to just give you the answer. That said, the death of discovery is worth mourning. I hope someone solves it but this was dying before ai came along. SEO killed the web, AI killed SEO, and so it goes…

↳ reply 1 — taurath:

> You used to get 10 pages of clickbait that made you scroll down endlessly for the answer.

And before that, you would get the an exact, human written page for what you searched for, which is why Google was able to make money in the first place.

This is a Google search problem, and they could have defeated SEO sites if it weren't more profitable for them. SEOs didn't force Google to put 8 ads between the search bar and the first non-ad result, Google did.

Whatever Google is now, nobody would actually choose it if there were alternatives that competed on product, but there aren't.

We all live in duopoly land where every extremely high margin software and hardware role is taken up by 2 of 7 companies.

↳↳ reply — smelendez:

> And before that, you would get the an exact, human written page for what you searched for, which is why Google was able to make money in the first place.

Google wasn’t really good for questions like “who is hosting SNL?” until pretty late in the game. The Huffington Post made a big deal in the early 2010s about posting articles like “What time is the Super Bowl?” The SEO wars started pretty much immediately after that.

But before that you probably would have had to go to a TV listings site or go to the NBC page for SNL, which may or may not have had the answer, possibly embedded in a Flash interactive.

↳↳↳ reply — xp84:

I remember that era. Honestly it was a bit more work but it wasn’t unpleasant work finding information. We 2000s-era netizens just learned the names of sites like IMDB, wunderground.com, WebMD, Mapquest, ZDNET… different sites for different purposes.

(Just as we had multiple big retailers, in different narrow categories, like CDNOW.com, before Amazon.) All the consolidation into Google for every information need is unhealthy at best.

↳ reply 2 — beefsack:

The big thing that scares me with this is how it's driving further traffic consolidation to the big players.

It feels like the web has just become either social media or AI. There isn't any room for smaller sites to find users anymore.

↳ reply 3 — neya:

It's not just death of discovery. This is theft. They scraped your website, built a knowledge base out of it with the promise of sending you people to you. But only now, they use it to answer the questions themselves and cut you off. Classic middleman play.

Top #2 — asdfasgasdgasdg:

If Google didn’t put those there, people would be going to other LLMs to get their answers quickly. I don’t know how this ends but I strongly doubt any unilateral effort to withhold llm service by Google changes the medium term outcome.

↳ reply 1 — slashdev:

I think it's actually wise of Google to disrupt themselves this way. If they don't the AI companies will do it for them, and they'll have no control over the process nor chance to recover lost ad income. As per the article, Google managed to pull this off without hurting ad revenue (surprise!)

Disclaimer: I wrote the blog post and submitted it

↳↳ reply — riffraff:

But ad revenue is hurt, according to google it self, isn't it?

https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cm9qzdqpxy48o

↳↳↳ reply — eli:

"total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn"

They made lots of money on ads, that was just a little market blip because that's an honest reason it wasn't even higher.

↳ reply 2 — fishfasell:

Exactly, people treated Google like it was AI long before the rise of LLMs. Now they actually get the answer they're looking for rather than searching through a sea of web links.

Top #3 — julenx:

When I first connected to the internet in the mid 90s the www was young, and there were still traces of pre-www internet information services such as Compuserve, AOL, etc. They acted as subscription-based computer networks that provided access to curated content (and more). I never got their point back then, but I understand they were walled gardens of information.

Fast forward to today, we have witnessed the open web grow, provide capabilities that were unthinkable of, but information-wise, it looks as though we are going back in time. AI answers/overviews shield users from the complexity and uneven quality of the raw internet, but at the expense of cannibalizing traffic to the origin, thus becoming the information gatekeeper and ending up owning the discourse.

Knowing that laymen use frontier chat providers as search engines too, all in all these are becoming centralized information brokers that filter the wider internet to keep users inside a single platform.

Ads died though.

On the other hand, Apple should have voluntarily done the archiving. Predictably they didn't and wouldn't, because the only single thing these companies care about is profit and everything else can happily go to shit.

In a just world, Apple's refusal to spend the absolutely miniscule amount of effort to archive the forum themselves would earn them a massive reputational stain and they'd face an enormous backlash for effectively spitting on the very people who allow them to exist.

That won't happen, because consumers simply don't care. Corporations have proven time and time again that consumers will tolerate - or even celebrate - being trampled upon as long as their new shiny baubles make them feel superior in some way.

It is a travesty that Apple's support forum was created virtually exclusively by volunteers, and it's a travesty that it's up to other volunteers to ensure its ongoing survival.

Fuck Apple, squarely and truly and wholeheartedly. Fuck Apple.

item.title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
item.description: 870 points, 419 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.cloudflare.com)

→ HN comments  ·  870 points  ·  419 comments  ·  comments as of 23h

Top #1 — hypfer:

I think a lot of discourse about these topics still assumes that the Internet is where the nerds and the good people live, which is why it fails.

The Internet has eaten the world and everyone is there. All the people are there.

Holding up the idea that all of its infra must be "neutral" like a road and pass through everything doesn't work when everyone is there.

For a stable world, the majority needs to be steered away from the most troublesome things in ways they do not comprehend or notice, because trying to convince them that they probably shouldn't do something is an exercise in futility.

Doing this on a DNS level is good, actually, precisely because it is so easy to bypass by people that matter and are more lucid, open to reason, etc.

Of course, providers don't like that. And there are risks like slippery slopes and all, but I do not see an alternative to this? I do see alternatives, but their either do not achieve what needs to be achieved or are actually worse.

The dream of the Internet is dead. Now we have something else. The sooner we accept that, the sooner we can start coming up with new and better dreams that ideally do not die the same death.

↳ reply 1 — Vinnl:

> Holding up the idea that all of its infra must be "neutral" like a road and pass through everything doesn't work when everyone is there.

I don't see how that follows? Everyone's on the road too, and it seems to work best to keep those neutral?

↳↳ reply — hypfer:

Huh? No, on the road you only find road-legal vehicles piloted by people with a driver's license, which is inaccessible to people known for doing crimes relating to the infrastructure etc etc.

Roads are then governed by strict rules and you lose your access to those if you do not comply.

Meaning that roads (just like all shared infrastructure) are already a state-filtered thing.

The filters are just calibrated sensibly, meaning that your first thought was not "they're policed and I am oppressed" but "huh, but roads are free, actually?"

__

I did feed this exchange into gemini after the fact and it painted this nice picture that I think might be helpful to better convey what I am trying to convey:

> Actual freedom on a highway would mean dodging uninspected, brake-less, 10-ton vehicles driven by 12-year-olds at 150 miles per hour. That would be terrifying.

> What the user calls "freedom" is actually just a highly restrictive environment where the restrictions perfectly align with his personal habits. Because the user doesn't want to drive a homemade tank drunk at 150mph, he never hits the invisible wall of state friction. Therefore, he assumes the wall doesn't exist.

↳↳↳ reply — Vinnl:

I don't know where Gemini got that I referred to freedom. But I don't think the roads themselves are technically/mechanically deciding who gets to use them.

(They sort-of can, of course - modal filters are a thing. But neutral roads seem to work just fine, too. Of course, we do have other methods of policing who uses them, but like in the DNS case, they do still get used for crime. We accept that.)

↳ reply 2 — zwarag:

> For a stable world, the majority needs to be steered away from the most troublesome things in ways they do not comprehend or notice, because trying to convince them that they probably shouldn't do something is an exercise in futility.

We live in a democracy. It is the duty of every one of us to face things for what they are. The whole safety thing that democracy gives us grew out of people facing reality. If we steer away from that it will be highjacked by people using the fears to control how you vote. We need brave people with agency. Not people that hide and get manipulated.

↳ reply 3 — lokar:

item.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
item.description: 311 points, 421 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (complexdiscovery.com)

→ HN comments  ·  311 points  ·  421 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — alkonaut:

I find AI writes code as least as well as I do (with 25yoe). So I'm now mostly reviewing. But I also find it reviews code better for issues than I do. A LOT better than I do. Now, finding "issues" isn't the only reason to review. It's also for understanding. But for "issue finding" my agent can just review it's own code (Or rather, agents review each other's code). It works, and produces acceptable quality code. I don't find there's a buggy and bloated mess left behind any more. It's by no means perfect, but this is like self driving cars: what's being replaced sure wasn't perfect either.

I'm very good at telling agents what to do. That's not a problem. I understand a code base I worked 20 years in like no one else. The problem creeps in slowly: the less I know about this code base, the worse I'll be at directing agents. They'll do ok on their own, and they can certainly help me understand code too in a way my colleagues never could. But still, I'm slowly becoming less and less familiar with my own code base. In a few years, it would be foreign to me. And I would be describing changes in terms of high level features instead of architectural changes, refactorings and so on, that I do now. And I don't yet trust the LLMs to do a good job with that. So right now there's sort of a honeymoon period when the human understanding of code is good, and the LLMs are finally good enough to write and modify code. But I wonder what will happen after that.

↳ reply 1 — cjonas:

The problem isn't its coding or its ability to review code... the problem is its ability to apply the right solutions. AI tends to do really well at high level architecture, but then starts to fall apart when there are 1000 mini decisions needed to implement that architecture. Further more, it will absolutely brute force whatever requirements it's been handed from an "authoritative" source. IOW, it's much more likely to be critical of design decision when they originated from its own context window, than those that are handed down from a ticket, design document, or another agent.

↳ reply 2 — gwbas1c:

I've found that the way I strike a balance is to:

1: Carefully pick critical areas that I do by hand, and have AI do the other 90%.

2: Make small changes by hand before / after doing the work with AI.

Most important: Slowly rotate the areas that I do by hand. This way, I keep my hands-on knowledge good enough to give AI knowledgeable instructions.

↳ reply 3 — osigurdson:

We should probably take a step back and think about why we ever did code review in the first place. I'd say there were two primary forms: "mentor review" and "peer review".

"Mentor review" describes the situation where there is a knowledge imbalance between the author and reviewer. It can represent an onboarding situation but it isn't static - there are always areas of the codebase that some people are more familiar with than others.

A "peer review" is more the situation where both the author and reviewer have similar knowledge in a given area. The purpose of the review here is primarily to look for oversights.

I'd say, the peer review should be deprecated at this point. AI can generally do a better job at looking for minor / localized problems. The "mentor" type review should stay however as it is still very valuable.

Top #2 — littlecranky67:

For a couple of year I have been reviewing code in my team and my job is only to review and coach other junior/intermediate members of the team - not to develop new features myself. The problem with AI is the merge requests now contain more code and often the chosen solution is overblown/overdesigned for what actually needs to be done.

With human coding, the lazyness of the developer and the urge to keep things simple and deliver faster often leads to simple solutions (with a time/effort/return tradeoff). With AI, I get overblown MRs that work, but oftentimes could be simpler (with said tradeoffs). So my work has become more difficult and time consuming, and the codebases grows faster. And I don't think my team members learn or grow at the same rate as they did before.

Now, I have no strong feelings against AI - it is just a tool afterall. And I have no experience what the long-term effects of this will be (just as anybody else).

↳ reply 1 — wombat-man:

Yeah this is my finding too. Sometimes it adds quite a bit that is only very marginally better.

↳ reply 2 — jijijijij:

>With human coding, the lazyness of the developer and the urge to keep things simple and deliver faster often leads to simple solutions (with a time/effort/return tradeoff).

I believe this will become one of the biggest tech debts generated right now. AI removes the pressure of inefficiencies and bad decisions across the board. There likely is even going to be a new equilibrium far worse than what we got today, only manageable by AI, but with "productivity" gains lost to inefficiency and complexity.

I don't see how any other outcome would be possible.

Top #3 — AlwaysRock:

All I do all day is review ai written code. my own or teammates. I really do not enjoy it.

↳ reply 1 — pmarreck:

The irony is that I actually don't mind reviewing code, but I've already taken that step out of the equation using a set of guidelines I've developed over the past year working with these things. The vast majority of which I have barely reviewed code in. In well-working results.

Your goal should be to automate and remove yourself out of the process as much as possible while maintaining quality, while also remaining confident that you will still be valuable.

↳↳ reply — pmg101:

This sounds good and is the sort of thing I hear a lot, but fundamentally I don't think it makes any sense.

Either I read, understand, and can therefore trust the code.

Or I don't read it, don't fully understand it, and I'm just trusting AI to get it right, but have no way to know if it has done.

So far I'm in Column A and it's working well. We're going much faster than we used to.

↳↳↳ reply — jwilliams:

Does it have to be one or the other for every PR? For me that is a _lot_ in the grey - i.e. LGTM and even if it was wrong, the blast radius is very small. Combined with auto testing and rollbacks.

↳ reply 2 — jayd16:

If AI makes the job 10% faster, it certainly makes it 10x less enjoyable.

Also — ★ simonw:

Here's the actual paper: https://fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf

Key methodology:

> We leverage a novel proprietary dataset from Jellyfish (JF), an analytics platform that companies use to understand the activity of their software engineering teams. Our data allows us to measure details of the software production process, covering 445 million work events of 720,542 workers across 655 firms, from January 2021 to August 2026. JF combines data from industry-standard software engineering tools, and we use four of these tools: (1) code version control systems, such as GitHub, which track engineers’ code; (2) issue management systems, such as Jira, which measure engineers’ progress on and completion of software tasks and projects; (3) scheduling tools, such as Google Calendar, which capture meeting activity and time allocation; and (4) generative AI usage at the firm and worker level, for GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code.

item.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
item.description: 1143 points, 317 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (calif.io)

→ HN comments  ·  1143 points  ·  317 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — lucasluitjes:

From the section on performing heap grooming over the network ("Remote Heap Feng Shui"):

> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.

And the "Limitations" section:

> There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.

Based on the complexity and constraints, short-term mass-exploitation seems unlikely. It will take some time before there are reliable exploits, and they may require running on infra close to the target.

But a long tail of unpatched java applications/services at high-value targets getting exploited, seems plausible to me.

↳ reply 1 — agilob:

>It will take some time before there are reliable exploits, and they may require running on infra close to the target.

Think that you're targeting KeyCloak and have a semi-working exploit that dumps some parts of heap memory with live tokens. You can go after 100s of banks globally, whole Tesco infra, dozens of gov.uk websites including HMRC and Home Office, azure containers... you know, anyone mature not do write their own auth server: https://www.shodan.io/search?query=keycloak

↳↳ reply — ptman:

https://www.keycloak.org/2026/11/java4shell-vulnerability-cv...

↳ reply 2 — afavour:

Yes, I guess the TL;DR is the chances of a drive by attack are low, but a sufficiently motivated actor with a specific target in mind might be able to exploit it.

So, patch your systems, governments!

↳ reply 3 — tru3_power:

Decoder route pretty low bar given basic auth right? I think the higher bar is the hardware requirements for exploitation

Top #2 — ievans:

Super impressive work by Calif as usual.

The exploit conditions are very specific but there are still going to be a lot of hosts impacted. We at Semgrep published some free detection scripts here: https://github.com/semgrep/detection-scripts/tree/main/CVE-2...

They look for these five conditions:

  * HotSpot VM: any OpenJDK build, Oracle JDK, or GraalVM JDK. Only HotSpot generates the stub. OpenJ9 and GCJ are OK. Azul Prime (Zing), which replaces C2 with its own JIT, and any VM name not recognized as HotSpot are [?], never [!].
  * x86-64 JVM on an x86-64 host.
  * Version 17.0.6 or later, not at or above a version listed in FIXED_IN, and no newer than the newest releases checked (see below). Newer versions are [?]: they may carry the fix.
  * The JVM reports avx512_vbmi and avx512bw, and UseAVX >= 3.
  * Base64 intrinsics are on and C2/JVMCI can compile. These turn it off: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, -Xint, -XX:TieredStopAtLevel below 4.

↳ reply 1 — bikezen:

The write-up itself matches your version assumption, however it also says:

> According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time.

So according to Oracle at least, JRE8 versions are affected as well.

↳↳ reply — xur17:

25.0.5.0.3 is the latest on the 25 version [0]. Does that mean no patch is available?

[0] https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/jdk25-archiv...

↳↳↳ reply — rhdunn:

That's the archive page for older downloads. The main download page [1] reports the latest version as 25.0.5.1.

[1] https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25

↳ reply 2 — ktm5j:

They mention GraalVM being affected, but it seems like it isn't when I run their PoC:

  kmiles@dora tmp.wdOJ2BRVwa % /opt/graalvm/bin/java Base64Trigger 
  runtime=21.0.5+9-LTS-jvmci-23.1-b48
  vm=Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM
  rejected=true changed=0 first=-1 last=-1
  NOT REPRODUCED

Top #3 — leca:

What’s that old Chinese proverb? “May you live in interesting times”? It feels like we’re living in interesting times. How long will it take for a bad actor to seriously compromise critical infrastructure? My bet is within six months.

The upside is that it’ll force legacy institutions and organizations with sub-par security to get good at security and modernize their legacy stacks. That, or get pwned in short order.

↳ reply 1 — nedt:

No single exploit should be able to take down critical infrastructure. If it does the setup is broken. Security is layers around it and the layers shouldn't trust each other nor should they be fully depended on them.

↳ reply 2 — tomkarho:

I always thought that was a curse. One of two-parter:

1. May you live in interesting times

2. May you find what you're looking for

Also — hypfer:

Given that this is AVX512-only...how many enterprises are out there that run vulnerable java applications on non-intel servers?

Genuine question. Everything I see is Intel all the time. I know that people at home switched to AMD, but they don't run enterprise java.

I also have been told that apparently EPYC was hyped for a while and some hosters give you that. But do corporations run the java applications there?

The name makes it sound like Log4J or the PHP thing, but from what I can tell right now, it kinda isn't all that relevant?

↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

The Log4j comparison is always a little frustrating, because it sets the bar somewhere in the neighborhood of "apocalyptic". If you're someone who believes our response to serious vulnerabilities is inadequate, you can see how Log4Shell gives a lot of cover to companies.

It is wild to find a generalizable (if platform-specific) memory corruption vulnerability in Java core Base64 handling; the tornado sirens should clearly be going off. But yes, it's not as bad as Log4Shell.

item.title: jQuery 4.1.0
item.description: 338 points, 177 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  338 points  ·  177 comments

Top #1 — noduerme:

The composability of jQuery has been an inspiration for the way I design my own frameworks and tools.

One thing I still regularly use jQuery for, though, that's rarely mentioned, is its event model. You can put a listener on any object, not just things in the DOM. Any data object can trigger an event. This is incredibly powerful for isolating logic from DOM elements and events. A frequent use case is for DOM elements to contain a reference to a data object that may be replicated elsewhere on the page. The data object sets up and tears down visual elements, listening for interaction, then dispatches a custom event. Your core logic listens for events on the data object instead of on every individual element that might refer to it. I usually delegate the draw routine for e.g. html snippets of a card or an interactive element to the data object itself in a draw() function that returns a string which incidentally jQuery handles quite nicely inserting into the DOM without needing to explicitly call createElement.

I wrote my own implementation of this a long time ago, but in the end, that feature plus the other ergonomics of jQuery still make it my go-to today over vanilla js. And pretty much everything I write is without any reactive framework (other than my own vanilla component/templating/remoting system), so the overhead is barely noticeable.

↳ reply — devsda:

> The composability of jQuery has been an inspiration for the way I design my own frameworks and tools

Not just as a framework but its documentation is also probably an inspiration for later libs. It was the first site for me where you could see the code and result together on the same page at the same place. And the discoverability of widgets was also great and exciting in a way.

Just open the firebug console, and try the examples for selectors, callbacks etc.

Top #2 — hax0ron3:

Although jQuery isn't very relevant these days, I still find its pattern of chaining a sequence of methods on a set chosen by a selector to be a beautiful example of going with a language's features.

↳ reply 1 — btown:

To that point, there was a conscious choice that the return type of most method invocations (except in specific "read a value" modes) should be a standardized container type.

That was, and still is, rare! And in a time without type checking and bundling, it was vital. Match your parentheses and quotes, and your jquery code might not find what you want, but it would (likely) not throw exceptions.

For those unfamiliar, I recommend looking at https://github.com/DefinitelyTyped/DefinitelyTyped/blob/mast... and searching for the 201 instances of

    : this
in that file. A remarkably fluent API. We could all be so elegant.

↳↳ reply — submain:

I'm just sitting and waiting until someone mentions "monads"...

↳↳↳ reply — hax0ron3:

I considered doing it in my top-level comment but I decided not to, since I don't actually know enough about monads to be sure that I know what I'm talking about, lol.

↳ reply 2 — franciscop:

This is one of the first things I learned in programming. A friend back in University showed me a bit of his code (neither of us were in CS), and I was like why are you returning `this`? Then he showed me this chaining. I only found it a "cool trick" at the moment, who'd told me that I'd end up loving it the more I learned programming. I've made two of my main libraries, `umbrellajs` and a plumbing one called `swear` (chaining but for promises, some chaining syntax sugar on top of promises basically), based on this. I stopped doing it too much in recent years, but still it's amazing.

Top #3 — CM30:

I'm a tad surprised jQuery still exists, though it's kinda neat it does. Always interesting to see historical projects with less and less modern day relevance get continued like this.

And while most of the use cases for jQuery have long since died out with things like classList, querySelector, etc, I do feel there's probably value in a framework that focuses on minor enhancements to a site rather than being the backbone of the whole thing. Like if you want a React or Angular or Vue equivalent, something like jQuery would be a terrible choice, but a lot of sites are static ones where the only scripting needed would be for minor things like dropdown menus or slideshows, and I can see a modern, lean library like this being a decent choice there.

↳ reply 1 — dalemhurley:

There is a heap of indie devs that swear by jQuery and avoid the frameworks like react. Each has their use cases.

↳↳ reply — smt88:

What’s a use case for jQuery over vanilla JS?

When most code is and will be written by AI, why would I sacrifice performance for syntactic sugar?

↳↳↳ reply — xp84:

Serious question: On modern hardware how much performance is jQuery actually taking away from you? Compared to the ridiculous overkill factor of using React for simple static pages, a practice I see everywhere now, the time it takes jQuery to parse seems inconsequential.

↳ reply 2 — liendolucas:

I would probably use Hyperscript for that use case: https://hyperscript.org/

There's a charming small museum just (west) outside Copenhagen, that used to be the Ole Rømer Museum, worth considering for a visit if you are nearby.

Site (https://kroppedal.dk/astronomi/) is only in Danish, rough translation of part:

"The museum is situated just a stone's throw from the astronomer Ole Rømer’s Observatorium Tusculanum, where the world’s first meridian circle was built—marking the beginning of a new chapter in the precise measurement of stellar positions. Ole Rømer had the observatory built on his father-in-law’s land in 1704, hoping to escape the disturbances of the big city. In 1973, the site of the observatory was rediscovered, leading to the establishment of an "Ole Rømer Museum" — the direct predecessor to the current Kroppedal Museum.

Today, Kroppedal Museum covers the entire history of Danish astronomy, from the time of Tycho Brahe to the present day."

Great if you like old astronomical instruments!

Top #3 — kstrauser:

I don’t quite understand this. The length of the eclipse would be the same, right? Or was it more like that the eclipse ended 10 minutes earlier on the wall clock than expected? I guess what would surprise me about that is:

1. I didn’t know clocks were that good by then to make that reliably measurable.

2. I didn’t realize clocks of the time could measure the period of the eclipse that accurately. Like say one took 24 hours and 7 minutes. If you’re off by 30 seconds, and you’re making a prediction today of when the eclipse would happen six months from now, you could easily be off 90 minutes just based on cumulative error.

The discovery seems easy enough given today’s widespread access to atomic clocks, but extra freaking impressive with clocks from the 1600s.

↳ reply 1 — adrian_b:

The pendulum clock had been invented by Christiaan Huygens a couple of decades earlier.

It became quickly widespread, especially at astronomical observatories.

It is likely that the recent availability of accurate pendulum clocks was essential for Rømer's measurements, so such a result about the speed of light would have been impossible for the previous generation of astronomers.

Nonetheless, inside a fixed astronomical observatory, where there has been built a meridian circle with a telescope, and if there is available a good catalogue of stars, it is possible to measure the current "sidereal time" and use differences in sidereal times to compute the corresponding differences in time, even without a clock. The sidereal time is not a time, but the angle of rotation of the Earth vs. the stars. The rotation of the Earth vs. the stars is much more uniform than the apparent movement of the Sun on the sky, which determines the days.

So it would have been possible, but in a much more difficult way, to measure accurately the duration of some astronomical events even without clocks, but only with accurate instruments for measuring angles, used to determine the celestial coordinates of the stars, then compute the difference in the transit times of some stars whose transits coincided with the beginning and the end of the duration that must be measured, from the angles between them.

When good clocks are available, it is easier to measure the transit times of the stars and compute the angles between them from the times, than the reverse procedure, which would be needed without good clocks.

↳↳ reply — dguest:

The "shoulders of giants" aren't just those of other scientists.

There's a whole view of history in which the major advances aren't caused by great people but rather by incremental improvements to measurement, manufacturing, and the economic base that powers them. Maybe it's less popular because asking students to memorize names and dates is easier than asking them to understand technology.

Something similar happened in end of the 1800s: searches for a luminiferous aether through which light propagated came back empty, which lead to Lorentz invariance and eventually special relativity. The whole development took a few decades. Physics wasn't just waiting around for Einstein to discover it, he just happened to be born at the right time.

↳ reply 2 — canpan:

To measure longer periods count the number of days. We have a built in clock which is relatively exact: The rotation of the earth. You only need a clock that measures time correctly during one day, much easier. Which existed at a time.

For the other point, and how he did, i guess the article is badly written. This should be better: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%B8mer%27s_determination_o... (he didnt need to measure months/years)

item.description: 333 points, 105 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (solidjs.com)

→ HN comments  ·  333 points  ·  105 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — wk_end:

What's amusing and/or interesting is that the stuff under "Built to Be Written by Agents" also would make it easier to write by hand, I imagine. It's just better debug diagnostics; nothing really to do with agentic development specifically.

Maybe that's just marketing, but it's really intriguing how human best practices are also agent best practices; how, maybe, we've reached a point where even devs aren't recognizing agent best practices as human best practices anymore; and how suddenly best practices are being prioritized in a way they often weren't - humans could/would/were expected to suck it up and deal with poor devex, but agents simply can't. A strange sort of victory for us folks who cared about it.

↳ reply 1 — lemming:

A friend of mine who works a lot with AI commented that working with AI was making him develop like a grownup for the first time. Turns out that all the best practices really do carry over, but the consequence of not doing it is greater with agents.

↳↳ reply — gwerbin:

Same here, bigtime.

AI has forced me to write out more planning documents. Not waterfall strategic planning, but tactical planning such as describing the desired behavior of a script before I write it, or pre-registering a data analysis and my expected findings in writing before I start querying data -- that goes in a PLAN.md within whatever folder I'm working on at the moment.

I now keep a systematic todo list that I call TASKS.md, which groups tasks into topical sections and every task has an ID, such as MD3 or EV7.

I also keep an append-only-ish journal of results, findings, unfinished thoughts, rejected ideas, etc.

All of that goes right into my project Git repo. It works great for both AI agents and humans.

But perhaps more interesting than my new workflows, is that I actually learn things from the AI. The idea to start pre-registering all my little analyses, not just the big tasks, was a Claude-ism that I've since adopted even when I'm not using AI.

↳↳↳ reply — hdjrudni:

I do TODO.md instead of TASKS.md but what's the benefit of giving each task an ID? Just easier for you to refer to a specific task? I usually just paste the whole line if I need to refer to it, but given it a short ID might not be a bad idea.

↳ reply 2 — novacrazy:

Kind of the same reason Rust works very well with agents, good error messages and strict type system. Harder to screw up for humans and bots alike.

↳ reply 3 — TheCapeGreek:

Sure, it can be marketing, but I think it's more that it has become evident that the best way to get agents to write code you can trust, at a scale that actually improves productivity, usually means adopting and enforcing best practices at a scale that the industry silently really wasn't doing at all.

I've spent the last few years banging on a drum about teams installing linters, static analyzers, and similar in Laravel teams. I get nods of agreement from seniors but little willpower from managers, who just want to see the number of commits line go up.

Surprise surprise, now that I am in charge of a project and have enforced these standards, the team has done incredibly well with even just partial AI adoption in their work - because the guard rails are there and agents don't get tired of hitting them.

Top #2 — altano:

If you're sensitive to bundle sizes (which you almost certainly aren't), heads up: the Solid 2 bundles are much bigger.

My counter component bundle test is:

↳ reply 2 — tommica:

Oh that is quite the leap

Top #3 — miguel-muniz:

Congrats to Ryan and the team. I never got deep enough into front-end to understand the nuance of these things but I still occasionally tuned into his Friday streams just to listen. You can tell he cares about this subject deeply and I enjoy listening to passionate people talk about their craft.

↳ reply — Tade0:

As a frontend developer it's a solid (heh) paradigm shift.

Turns out the secret to fine-grained reactivity all this time was just a tree structure describing the dependencies.

I'm using signals in Angular and while they don't cover every use case cleanly, they're a huge upgrade compared to RxJS Observables - particularly due to how simple and debuggable they are in comparison.

Edit: It's about the same ratio on AA. That's nuts.

The per-token price difference is exactly 2x (on all fronts incl. caching, though I'm assuming the caching mechanisms differ). I guess Sol uses way fewer tokens then. (About 4x according to AA. Math checks out.)

↳ reply 1 — rbehrends:

> Does anyone use both Claude and Codex and can compare what that's like in practice?

Be aware that this can vary greatly by benchmark to the poin where it is not possible to make a general comparison. Generally, however, Opus is considerably more expensive than Sol even for the benchmarks where it does best. That said, this comes with slightly better performance on benchmarks.

For subscriptions, it matters that Anthropic offers much higher discounts than OpenAI, partly or totally offsetting it. In my case, with $20 subscriptions for both (which is the worst-case scenario for OpenAI, they give bigger discounts on their $100/$200 plans), and on some tasks that I tried on both, 5h usage percentage is mostly a wash on average, with considerable variations either way. Again, I need to emphasize that this is for my tasks and cannot be generalized.

For example, on one task Sol decided to do extensive fuzzing to check its implementation while Opus didn't, so that drove up the usage for Sol a bit.

item.title: Not Everything Needs an LLM
item.description: 164 points, 71 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (newsletter.posthog.com)

→ HN comments  ·  164 points  ·  71 comments

Top #1 — socketcluster:

It is true that they don't tend to give simple answers.

But it reveals something about human biases that we tend to seek out simple answers to complex questions. We tend to think that because a question is short, that it's simple. We forgot how many details are involved and how much is actually going on underneath. Reality itself is often annoyingly complex.

All living creatures, including humans, are conditioned to simplify extremely complex things into simple concepts which we can react to. We only understand things to the extent that we believe they affect us.

↳ reply 1 — kzrdude:

In a lot of sciences we actually give simple answers, while keeping the door open for "it's complicated, go this way to find out more". And you can repeat that with four or five layers, always adding details to make it 'more correct'.

Our whole academic system is structured that way :)

↳ reply 2 — proc0:

Simple answers are the result of a problem being solved all the way through. It abstracts away all the details and exposes the essential part of the solution. This is the compression perspective of intelligence. We want things as compressed as possible because it's how intelligence more or less works.

↳ reply 3 — wolvesechoes:

But the things their answers are not detailed and nuanced, but trivial and verbose. They lay down the most banal stuff like it some enlightening wisdom.

Top #2 — throwawayffffas:

Using these decision models as a model router sounds really bad to me the models will most likely be newer than the decision model and thus the decision model will have no information about the capabilities of the model other than the short blurb you feed it.

In their defence, the incoming tickets weren't supposed to contain PII in the first place. That means whoever wrote the ticket included too much personal info.

Maybe a local/on-prem Jev is ideal?

↳↳ reply — The-Bus:

"We are also seeing a lot of noise in the computer industry that the solution to reducing complexity is a simplistic approach, that is, running all software on the server, and giving users nothing but dumb terminals. It generally is not the customer's desire to throw away the billions of dollars they have invested in their current computing environment, turn all their currently productive PCs into dumb terminals and run all of their software on expensive new servers. Customers soundly rejected this model of computing when the Unix vendors tried to convince them to buy network computers."

"Putting everything on a server (and asking the world to rewrite all of its software along the way) may seem attractive if you build servers, but it ignores the real concerns and needs of many customers."

These were quotes from Paul Maritz (a VP at Microsoft) made about 27 years ago to the WSJ[1] in a back-and-forth discussion with a Sun executive (Pat Sueltz). Some of the comments were quite prescient, others aren't.

1 = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB942104638509774099

↳↳↳ reply — linguae:

"It generally is not the customer's desire to throw away the billions of dollars they have invested in their current computing environment...."

This is true. However:

1. We now have tens of millions, maybe even hundreds of millions, of users who have little experience with traditional desktop computing. They grew up on Web services that they access primarily using smartphones, Chromebooks, or web browsers on desktop computers. There are many people with little-to-no experience with desktop applications like Microsoft Office and the Adobe Creative Suite, but they do their work on Web applications such as Office 365 and Google's suite.

2. Even for traditional desktop computer users, they often spend considerable amounts of money updating their environments once every few years. Windows has excellent backwards compatibility, but most people aren't interested in running Office 97 and Photoshop 5.5 on Windows 11 even if those programs can run on Windows 11. I like Office 97, but I need to deal with modern Office documents, plus I want the improved multi-language support and extra features that have been added in newer versions of Office. The Mac is much more aggressive about cutting off support for old programs; my PowerPC Mac OS X software can't run on my Apple Silicon Macs, and even support for Intel Mac programs will be dropped soon.

Because so many computer users these days didn't start off with traditional desktops, and also because of upgrade churn, this is how we ended up with the current situation, where many people rely on centralized solutions.

↳ reply 2 — AceJohnny2:

Efficiency and resilience are often in competition.

Price is vaguely related to efficiency, so that's what the private sector optimizes for. Think about that next time people complain about Government efficiency.

As one NASA chief said: "if we could blow up rockets as much as SpaceX did, yeah we'd be much faster and cheaper"

Top #3 — mkhalil:

https://www.apple.com/support/systemstatus/

Interesting that HomeKit makes the general status page and not the developer one. Makes me wonder how they define each entry, and what makes up a system in one vs. the other.

↳ reply — trickypr:

My guess is that it is something along the lines of "Would a normal user be affected by it".

A normal user might expect to access their home devices from outside the house (which is what I presume "HomeKit" covers). But only a "publisher" (for want of a better term) would need to access App Store Connect, or News Publisher or similar.
